i would like to inform you that a new political group has been set up in the european parliament, entitled 'identity, tradition and sovereignty'. this group is composed of 20 members, representing more than one fifth of the member states, and therefore fulfils the conditions laid down in the regulation. the composition of this group shall be published in the minutes of this meeting.
mr schulz, mr gollnisch, rule 29 and the footnote clarifying the scope of its provisions state that parliament does not assess the political affinities of the members of a group, and only when any of the members concerned deny sharing the political affinities declared by the group, does parliament have to verify whether the group is formed in accordance with the rules of procedure. i do not think that is the case; the group has made a statement of principles, a political statement which has been communicated to me, which will be published in the official journal and signed by all the members of this group. i understand that at the present time that is sufficient proof of political affinity between its members and i cannot therefore continue with your approach, mr schulz.
ladies and gentlemen, after welcoming our bulgarian and romanian colleagues, allow me a few minutes to assess the work we have done during the first half of this parliamentary term. i think there is a broad consensus on the growing importance and the greater prominence of the european parliament. the european parliament is better known and better recognised for its work. we have overcome the challenge of enlargement and solved important internal problems. we owe it to the work of all of you, the secretary-general, the parliament's administration. i want to thank you all. i would also like to recall the doubts we had, 30 months ago, about our ability to work with more members, with nine more languages then - now there are 12 more languages - and with even more diverse parliamentary cultures. i think we can now see that we have overcome these difficulties and that the enlarged parliament is functioning. there has been no division between old and new europe. meps from the new member states have been perfectly integrated into the various transnational political groups, working at european level and from a european perspective. we have played an important role in cushioning east-west tensions, and this has enabled us to reach important agreements, such as the paradigmatic case of the services directive. the members of the 10 new member states have now taken up the highest political posts in our parliament and there are a large number of rapporteurs among them. i hope that this inclusive participation will continue in the future. you will also remember that at the beginning of the legislature i told you that the statute for members would be a priority. i said that in the face of some scepticism from more experienced members, but today we have a statute which will guarantee, when it is applied, equal treatment between members and transparency of their expenditure. it was a difficult issue which seriously tarnished the image of the european parliament and i think we were all very pleased to have resolved it. in order to be able to function with more members, we have had to carry out important internal reforms. more planning, more selectivity, more political orientation of the debates, more speed in taking a stand on international events and on the decisions and proposals of the commission, more efficiency in our delegations in third countries, more dynamic work in our parliamentary committees. each of them has done their part to find and implement original and effective solutions. i thank everyone, and especially the chairmen of the political groups, the vice-chairmen and the managers who have accompanied me to the table, the committee chairmen, and also - let me say this now - very particularly the secretary-general, mr priestley, who will soon be leaving us. (applause) believe me -- and i say this with the knowledge that the position i have held has given me -- he, julian, and his collaborators are the real architects of that everyday miracle that is the functioning of this complex institution. to make it work, we also had to develop a major real estate policy, which has not ceased to provoke controversy. we have made major investments in works in brussels and luxembourg which my successor will have the pleasure of inaugurating shortly. we have acquired buildings at all three headquarters and in the 27 countries where we have information offices. we are a major real estate powerhouse throughout europe, and i can tell you that this policy will enable us to save 100 million euros a year, compared to what a rent policy would be, and that will enable us to apply the statute for members without having to ask for additional resources from the european taxpayer. i would like to thank the vice-president, mr onesta, and the staff of the general secretariat for their work in this area. madam president, i congratulate you on having a seat at this table. the socialist group considers extremely serious the sentence confirming the death sentences of the bulgarian nurses and the palestinian doctor, who are unjustly accused of infecting hundreds of children with the aids virus. this condemnation, which is totally unacceptable to all european democrats, is intended to condemn not only the accused but also medicine and humanitarian aid in libya. we therefore express our utmost opposition to the death penalty under any circumstances and reiterate the european union's commitment to the fight for its abolition or a global moratorium on its application. the death sentence is particularly unfair in this case; first, because the process did not meet the rules of independence and impartiality of the court, a rather widespread issue in the case of libya, and second, because the sentence goes against the tangible evidence presented by neutral experts, which proves that the accused are innocent. in addition, as i said, medicine and public health are being condemned because the real causes of the aids virus in children are being kept hidden. we appeal to the tragedy of these convicts, who after eight years in libyan prisons are suffering in inhuman conditions and reporting ill-treatment; and we also recall the tragedy of the sick children and the families of the deceased children, to whom my group expresses its full solidarity, as well as support for the european commission's programmes in libya to combat aids. we call for the immediate release of the nurses and the doctor, who are innocent, and we demand that the libyan authorities concentrate on the infected children. we therefore promote amongst all of us a human rights policy which is truly coherent, credible and firm.

the president of the council. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i am speaking to you today about one of the most fundamental aspects of the european union's human rights policy. the timeliness of this subject is also reflected in several motions for resolutions tabled by the various groups in the european parliament. on the basis of the guidelines for a union policy towards third countries on the death penalty adopted by the council of ministers of the european union in 1998, the european union is committed to the abolition of the death penalty in all circumstances throughout the world. the establishment of moratoriums has also been an integral part of the fight against the death penalty for many years, but not as the main objective, but as an intermediate step towards its final abolition. the european union will continue its policy of protecting human rights under the german presidency of the council, and in this spirit will continue to advocate both a moratorium and the final abolition of the death penalty. this means, on the one hand, that the debate on principles will continue to be conducted decisively in bilateral contacts as well as in multilateral fora, in particular in the united nations. this also means continuing to actively approach and intervene in countries at a turning point, i.e. where there is a positive or negative development with regard to the death penalty, and this means very concretely taking action in many urgent individual cases. i know that the european parliament has always supported this policy and i am glad to say that we have already achieved a great deal together. the fact that the death penalty has been abolished in law or in practice in some two thirds of the countries of the world is also the result of the consistent efforts of all those who are actively fighting against it. this - i would like to emphasise this - includes active involvement in the council of europe. the 13th additional protocol to the european convention on human rights, which also abolishes the death penalty in wartime within the european council's competence, has now been ratified by 33 states. but i would also like to mention that there are still too many countries, 66 in number, which continue to use the death penalty, and unfortunately also some declining trends in the observance of moratoriums. it is therefore important that we do not relent in our efforts and campaign specifically - especially in international forums - for the abolition of the death penalty. in this spirit, the european union has submitted a resolution to the commission on human rights, which was dissolved in 2005, every year since 1999. over the years, a stable majority in favour of this resolution has been secured. after the dissolution of this body, we must look for new ways to advance the debate on the abolition of the death penalty. but there are no easy answers. we must be very careful about what we do, because the first thing to do is to avoid going backwards. there is a clear consensus on this line in the european union so far. the european union has therefore so far refrained from introducing a resolution to the un general assembly because of the continued high risk of failure. instead, on 19 december last year, at the initiative of the european union, a unilateral declaration against the death penalty was presented for the first time at the united nations general assembly, which was supported by 85 states of all geographical groups. this is an encouraging result, but it also confirms that the chances of success of an eu resolution in the un general assembly cannot yet be considered as assured. what's the next step? it is clear to all our partners in the european union that we want to continue to actively promote our cause, the fight against the death penalty, also at the level of the united nations. at the same time, however, i would like to make it clear that the environment remains very difficult and that, therefore, success in the fight against the death penalty can only be achieved through well-considered and gradual action by the european union. the aim should continue to be to avoid the failure of any new eu initiative as far as possible, because a failure of the european union would be a success for the proponents of the death penalty and thus a step backwards in the fight against this inhuman punishment. we cannot and must not allow this to happen! i think we're getting support, too. some key ngos, such as amnesty international, also warn against hasty action and say it could be counterproductive for the european union to push for a new debate on the subject in the un general assembly. the general council of 22 january therefore agreed to develop a well-thought-out approach which would gradually enable us to give greater emphasis to our concerns in the united nations. the ambassadors in new york and geneva were accordingly instructed to examine immediately all possibilities for furthering the discussion at the level of the united nations. it is also important to obtain up-to-date assessments from relevant non-governmental organisations on the next steps to be taken in the fight against the death penalty at the un level. on this basis, the eu presidency will then make proposals to the eu partners in february for further action. i think this is an important first step and i hope that we will also find support for this approach! (applause from the centre)
member of the commission. mr president, i also welcome this opportunity to exchange views on the issue of the death penalty and on the means to promote the universal abolition of this odious practice. as you know, the abolition of the death penalty worldwide represents a key objective of the external human rights policy of the european union, and i am personally committed to seeing the eu continue to play a lead role, as we have just heard, in this global effort. since all of us here agree on the ultimate goal of our action in this field, namely universal abolition, i wish to provide some thoughts on this process of abolition and on the means to reach our common goal. firstly, let us not forget that the experience of abolition on the european continent has been a slow, often tortuous and protracted process, which has been, for most of our member states, driven by a combination of strong political leadership and a mature level of development of human rights protection, the rule of law and democratic institutions. with some notable exceptions, including the united states of america and japan, the global map of abolitionist countries also closely follows that of democratic pluralism. visionary leadership and political courage are key to abolishing the death penalty. these efforts often need to be bolstered by a dynamic and open nationwide debate to ensure that the ultimate political decision to abolish the death penalty in a country is also a permanent one. in the philippines, and to some extent kyrgyzstan, the recent abolition of the death penalty was precisely the result both of remarkable courage on the part of the political leadership and a profound nationwide debate, which witnessed wide participation from civil society actors – which has been mentioned – and institutions. in the united states of america, there are also some encouraging trends in some states, like new jersey and maryland. on the other hand, it is not excluded that a country falls back into the practice of death penalty as we, unfortunately, have witnessed in bahrain and need to fear in peru. and in many other countries our appeals to abolish the death penalty have fallen on deaf ears until now. the execution of saddam hussein and his henchmen has now sparked a renewed debate on the death penalty. the horrific videos of his undignified end upset even some supporters of the death penalty. but let us not forget that every year thousands are executed, most of whom are certainly somewhat better people than saddam and many are even innocent. their deaths should outrage us even more! while evidently the abolition of the death penalty in any country is, to quote robert badinter, ‘a victory of humanity over itself’, one must remain realistic as to the influence of external actors, such as the european union, in this process, because this process remains first and foremost a domestic one. this is not to say that the european union will sit on the fence. on the contrary, the eu has been and will remain at the very forefront of international efforts, notably at the united nations, as was mentioned, to fight the death penalty. last december, the eu presented a declaration on the death penalty at the un general assembly, which received the support of a record 85 states. in line with our guidelines on the death penalty, the european union has carried out numerous demarches on individual death penalty cases, including in countries such as the united states of america, iran and indonesia, and will continue to do so in the future. the eu is also the leading source of funding for abolitionist projects run by civil society, and over the past ten years, we have spent over eur 15 million supporting such projects around the world. the european parliament and civil society actors have traditionally played a crucial role in both supporting the abolitionist efforts of the european union and in stimulating the debate on the means to enhance our policy. it is of prime importance to listen carefully to those voices when discussing possible initiatives in various international forums, as the council is currently doing. this has certainly been illustrated most recently by the italian proposal for a universal moratorium on the death penalty at the un general assembly. without prejudging the final outcome of this process of reflection, i wish to share three observations made by abolitionist actors on the moratorium which have struck me as relevant for feeding today’s discussion. while representing a key element in the eu’s strategy towards universal abolition, leading ngos have stressed that a moratorium is not a panacea. they claim it is by essence fragile, reversible and must be followed by abolition in law. they refer to the example of kyrgyzstan, where the regularly extended moratorium on executions has not prevented the number of prisoners on death row from increasing. i think we need moratoria that hold firm. secondly, some ngos underline the fact that the moratorium is one abolitionist tool among others. i agree that, in this context, the promotion of the second optional protocol providing for abolition, the support for legal counselling for death row convicts and other efforts have to be included in our toolbox. hence, we should avoid the current discussion on the moratorium to eclipse the fact that abolition is a multi-faceted process. lastly, when bringing the issue back to the un general assembly, we need to be cautious as to the possible outcome. it is paramount to secure a positive result. we need to be alive, however, to the risk of an ambiguous or even a counterproductive outcome – and the council presidency has alluded to it – given international divisions on this subject. failing in such an effort could have negative consequences which will be difficult to repair. therefore, we need to assess the situation and possible scenarios thoroughly before moving. in conclusion, i wish to underline the importance of maintaining a common eu approach towards the universal abolition of the death penalty. the commission will spare no efforts to work with the presidency and parliament to this end.

madam president, yesterday, 24-year-old robert wilson was sentenced to death by a new york jury. this is the first death sentence handed down in that state in the last 50 years. and this is also a sad example of the insecurity that today weighs on the universal values that we all stand for here today, despite very significant progress that has been made in countries like liberia, mexico, the philippines and moldova. but we must continue to fight so that others, such as china, with about two thousand official executions a year - eight thousand, according to unofficial figures - join the global moratorium and suspend their executions. we must support civil society in iran, which is mobilizing against capital punishment. iran has one of the highest execution rates: 177 in 2006; it has also broken the moratorium on stoning and, to this day, maintains six women condemned to death by stoning. we call in particular on the united states, a country whose decisions have a very great influence on world politics, to support the italian initiative establishing a universal moratorium on the death penalty, which will be adopted - i hope with the support of this parliament - at the united nations general assembly. the moratorium, as has been said here today, is an unavoidable first step towards abolition. this is probably one of the most important challenges facing human beings at the beginning of this century.

this system would begin by december and that was the case. the trial has been initiated between the us administration, customer border protection system, and amadeus. there is a technical aspect to the request for ad hoc data but this is a technical problem while the testing of the push system has been started, as we were promised. as regards the number of data, i have listened with interest to what many of you have said about the 34 data currently covered by the pnr agreement. i can say quite clearly that, as far as my role in the negotiations is concerned, i intend to ask for a reduction in the number of data in question, but i do not do so because i share the view that the americans are asking us for too much data. if all 34 of these pieces of data were useful in pursuing terrorists, i wouldn't be afraid to tell you that we need 34. instead, the really useful data are probably those 19 that have been indicated, that is, a much smaller number. however, believe me, it is not the principle of numbers that makes the difference in the data to be processed, but the principle of the usefulness of the data, and it is in this sense that i intend to conduct my negotiating action. i'm not going to go along with the idea that if we go from 34 data to 15, we've done a good job. we may have done a bad job if some of the data that we've excluded has some of the data that could prevent a terrorist attack. i have no doubt about that . i am absolutely convinced that the main objective is to make the system work. who has access to the data? on what grounds? how much data and for how long? these are the points of an agreement which we shall be negotiating shortly, informing parliament as we have said. ladies and gentlemen, many of you feel that passenger information is the missing criterion in the pnr system. it is conceivable that, in the absence of a consensus between the two parties, no agreement will be reached by the end of july. on a purely imaginative level, i envision a very simple solution: the commission has also proposed that the united states should provide a paper to be signed by the passenger when he purchases a ticket to the united states, informing him that his data will be processed in a certain way. if that were to happen - and i sincerely hope it never happens - we would have guaranteed passenger information, but without an agreement at european level, passenger rights would be limited to the private sphere of the air transport contract. this is an eventuality which we must prevent by all means, which is why we must strive to achieve a new european agreement. the alternative would be very simple: i think that the commission has a duty to ensure that the european parliament is given the opportunity to express its views on the matter. but we would lose a european role which they have already played and which we are urged to play again. that is why we need to renegotiate, even if we reduce the number of data, provided that the reduction of data does not affect the fight against terrorism. i have informed the libe committee that, as regards the ats system, i have received written assurances from the united states of america that the pnr agreement is being respected. in a speech in this house i was reproached for not having checked the veracity of this statement. if i had the power to investigate the behaviour of the united states of america from brussels on american soil, i would have powers that no european or national authority has ever had or ever will have. everything is possible except to ascertain, as i am asked to do in the above speech, the veracity of that letter. when i am formally told that the rule is respected, i am obliged, until proven otherwise, to believe that to be the truth. that is what you do between allies, unless you have evidence to the contrary - which i frankly do not have, and i must say this with absolute sincerity - because otherwise we open a permanent investigation into every single reference in the letters we receive from the united states of america. mr roure asked me if we could pass on to parliament the information on the negotiating mandate. you know this is classified information: however, i repeat, even if it is classified, we will find a way of informing parliament, that is, a way of providing political information without violating a rule laid down in the treaties, according to which classified information ('eu restricted') cannot be published. this is the political solution i propose: if the treaty is amended to provide for a mechanism for communicating classified documents to parliament, i will apply those rules without fear. the aim is to overcome the obstacle of not being able to inform parliament in the presence of classified documents: i intend to keep you informed. many people have called for a framework agreement, mr president, and i believe that this is the right way forward. the framework agreement on data transmission is exactly what we have started to work on with the presidency, creating a joint working group to deal with certain issues relating to the processing of personal data, thus leaving aside the swift and pnr cases, which have parallel routes. we believe that the time has come to conclude a euro-atlantic political agreement with the united states - a framework agreement - on the processing of personal data, and we intend to work on this agreement to identify the types of data to be transmitted, for what reasons and for how long. however, ladies and gentlemen, there is also one point which has not been dealt with in this debate and which needs to be dealt with: how can we preserve the confidentiality of the technical information which is part of this agreement and the disclosure of which, as a means of investigation, would be of great benefit to the criminals? it is necessary that such information be kept confidential. so there is another problem, because it is clear that if we reveal the actual control mechanisms of suspected terrorists, we would be giving them a powerful tool. can a solution be found? i am absolutely convinced of that, but we need a common political will. i would like to conclude with one final thought: this does not justify the individual breaches of european law and the legislative shortcomings in the swift case. you will remember that when no one was talking about a european agreement, i spoke to the libe committee about the need for such an agreement because it is much better to fill a legislative vacuum with a european rule than to leave it to each member state to regulate itself as it pleases. the swift case is emblematic: i have received a reply from only seven of the 27 member states. this is a symptom that the issue must be addressed at european level. i therefore feel that a political agreement is essential and that without parliament such an agreement would have less legitimacy. the european parliament has already expressed its views on the commission's proposal for a regulation on the protection of the environment. but the problem, ladies and gentlemen, is the terrorists, not the united states.

the reason why we have put our oral question on the renegotiation of the public procurement agreement, which will be concluded in march next year, is that we are at a crucial juncture. in addition, in view of the importance of this agreement and its duration, which will again be 10 or 12 years, it was necessary to raise it here in this parliament with the commission. the public procurement markets are becoming increasingly important in the world, because of their volume, which can reach up to 25% of world gdp, and also because for the european union they represent a comparative advantage, since in this sector, at the moment, we can be competitive, as i say, against other competencies that we are suffering from other countries in other sectors, such as agriculture and industry. if we are to adapt to globalisation, it is therefore important to develop the sectors in which the european union can be internationally competitive and thus create fair and favourable conditions for european businesses. these markets are, in most countries, reserved for domestic firms, which constitutes one of the main non-tariff barriers to international trade. there are two aspects of this renegotiation which i would particularly like to stress. firstly, the geographical extension of this agreement, with the entry of important players such as china or the developing countries, and secondly, the need to ensure that there are fair, balanced and reciprocal conditions for companies from different countries. as regards the first point, the greater the geographical coverage of the public procurement agreement, the greater its validity. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the conclusion of the agreement on the free movement of goods between the european community and the republic of korea. let us not forget that china has committed itself to opening up its public procurement market - which remains largely closed or with unacceptable requirements for european companies - and to launch accession negotiations to the public procurement agreement in 2008, after its accession to the world trade organisation. secondly, as regards fair and reciprocal conditions, we must remember that the public markets of the european union are already very open to international competition. this has considerable advantages for contracting public entities, as this openness means that they have more choice and therefore a greater chance of finding goods and services of higher quality at lower cost. but on the other hand, let us not forget that european companies may be thus disadvantaged in cases where their foreign competitors are preferred. the union's trade policy is to open up international markets in all their aspects. the solution is not to close public markets to foreign companies. that is why we have a legitimate right to ask that our companies enjoy similar conditions of access to public markets to those of our main trading partners, those whose companies already enjoy access to our public markets. however, this is not the case at present, with the commitments made by our trading partners being very limited compared to those of the european union. commissioner mandelson also referred to this imbalance in his communication on a competitive europe in a globalised economy. it suggests the possibility of introducing specific restrictions on access to certain parts of the union's public markets, in order to allow our trading partners to offer reciprocal opening of their markets. all that said, i think it is timely - and more than appropriate - that this oral question be put to the european commission on behalf of the committee on international trade, so that we can know what its strategy is in this renegotiation of the agreement, which i stress is at a crucial juncture, because of the need to reach an agreement in the coming weeks. how will the commission defend the interests of european companies in the markets of sectors where we are highly competitive, such as transport, energy or public works, in the context of the objective of continuing on the path of greater commercial openness, and not the other way around? and in this same context, how will the situation of european smes, which are already at a disadvantage compared with large companies, be considered in relation to the situation of other smes in other countries whose governments reserve a part of their public contracts for them, as is the case in the united states? given the lack of reciprocity, the disadvantageous situation for european smes and the importance they have in the main objectives of the so-called lisbon strategy, we ask the commission to demand that the other parties to the negotiation give up their own exceptions or, if this is not possible, that they accept that we apply a similar exception for the benefit of european smes. in any case, let us achieve that reciprocity which is currently working against european companies. i therefore ask the commission to inform us of the state of these negotiations, particularly on the issues i have highlighted and to which the text of our question refers; and also to take note of the concerns expressed by the european parliament and to take them into account in its negotiations in geneva.

order to fight climate change. the 30% cut in developed countries’ emissions by 2020 is a necessary step towards the longer-term objective of reducing them by as much as 50% below 1990 levels by 2050. it is necessary to see that this is a step in that direction. this reduction is essential if we are to meet the 2°c objective, which we know, in turn, should prevent massive and irreversible disruption of the global climate system. it is the developed countries that should continue to shoulder most of this global effort to reduce emissions over the next decade or so, as they are already doing under the kyoto protocol, so as both to be credible and motivate those poorer countries in the world that will have to follow suit. we asked the group of developed countries to reduce by 30%. let us ask ourselves whether this is ambitious. compared to 1990, us emissions are currently up by 15%, those of the eu-25 are down by 5% and those of russia are down by 30%. it will not be easy, and you cannot see it individually, but it represents a huge challenge. let me also mention the costs, because many of you have referred to the costs for industry. the commission has made impact assessments that show that taking action to limit climate change is fully compatible with sustaining global growth. investment in a low-carbon economy will require around half a percent of global gdp over the period from 2013 to 2030 and would reduce global gdp growth by 0.19% per year, which is a fraction of the expected annual gdp growth rate of 2.8%. this is without associated health benefits, greater energy security and reduced damage from avoided climate change being taken into account. this is a small insurance premium to pay for significantly reducing the risk of irreversible damage to our economy and to our planet, and especially if you compare it with the stern review’s estimate that uncontrolled climate change will cost between 5 and 20% of gdp in the longer term. so we must consider the cost of inaction! climate change is already costing us – just ask insurance companies all over the world. finally, the spring council is about the lisbon strategy. you are absolutely right that, if we want to communicate, we have to mention that it is about jobs and growth. lisbon is also about the courage of reform. i fully agree with mr watson that there is ample evidence that reforms work. however, we also have evidence that societies dominated by fears and insecurity are not easy to reform: they are afraid of change. that is also what we see in europe and that is why we have to build confidence and remember that the lisbon strategy – the jobs and growth strategy – is also about fighting social exclusion and poverty; fighting poverty in europe as well, improving quality of work, investing in education, building civic competence and investing in people. that is the only way to overcome the fears. listening to all these interesting speeches, i am reminded of the intimate link between the growth and jobs strategy and sustainable development, because we have heard all the arguments for why we as europeans would like to see economic growth, coupled with social security and maintenance of a high level of environmental protection, while continuing to be ambitious. i think that sustainable development is an objective which is gaining ground more and more as the vision for europe and for the world.

member of the commission. madam president, i am very grateful to the european parliament and in particular to the rapporteur, mrs batzeli, and the committee on agriculture and rural development, the committee on international trade and the committee on regional development for their work in preparing an own-initiative report on the commission’s communication ‘towards a sustainable european wine sector’. i knew before i started the reform process that it would be difficult and complex. these last few months have certainly confirmed this impression. my debates in the committee on agriculture and with a number of members in the intergroup on wine here and in their constituencies have shown me that we are dealing with difficult and sensitive issues. i therefore welcome the report. it is an ambitious report that covers the whole range of aspects addressed in the communication. i believe that i am not saying too much by noting that mrs batzeli has grasped the many conflicting concerns that we need to reconcile in the course of the reform. it has been a valiant effort and we will now study the report carefully. i shall make a few initial observations tonight based on our first reading of the report. firstly, i should like to express a little regret. the report initially states that the commission, by advocating the need for the reform within the european union, is not paying sufficient homage to the image of european wines. let me, therefore, be completely clear. the european union’s wine sector is second to none: it delivers the best quality wine in the world, it is extremely diverse and it is an important part of our cultural heritage. however, some parts of the sector are struggling. millions of hectolitres go into crisis distillation every year. that is hardly a sign of a sector that is in good shape, which is what i want it to be. i want the sector to be able to compete so that europe will continue to be the world’s leading producer of wine. that is why the current regime simply has to be changed. it is no longer sustainable. i think we can agree that it has resulted in a structural imbalance. stocks are high and, as a result, prices for many wines are low and income for wine-growers has been reduced. these developments, combined with falling consumption, changing lifestyles and increasing imports from third countries, have forced changes upon us. i think this is widely accepted. the direction we all want to take is described in recital k of your report. it suggests that the principal aims of the reform should be to strengthen the dynamism and competitiveness of the sector without losing its market share in international markets, but, equally, to take account of the interests of producers and consumers, while respecting the objectives of maintaining tradition, quality and authenticity. it goes without saying that you are critical of certain elements of the communication, including matters such as the consumption forecast and the alerts, and the contradiction between the policies of grubbing-up and competitiveness. the commission agrees that one of the main challenges is to revive demand, but profitability is even more vital and the pattern of structural surplus leading to lower prices and negative incomes needs to be stopped first. profitability is not a question of concentrating production in a few hands and then standardising the wine. there are small producers who make wine of a wonderful quality and who are also very profitable and i see no reason why this should not still be the case in future. however, grubbing-up allows those wine producers who are never going to be able to be competitive and who are not able to respond to consumer demand to leave with dignity and compensation. surely no one here wants to force those producers who have no profitable, predictable future in the sector just to remain because they cannot afford to leave. i fully understand that grubbing-up is a sensitive question. i therefore particularly appreciate the constructiveness that the european parliament has already shown on this issue. i welcome your recognition that the decision to grub up must lie with the grower and, having said this, i have also studied your different suggestions very attentively. you also state very clearly that the decision to grub up cannot, and should not, be taken in a vacuum. i completely agree. you have put forward suggestions on how to ensure that grubbing-up complies with a certain number of social and environmental aspects and i can assure you that these will serve as a useful inspiration when we consider how better to frame grubbing-up within our legislative proposal. i have also noted that you propose to operate a reform in two stages. we will have plenty of time to discuss the timing and how to calibrate the various instruments at the different stages, but i agree on the concept that we need initially to address the structural imbalances that weigh heavily on our sector today. one issue that you come back to in the report, and which was also a key factor in our earlier debates, is your strong preference for maintaining the wine budget within the first pillar. first of all, i believe that this is at odds with the community position that rural development measures can make a substantial contribution to the required improvements in the wine-growing regions. let us not forget that we can ring-fence funds for wine regions in the rural development budget. but i also believe that your position on this issue rests on a false perception that i want to shift considerable funds away from the first pillar, and this is not the case. i have said on several occasions, and will repeat tonight that in the future the majority of funding to the sector will continue to come through the first pillar, but this should not prevent us from drawing on the obvious benefits of also having recourse to the second pillar. i know that in this parliament there is a strong push for more community efforts on promotion. it is indeed important that we improve information about the advantages of moderate and responsible wine consumption and that we promote opportunities in third countries more aggressively. i think that you will agree with me that we need a more progressive and a more modern approach. this is something to which i will certainly give due attention in the legal proposal. finally, i would like to say that i have worked with this parliament for two and a half years. you have clearly demonstrated your ability to be progressive and creative, even on sensitive matters such as the sugar reform, in the pursuit of balanced reform solutions that properly prepare the european union’s agriculture to face up to its present and future challenges. but when i look at many of your positions, notably on enrichment, distillation, and private storage, i must admit that i find you to be a little more timid than usual in your zeal for reform. i do not expect us to agree on these issues now, but these are areas where i believe we will need to be innovative and creative. much difficult work therefore lies ahead of us, but i look forward to your continued and very valuable input. i welcome this opportunity for a debate here tonight. my apologies to the chair for being more lengthy than usual, but this is a very important issue which is the focus of huge attention in all the regions of europe and that is why i took the liberty of speaking for a little longer than usual.
the committee on regional development has in its opinion wanted to stress certain issues which we consider important from the point of view of territorial cohesion, when implementing a reform which will have important consequences for certain european regions. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to apply the principle of subsidiarity to the wine sector, in particular by introducing a system of regional aid for the production of wine. we therefore want to draw attention to the commission's proposed grubbing-up scheme, which would seriously damage the economic and social situation of certain regions where the wine sector is the main source of employment and prosperity. we believe that the commission should propose measures to modernise wine production techniques and marketing methods. finally, it must be a reform which is applied in a progressive manner and includes transitional periods and a permanent assessment of the effects of the reform on the economic and social situation of the regions of the european union.

wine is not made, wine is made and raised. it's a subtle difference, but it's an important one, because it says a lot about who's talking to you and it says a lot about the person's point of view and their sensitivity to the sector. the european wine sector is certainly in trouble and the fundamental problem it is facing at the moment is the difficulty created by the increase in domestic demand, because consumption internationally is still increasing. however, this problem must be solved, and it must be solved in the light of its many implications, because the sector in europe is increasingly importing. so it's not a problem of what we produce, but of the price at which we sell it. and why do we sell at different prices? vice-president of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, after the tragic terrorist attacks in the world, security has become an essential right of citizens, because we can all live in a world of freedom and rights. and it is undeniable that security is one of the fundamental rights of citizens, which makes the exercise of freedoms possible, but we must never forget, as we have said many times in this house, that legality is the precondition for guaranteeing the right to security of citizens. in other words, ladies and gentlemen, security is not and can never be at any price. these being our values, we should not be afraid or ashamed to deal with such a matter in this house, a matter which we have tried to clarify and explain thanks to the work of parliament and the contribution of many of us. we must never forget, first of all, that the search for truth in the rule of law is based on the identification of precise facts, which are called upon to be investigated by free and independent courts. and in the face of reports, complaints and facts, it was and is the duty of national investigations to ascertain the truth and, where it appears that the law has been violated, to ensure that those responsible are punished. it is undeniable that there were those responsible, but it is not for the european institutions, this parliament or the commission, to pass judgments but to ask for the truth to be established. it is clear that the truth that will emerge from the conduct of the trials in accordance with the rule of law may have consequences, both at the institutional and political level. i welcome the fact that parliament's inquiry has provided, as the rapporteur, mr fava, has just said, factual information which is useful for the continuation of the inquiry. it is therefore the task of the magistrates to investigate and it is the task of the governments - both of those who have done so and of those who have not yet done so - to conduct administrative investigations and punish unfaithful officials, because an official who commits violations with the cover of secrecy betrays his institutions, betrays the state, and is therefore an unfaithful official. it is the duty of governments, however, once the facts are finally settled, to reveal the truth, even if it is an uncomfortable and unpleasant truth. the european commission's task has been to contribute to parliament's work by providing concrete elements which have proved useful to parliament's inquiry. but the commission's task will also be, once the truth is known, if it is known, to draw conclusions from the judgments and then to make proposals. i believe that it is also and above all the responsibility of parliaments and politics to look to the future and to suggest solutions so that these events will never happen again. i am sure that all those who have engaged in this investigation have done so primarily to serve the purpose of security in legality and law-abiding, and to serve security as a right: security is not an optional right after 9/11, it's a fundamental right. i trust in the will of all those who have worked on this aspect to continue to do so. that is why we need to reflect on the role of services. the president-in-office of the council has rightly said that there can be no european law on secret services, but that political reflection is required on the role of these services, which i am deeply convinced are essential institutions for combating terrorism, but which must operate under the responsibility and clear mandate of governments. national rules are therefore needed: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i am sure that the council will be able to accept them, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. so we do not want to know the secret information, but we want to know the overall record of the activities of an institution which must be confirmed and cannot be discredited, as if it were an association of criminals. however, i believe that political control by the parliaments is essential. there are other aspects which could be considered at european level: i'm talking about the use of airspace. the use of airspace is one of the points highlighted in the fava report. how are state aircraft, or those used for state services, classified? how do we tell them from civilian airplanes? this is a point on which the european commission can make a contribution, because our responsibility for air traffic can help to define safer criteria, which make it possible to ascertain whether a legitimate use is possible and prevent the misuse of the purpose of covering an aircraft for state services, when it is not a matter of state services. this is a concrete contribution we can make. let me now make a purely political point. i think it would be a political mistake to give the impression - and this is not the intention of the rapporteur - that the united states of america is on the defendants' stand. that would be a political mistake, and i would not agree with that - i say this sincerely - because we should rather emphasize first of all that the defendants are the terrorists, that is, those who have broken the law and who are ready to strike once again at our democratic institutions. i say this because we all know that this dark affair, certainly full of violations, was born precisely thanks to the great american democracy, thanks to the free press in the united states which has allowed the disclosure of facts that have been investigated by the european parliament and other institutions, including the judiciary. you are well aware that the united states congress is still dealing with the matter and that it is our intention, during the german presidency, to work with the presidency to relaunch euro-atlantic cooperation based on two pillars: the european union is a democratic country. i believe that we will continue to seek the truth and to cooperate, as is our duty, with the united states of america, as sincere allies, who tell the truth even when the truth is inconvenient, and who demand punishment for those responsible in case of violations. let me conclude by saying that if this parliament is divided today on such a sensitive issue, its message will be weakened. if, on the other hand, it is united in its words of firmness on the one hand and of a revival of cooperation on 'rights and security' on the other, it will prove to be a stronger parliament.

the rapporteur. - madam president, international terrorism is the most dangerous threat to peace, security, integrity and human dignity. as an invisible, geographically diffuse enemy, located both within and outside our borders, the way we are fighting it is different from how the european union has faced enemies in the past. the european union's counter-terrorism strategy must be global, multilateral and based on the united nations system. any unilateral and exclusively military response is doomed to failure. the fight against terrorism will be won in the field of values. it is therefore essential for the moral defeat of terrorism to raise awareness and mobilize our public opinion. you must never let your guard down. we must not react only after a major attack, but permanently and proactively. a strengthened cfsp is a necessary condition for success. this means improving, equipping and coordinating european intelligence and information services and deepening the detection of terrorist financing channels. the union's external action must concentrate on stopping the support of terrorist groups by sanctions and coercive measures in those states which do so, and on helping weak states to strengthen their institutions and strengthen democracy so as to prevent terrorist groups from taking root there. madam president, preserving the rule of law and human rights in the fight against terrorism is not only the moral barrier, it is the raison d'être of our strategy, because it is precisely what the terrorists want to destroy: the values on which our coexistence is based. if we give in on that ground, as has happened with the war in iraq, guantanamo, abu ghraib or the illegal flights of the cia, we will be giving excuses to the terrorists, who will try to justify themselves, and we will be providing fuel for terrorism. the limitation of fundamental rights does not produce more security, but more fear. we need free, self-reliant societies. fearful societies lose the fight against terrorism in advance. the safety/freedom dilemma is false. we will be safer if we are freer, more open and more inclusive. prevention, which is so important and which failed on 11 september in new york and 11 march in madrid, is essential, as is greater efficiency in police and judicial action. our cfsp must help to remove the breeding ground from which international terrorism is fed. terrorism is always unjustifiable. we should never talk about causes, but there are circumstances that feed it, the first of which is the humiliation and contempt felt by millions of muslims, in the face of what they understand as the arrogance and arrogance of the west, and the aggravation of endemic conflicts such as the israel-palestine conflict. it is also contempt for a religion that is peacefully believed by over 1.3 billion people in the world. we are facing fundamentalist, dogmatic fanatics, but not a religion or belief. we sometimes forget that more muslim victims have fallen at the hands of islamist terrorism than western victims. this explains the international success of initiatives such as the alliance of civilizations, adopted by the united nations, in the face of the clash of civilizations that advocate fundamentalists of one sign and the other. in addition to better means, international terrorism must be defeated with intelligence and tenacity, not with incendiary speeches that only demonstrate underlying weakness. fascism, first, and stalinism, decades later, were defeated on the ideological terrain, without renouncing the principles that inspire our societies, among them freedom of expression exercised responsibly. in this report i place particular emphasis on the recognition of victims as the main actors whose voice is heard by the public authorities. that is why we are joined today in the gallery by four direct victims of the march 11 attack in madrid: jesús ramírez castanedo, jesús abril escusa, isabel casanova ortega and euclides antonio río grajales. to them, thank you very much for coming.
the president of the council. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr luis yañez-barnuevo garcia, and the committee on foreign affairs of the european parliament for the report on the external dimension of the fight against terrorism which is being presented today. the report is very comprehensive and deals with some very important issues on which we share broadly the same views. the terrorist threat is more international than ever. the measures taken by the european union to deal with this threat can only be truly successful if they are part of a coordinated global effort to combat terrorism. the european council of december 2005 adopted the european union counter-terrorism strategy, which sets out the general framework for european union action in the field of counter-terrorism. at the same meeting, the european council adopted the european union strategy to combat radicalisation and recruitment for terrorism. both documents deal in detail with the external dimension of the fight against terrorism. as regards the external aspects, i would like to highlight three important points: radicalisation and recruitment, cooperation with external partners and the international legal framework. first, the overarching objective of the counter-terrorism strategy is to prevent people from turning to terrorism, and to do this we need to address the factors that contribute to radicalisation and recruitment for terrorism. the union has continued to seek to ensure that issues related to radicalisation and recruitment are taken into account in its external action to combat terrorism. it has exchanged experience and practices with external partners in dealing with the problem of radicalisation. the european union has for the first time also included the fight against radicalisation in a specific technical assistance programme to combat terrorism. meetings devoted to interreligious and intercultural dialogue have been held within the framework of the asia-europe meetings, the barcelona process and the anna lindh foundation. the union has also undertaken a thorough reflection at the working level on how to improve its public diplomacy and contacts with islam, both within and outside the union. we are determined to continue this. radicalisation and recruitment will continue to be addressed in future programmes of technical assistance in the field of counter-terrorism and will remain an important topic of dialogue with third countries. secondly, cooperation with external partners: in pursuing its objectives in the field of counter-terrorism, the european union has continued to work closely with partners outside the european union. political dialogue with partners is an essential component of the european union's external action in the fight against terrorism. respect for the rule of law and the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms in the fight against terrorism were key themes of this dialogue. i am also reminded of the debate we had this morning, where there was a great deal of agreement. a considerable amount of work has been done with a number of countries to strengthen cooperation in the fight against terrorism. the european union and its member states have agreed to provide technical assistance in the fight against terrorism to a number of countries which should be given priority. progress has been made in the political consultations with other priority countries. the european union has also contributed to capacity building at regional level. i would just like to remind you of the jakarta centre for law enforcement cooperation (jclec) in indonesia and the african union counter-terrorism centre in algiers. cooperation with the united states in the fight against terrorism remains a high priority. the european union and the united states have worked together at both political and expert level to deepen their dialogue. the union has also expanded its counter-terrorism dialogue with other partner countries such as israel, australia, canada and russia, and within the framework of the euro-mediterranean partnership. areas of common interest and options for cooperation in particular the provision of technical assistance to other countries have been considered. the third is the international legal framework. the european union has continued to advocate that the united nations play a key role in the fight against terrorism. the adoption of a comprehensive convention on international terrorism, with a clear and unambiguous definition of terrorism in all its forms and manifestations, would indeed be an important signal that the international community is united in confronting the terrorist threat. the european union will therefore continue to make every effort to achieve international consensus on the comprehensive convention. the recent adoption of a united nations strategy to combat terrorism is also an important step forward in the intensification of international cooperation with third countries in the fight against terrorism. the european union is ready to implement the strategy together with all member states of the united nations. this is one of the european union's priorities for the future. the european union will use its dialogue with external partners to promote the full implementation of this strategy and to exchange views on how best to achieve this objective. i believe that you would make a very valuable contribution to this by raising this issue with your counterparts in third countries. the institutions of the european union - as i said at the beginning - have reached a broad consensus on the priorities for combating international terrorism. your report, mr rapporteur, and a long-term exchange of views such as the one we have today, will help to deepen our common understanding and help us to develop appropriate measures to combat international terrorism. it would also be a sign to those who have been victims of terrorist attacks.
member of the commission. mr president, firstly i would like to commend the rapporteur, mr yañez-barnuevo garcía, for his report. let there be no doubt: terrorism is a threat to all states and to all peoples. it is criminal and it is unjustifiable under any circumstances. the commission therefore fully shares the view of the report that terrorism constitutes an important threat to security, to peace, stability and the democratic values on which the european union is founded. the commission also shares the objective of combating terrorism globally while respecting human rights. all anti-terrorist measures must be consistent with both international humanitarian law and international human rights law. while largely agreeing with the report, i would like to comment on two points. firstly, the report is calling for the adoption of a definition of terrorism. since the un has not yet agreed on a definition and since such an agreement still seems distant, although we are working towards that, i would like to recall that relevant universal conventions and protocols already provide a common legal understanding of what constitutes an act of terrorism. the union also has a definition of terrorist acts in its framework decision on terrorism. these are solid legal foundations. secondly, the report calls for the extension of the jurisdiction of the international criminal court to include acts of terrorism as crimes against humanity. i think we should be cautious, before altering the definition of crimes against humanity included in the icc statute. such an endeavour might be counter-productive in the efforts to broaden support for the court. the complex relationship between international humanitarian law and the definition of terrorism may lead to further complications. the commission welcomes the interest of the parliament on the external aspects of the fight against terrorism. in the current environment of open borders, efforts to fight against terrorism, internally and externally, are aspects that are closely linked. it goes without saying that vice-president frattini and i are working closely together in order to make these efforts mutually reinforcing. we strongly agree on the need to support the united nations consistently with our policy of effective multilateralism. equally, the emphasis put on prevention is very important for the commission. conditions conducive to the spread of terrorism need to be tackled. tackling the root causes of terrorism lies at the heart of our external policies, and the report’s recommendations for a more coherent and effective eu policy also largely go in the right direction. let me highlight the important contribution that the commission makes to the fight against terrorism. firstly, with member states, the commission is implementing the 2005 eu counter-terrorism strategy, of which our colleague and president has talked. terrorism also features regularly during meetings with our partners and in international organisations. for example, as i speak, a major meeting is under way with commission participation in berlin in order to prepare the heiligendamm summit of the g8 in the areas of terrorism and organised crime. secondly, the commission is an important provider of capacity-building assistance to some 80 third countries aimed at improving governance and administrative capacities in related areas. a number of priority fields mentioned in the report, such as border management and terrorist financing, are priorities for community assistance. thirdly, the commission is working in new areas which should improve eu action in the fight against terrorism, such as the protection of critical infrastructure, the fight against violent radicalisation and terrorist recruitment, bioterrorism, radiological threats, explosive detection technologies, terrorist use of the internet, as well as terrorism in the context of crisis management, and there are obvious links to our efforts in fighting organised crime and drug trafficking. afghanistan is, for instance, a serious case in point. finally, and in reply to one of the requests of this report, the commission wishes to confirm that it intends to produce a communication in the course of 2007 focusing on global and trans-regional security challenges. the focus will include key aspects relevant to human security and focus on counter-terrorism. you may be aware of my personal commitment to support the human security discourse. what better way could there be to address conditions conducive to the spread of terrorism than to promote both freedom from fear and freedom from want. despite what is being done, i think we can all agree that we must work together and enhance our collective performance in fighting against terrorism. we will try to play our part, but we are certain that the collective effort with parliament will be a more important one.
opinion of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs. the fight against terrorism is a priority requiring the solidarity of all member states and the commitment of democratic countries. security is a genuine and essential right which can never be exercised at any cost, but only in strict subordination to the law and respect for human rights. international terrorism is a threat to freedom and human rights. the sinister distinction between lethal terrorists and political terrorists, armed arms and political arms, only contributes to strengthening the criminal whole to the detriment of law and order. dialogue with terror in any form or formula is an unequal, useless and offensive dialogue for the victims. member states should pay particular attention to the promotion of intercultural relations and to strengthening interfaith dialogue among members of civil society with a view to improving coexistence, tolerance and mutual understanding. the union should streamline, coordinate and facilitate the action of the instruments at its disposal, europol, eurojust, ecpol and the situation centre, and others with the same purpose to detect and prevent interconnections between terrorism and other forms of crime. i ask, madam president, that the very difficult experience of the victims be respected and taken into account, especially as i say in my report, when drawing up prevention strategies. victims need to be recognized and protected. terrorists start to lose when victims tell the truth and society listens. and as regards prevention, madam president, prevention cannot and must not be a weapon of war between democratic countries and states. the last time prevention failed was on december 30, 2006 in madrid. we do not criticize failures in prevention, we strive to ensure that failures in prevention never happen again. and i conclude, madam president. we will only be able to confront terrorism with determination if we all - and together - democratic countries, and the union in particular, have a clear perception of the threat, and the threat is lethal, permanent and persistent over time.

strategy - efforts which have not always been easy to accept or understand - are bearing fruit and contributing to strengthening the european social model in the context of globalisation. many of the difficulties which public opinion has recently encountered in the european project stem precisely from the fear of citizens, of certain sectors of our society, that globalisation will impose a labour markets are holding back job creation are also wrong. the facts show that since the euro was introduced on 1 january 1999, eight years ago, the european union has created four times as many jobs as in the previous eight years. and in the years since the lisbon strategy was launched until now, the european union has clearly created more jobs than the united states. some people call both in the euro area and in the european union as a whole, have long been the ones with the highest rates of economic growth. the fact is that fiscal consolidation is progressing, progressing, improving in parallel with the increase in our growth and job creation figures. there has been much talk lately of the strength of the euro against the dollar or the yen as an obstacle to our exports, but the fact is that the trade balance of the euro area against the united states has improved again in 2006 and the rise in oil prices has been partly offset by the revaluation of the euro against the dollar. in short, ladies and gentlemen, the improvement in our economies and the acceleration in job creation are clear proof that the european economic and social model, with its high degree of social protection and environmental requirements, is perfectly compatible with the globalisation of the economy and economic growth. europe, european countries and our economies have always done better when they have opened up to the world and, now that the world economy is experiencing an unprecedented expansion phase, europe and european citizens have much to gain from this bet on the opening up of our borders and the growing integration of our economies into a global sphere. reaching out to citizens is not just a way of vindicating the economic and social policies we have advocated in recent years: it is a key issue to reinforce confidence in europe's ability to provide well-being to european citizens and offers us a solid basis to reinforce the necessary political will to deepen the path of structural reforms defined by the lisbon strategy. the second fundamental coincidence between the reports we are debating today and our own opinion in the european commission is precisely the need to consolidate the reforms initiated by the implementation by the member states of the national reform plans. in this sense, the dynamism of emerging economies, the ageing of the population, the low growth potential in many european economies, the budgetary imbalances still existing in some member states, the low growth of productivity and the segmentation of the labour market are, among others, very powerful reasons to continue to pursue policies leading to a greater capacity for innovation, to greater opportunities for lifelong learning, to an improved community waters. first of all, i welcome the fact that the report stresses that the fight against illegal fishing must start in our own waters and that it must also concern our vessels. community waters are regulated, but that does not mean that illegal practices are not carried out in them. the report also recognizes another very important aspect, namely how to prevent the entry into the community of fishery products from third countries that have been caught illegally. as the world's largest market and importer of fishery products, the community has a specific responsibility to ensure that products that end up on the tables of european consumers do not come from illegal activities. this implies that a new approach should be established to adequately control the legality of fishery products imported into the territory of the community. another aspect to be highlighted is the need, as noted in the report, to create more synergies to improve the monitoring, control and surveillance of fishing activities. illegal operators often use clandestine and international channels to disguise their activities. the success of the investigation of these activities depends on the cooperation of the various services involved in maritime surveillance at international level and also at community level. i cannot list all the points in the report here, but i would like to highlight, for example, the call for greater consistency in the sanctions imposed by member states for serious offences in relation to fisheries laws, or the need to solve the main problems caused by public fishing flags, which demonstrate that parliament and the commission are on the same wavelength as regards priorities for future action. the commission has not been idle over the years. the european community has made considerable progress since the adoption in 2002 of its action plan against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. progress is mainly seen in our work at international level, through which the community has promoted measures against illegal fishing in all bodies responsible for fisheries and the law of the sea. however, the most significant progress against illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing has been made in relation to regional fisheries management organisations, most of which, thanks to the community's efforts, have already adopted a comprehensive set of measures against illegal fishing. the community has also improved its policy of assistance to developing coastal states, which are the main victims of the type of fishing we are discussing today. the strengthening of the capacity of these countries to exercise adequate control over fishing activities in their waters has been financed from the eu budget through a fisheries partnership agreement, both at national and regional level, modelled on the recently agreed regional fisheries surveillance plan for the south-west indian ocean. at community level, the 2002 reform of the common fisheries policy also gave a boost to the policy against illegal fishing by adopting provisions on monitoring compliance with community rules and the creation of the fisheries control agency. however, despite significant progress against illegal fishing, it is far from eradicated and remains one of the most serious global threats to the sustainable management of fisheries resources and marine biodiversity. the commission therefore considers that, almost five years after the adoption of the 2002 action plan, the time has come to devise a new strategy against this type of fishing. in this context, the commission has decided that illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing will be one of the main priorities in the area of the common fisheries policy and the maritime policy this year. the commission will draw up proposals in this respect and will submit them to the member states and to this parliament during the second half of this year. the report we are discussing today is a particularly timely contribution to the work on which the commission will base its proposals. i am not saying that we should not be concerned about the problem of illegal, unreported and unregulated fishing. the report by mrs aubert and the committee on fisheries is an extremely important and encouraging step in this direction.
