i would like to refer to the community plan to eradicate illegal fishing, which is mainly carried out at international level in the waters of developing countries, which are too poor and lack the means to control fishing activities in their jurisdiction. failure to prevent such illegal fishing results in losses and hardship for their coastal populations which depend on fish for their livelihoods and food security. at the same time, these illegal practices cause direct losses also to legitimate fishermen. and in this connection i would like to stress once again that one of the virtues of the fisheries association agreements concluded between the european union and other countries is precisely that the community deep-sea fleets have accepted the code of conduct for responsible fishing promoted by the united nations, and that their presence in those waters also means that other illegal vessels do not act with such impunity. i therefore voted in favour of the plan to eradicate illegal fishing, arguing that all fisheries agreements with third countries should be renewed, since the benefits are important and mutual, because it seriously undermines the biological balance of the seas and that this represents a high environmental risk which we cannot afford.
on behalf of the green group, although there have been five rounds of dialogue between the government of the people's republic of china and the representatives of the dalai lama since 2002, it is clear that there are fundamental differences which make it difficult to reach a final agreement that will clarify the situation in tibet in a way that is satisfactory for all parties, but at the same time fair and dignified, especially for the tibetan people. however, i am of the opinion that the responsibility of each of the two parties for not having reached an agreement is not comparable. the dalai lama, as the temporary representative of the tibetan people, has on more than one occasion expressed his desire for dialogue and agreement, and has even given up calling for complete independence in favour of genuine autonomy which guarantees respect for tibet's ethnic, linguistic, cultural and religious identity. in this respect, i believe it is the chinese government which should show a better will and at least accept the resumption of dialogue with the will to reach a good final agreement. i therefore urge the european commission, the council and the member states to use all the existing spaces to support a new round of sino-tibetan dialogue, and i believe it is particularly important, as has been said, to use the negotiations on a framework agreement on partnership and cooperation between the european union and china, which began on 17 january, to demonstrate the community's commitment to dialogue and a just and lasting solution in relation to tibet.
mr president, in the bay of cádiz, in the municipality of puerto real, in spain, the multinational delphi is threatening to close down the plant and put 1,600 workers on the street, and 4,500 indirectly. it is one of many multinationals that have received public subsidies, over 60 million euros, to be able to carry out all production. moreover, the company had committed itself to maintaining these jobs until 2010. we are faced with the scandalous case of yet another relocation affecting the european union. i would ask the commission, and parliament itself, to try to legislate clearly to prevent a new kind of piracy. these are companies that benefit from public subsidies and then immediately afterwards they close the company, relocate it and leave thousands of workers on the street. the bay of cadiz region cannot withstand this crisis. i therefore call directly on the european commission to help us, together with the institutions, in this case the junta de andalucía, the municipalities concerned and the trade unions, to prevent this employers' strike.
mr. chairman, ladies and gentlemen, at last in this year's wimbledon tennis tournament the female winner will receive the same amount of money as her male counterpart. it is a victory for women, to which we have contributed in this parliament. consciously and deliberately paying women less is just one of the reasons why women in the european union earn 15% less than men. there are other reasons behind the scenes: more women working part-time, on temporary contracts, in the lowest paid sectors, more difficulty in accessing positions of responsibility, etc. equal pay has been part of european law since its inception, but prohibiting discrimination has not eliminated the pay gap. to achieve this, courageous responses are needed, such as the one given by the socialist government in my country, spain, by passing a law on equality. i am also pleased that the socialist party has launched a campaign to denounce this situation on 8 march. i ask you to join her in putting an end to wage discrimination against women once and for all. in the european year of equality, this can be our challenge.
opinion of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection. madam president, i am speaking at this sitting as the opinion of the committee on the internal market, which adopted the opinion by a large majority. some of its contents have been incorporated, either in the spirit or in a more explicit way, into the report which mr hasse ferreira has presented to us here this afternoon. i would like to highlight some of the concepts contained in the report of the committee on the internal market and consumer protection or the characteristics of what are called social services of general interest. all these services are undoubtedly part of what is broadly and perhaps difficultly defined as the european social model, a model which they have helped to shape. another aspect that nobody disputes is that the principle of subsidiarity must be applied to these services in full and that it is therefore up to the member states to define not only the field in which they are applied but also the model and the system. there is also one issue which i consider to be fully accepted and that is that we are in a dynamic environment in which both the demands of society and, therefore, the incorporation of new social services are constantly evolving and changing. as rapporteur for the committee on the internal market and consumer protection, i would like to draw attention to the need to make the provision of these social services compatible with legal certainty and free competition. because we must not forget that each state has different models for implementing services. in public services, social services must be provided by public administrations, but they do not necessarily have to provide them directly. i believe that this parliament and the commission must be aware of the need to ensure, while respecting the specific nature of these social services of general interest - especially because of the job creation that this entails - the legal certainty of those service providers who wish to do so throughout the european union.

member of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, allow me to thank the european parliament, in particular the committee on women's rights and gender equality and the rapporteur, mrs sartori, as well as the other committees of the parliament, for their opinion on the report on the roadmap for equality between women and men. this plurality and diversity of views reflects the intention of the plan, which concerns all the policies of the european union, both internal and external. this plurality also reflects the fact that gender equality concerns all of us and is far from being a women's issue. parliament's report is an expression of our shared commitment to work towards greater equality between women and men, thanks to the instruments that the treaty gives us. with the plan, we reaffirm the need to develop a strategic and multiannual approach to equality issues. we also reaffirm the need for an approach that includes specific measures and promotion of gender equality in all areas. the commission notes and welcomes convergence of views on many issues between the institutions, as your report shows. let me point out some of them. gender equality is primarily a question of women's rights and status in society. equality is first and foremost a requirement and an unconditional right. legislation is a prerequisite if we are to establish the foundations and conditions of genuine equality. in this developed environment, the community has a legal framework in this area that ranks among the most advanced in the world. however, it is still necessary for these laws to translate into practice in terms of reducing inequalities and actually improving the status of women. the existence of laws and rights does not automatically mean the full exercise of those rights for our citizens. our efforts to ensure the realisation of these rights in everyday life must be stepped up. the plan and the report of parliament show that the commission and the european parliament will continue to be allies in this respect, and i welcome that. this legal framework must also reflect and respond to current challenges and needs and adapt where necessary. the commission therefore committed itself in the plan to review the part of the legislation that was not subject to recasting with a view to modernising it if necessary. we took the first important step with regard to the maternity and parental leave directive and in october last year we launched the first phase of formal consultations with the social partners. we are also currently assessing the application of directive 86613 on selfemployed women and women who contribute to the pursuit of this activity, as well as directive 797 on equal treatment for men and women in matters of social security, in order to decide whether any amendments need to be proposed. but there is an economic issue besides the rights issue, because it is very important for women to be economically independent throughout their lives. the lisbon strategy for growth and jobs sets out a framework and objectives for improving the position of women in the labour market. although we have recently seen a very significant increase in women's participation in the labour market, women still face differences and disadvantages simply because they are women. for example, in the area of pay, despite the existence of legislation, women continue to be paid less for the same work, on average by 15%. the commission has already started to address the issue of equal pay for equal work and intends to continue in this direction. we'll be working on the pay gap statement for the next few months. the aim is to begin to address the causes of this disparity, despite years of legislation, and to propose changes and directions for action in this area. however, economic independence will only be achieved by developing genuine policies on reconciling work, private and family life, not only for women but also for men. we know that one of the main obstacles to women planning to enter or continue their careers in a relaxed way is related to the difficulty of reconciling family and work life, especially when we know that women continue to carry out a large part of family and domestic responsibilities. the commission has therefore consulted the social partners to see whether there is a need to modernise the legislation in this respect. the proposals of the social partners will be important for possible further developments. we believe that this is an area where substantial progress can be made. in addition, we have quantified targets for childcare services, the barcelona targets. e year 2010 is approaching and therefore efforts need to be stepped up, including through the possibilities offered by the structural funds to support member states to develop childcare structures. it then falls within the framework of activities eligible for funding from the european social fund. as regards decision-making, it is clear that women are still missing from boards or high-level positions of responsibility, whether at the political or economic level. i'm a strong believer in the importance of role models and i'm convinced of the importance of informal networks in a working career. one of the priorities will be to create networks for women in economic and political decision-making and to collect and disseminate data on women's participation through our database. the report also addresses a very important aspect, gender budgeting. we need to be able to know the resources allocated to our priorities and to ensure that the necessary financial resources are allocated to support those priorities. gender budgeting is an excellent tool because it could allow us to use this data. in the light of methodological progress, there is therefore a need to improve the availability and collection of such data and the exchange of best practices. we are aware of this and therefore recommend a pragmatic approach in this area. we are launching a study to assess the feasibility of including a gender perspective in the budget process. let me assure you of the commission's commitment to support the implementation of the policy objectives in the area of gender equality by making appropriate funding available. many programmes or grants already cover measures in the area of gender equality. i am of course referring to the european social fund, which aims to support measures in favour of equality between men and women, but also to other smaller programmes aimed at supporting the development of public policies on equality, such as the new integrated programme progress, and i am confident that the european institute for gender equality will play a major role in raising awareness of these issues in the coming years, in particular by collecting and providing data on the situation and status of women. at this level, the aim is to ensure that all these funds are complementary in support of a single objective. i share your view that the increasing diversity of our society, for example in terms of ethnicity, is posing new challenges. we need to study better the issue of the various forms of discrimination to which migrant women are exposed. the european year of equal opportunities will provide us with a platform to exchange views on this topic, as one of the issues it addresses is multiple discrimination. combating violence against women and trafficking in women is also a priority for the union. we have developed a set of measures, mainly under the daphne programme, which is concerned with combating all forms of violence against women in europe, such as sexual exploitation, female genital mutilation or trafficking in women. promoting equality in development and external policies is also very important, as the european union is the world's leading donor. the values that guide our actions within the union must be the values we defend towards third countries. we need to make better use of our funding, for example, to strengthen the capacity and reach of organisations fighting for women's rights around the world. as you know, this issue is at the heart of the communication on gender equality and development policy, which the commission adopted on 8 march to mark international women's day. the gender equality plan shall provide for control mechanisms in the form of an annual work programme, a mid-term review and a final review. i attach great importance to these mechanisms, since they are important tools for the good news. through such tools, european citizens can monitor the implementation of our commitments on gender equality.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, both the report by the rapporteur of the committee responsible for the subject, the committee on legal affairs, mrs lévai, and the opinion of the committee on culture, mr mavrommatis, and the various speeches we have heard so far, show that the european parliamentarians are taking a fairly uniform line with regard to the commission's recommendation. firstly, there is a formal objection: the use of a recommendation, of an instrument called 'soft law' in the european union, is always very dangerous, given that the european union has its own legislative instruments, such as the framework directive proposed by mrs lévai. and secondly, there is a fundamental objection. because at this point in time the commission's recommendation may already be having undesirable effects on the structure of the intellectual property market, which is subject to certain oligopolies, i.e. the so-called 'big ones', the main organisations controlling broadcasting. the commission's recommendation may lead these 'adults' to withdraw their repertoires from the existing system of collective management organisations which allow for a guarantee of rights, and if that were to happen, the result would be that 'adults', i.e. small organisations for the protection of intellectual property, would not be able to protect intellectual rights. and in the matter of culture, in the matter of music, the most important thing is not the market, the most important thing is the production of music. the culture of each of the peoples making up the peoples of europe. it is not a question of creating a large market, because in that large market the so-called gresham's law is applied, under which bad currency displaces good. in other words, we are about to reach a situation in which a completely unified market, with a few 'larger' or very important organisations, ends up monopolizing the market, imposing its conditions on authors and ultimately preventing intellectual creation from taking place in the european union. we therefore support mrs lévai's report and mr mavrommatis's opinion and do not think it appropriate at this stage to adopt any amendments to those reports.

the following is the report by wolf klinz, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 92/49/eec and directives 2002/83/ec, 2004/39/ec, 2005/68/ec and 2006/48/ec as regards the procedural rules and the criteria for prudential assessment of acquisitions and increases in shareholdings in the financial sector (com ((2006) 0507 - c6-0298/2006 - 2006/0166 (cod)) (a6-0027/2007).
mr president, crossborder issues and the acquisition of shares in banks, insurance and investment companies are less common than in other sectors. one barrier is the uncertainty in the prudential assessment processes before national supervisors due to the absence of criteria on the suitability of the acquirer and the detailed regulation of the procedures. the proposal for a directive addresses these problems and harmonises their treatment. the amendments adopted by the committee on economic and monetary affairs clarify the requirements, facilitate supervisory action, protect confidentiality and improve control. the overall result is positive and i congratulate the rapporteur, mr klinz. a sensitive issue is that in cases of large dilution of ownership with low participation, a lot of influence can be achieved. we have therefore defended the obligation to notify any significant participation and we welcome the possibility for member states to set a transparency threshold below 10% in order to receive information and to determine its existence.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 12 noon.
the next item is the debate on the oral question to the commission on community action on the provision of crossborder health services, by karl-heinz florenz, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety (o-0001/2007 - b6-0013/2007).
member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank members for a very interesting debate, which will be very useful and will provide guidance for us in the next steps of drafting a proposal, along with the outcome of contributions from the other stakeholders, from consultations and from the member states. just to cover a few issues: first of all, we will certainly be taking into account the health objectives and social values adopted by the health ministers last june, and this will be one of the considerations in our proposal. at the same time, we will also be looking at the important issue of patients’ rights, which is part of our consultation on community action. it is clear that we will look at these issues; what tools will be used will, of course, be decided after proper analysis of the consultation and based on the responses provided. i would like to confirm that what we plan to do is to take a step forward and not to reduce or undermine patients’ rights as recognised by the court, but to improve them and make them work, make them more concrete, and to make it possible to apply them equally among all european citizens. information is an important factor in this respect. as we have already stated, we will take subsidiarity into account. however, i have to remind you first of all that we do not propose harmonisation of national health assistance – this is not the intention. but, at the same time, i have to remind you of the european court of justice judgment on the watts case, which provided that there are situations where member states, based on other treaty provisions, will have to apply to amend and adjust their national healthcare systems. finally, i think there is a misunderstanding here. first of all, there are no proposals in the communication because it is precisely a consultation document. we did not want to pre-empt the positions of parliament, the member states and the stakeholders, so it is intentional that there is no proposal at this stage. it is just a description of the problems. freedom of movement and patient mobility is not something which is being introduced by the european commission – i think we discussed that in the past as well – it is something which has been recognised, whether we like it or not – and i hope we like it! – by the european court of justice, which has established that the internal market rules apply also to health, even if this is publicly funded. so this is not a question of a commission initiative introducing a new concept but how we in the commission, together with parliament and the member states, can make this concept, this reality, work for the benefit of patients without being to the detriment of the national healthcare systems, their viability and their operation. this is a big challenge for us but i think it is a big opportunity as well, and we can make it work for the benefit of citizens.

the next item is the joint debate on - the oral question to the commission on one action, one vote, by pervenche berès, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs (o-0004/2007 - b6-0014/2007), and - the oral question to the commission on proportionality between ownership and control in eu listed companies, by giuseppe gargani, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs (o-0014/2007 - b6-0016/2007).
member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank members for their questions. my colleague, mr mccreevy, regrets that he cannot be here this evening, but i can assure you that he will be informed of the results and content of the debate this evening. it is true that a study was launched in september, and its intention is to cover the various aspects of proportionality between capital and control, how this is applied or not applied in the member states, how it affects the deviation from the principle and how it affects institutional investors. the study was also designed to analyse the relevant regulatory national frameworks. the contractors were chosen in the usual simple way. there was a public invitation to tender and the choice was simple. the best author was chosen and the specific contractors made and presented the best offer. however, i have to clarify two things: there will not be an impact study, so research will be carried out in a factual way on the current situation in the member states, and no proposals or recommendations will be brought forward. both the contractors and the subcontractors have a strong record of original, independent, high-quality research in areas of company law and corporate governance, and their european presence constitutes a significant advantage in terms of providing comparative analysis covering different legal traditions. the subcontractors are of high standing and specialise in corporate law and securities regulation, and the study team provided the best offer based on scientific competence, professional reputation and integrity. as already mentioned, the study will cover multiple voting rights, non-voting preferential shares, company pyramids and other instruments which fulfil the same function of protecting controlling shareholders, and the study will include golden shares and the attribution of special rights for public authorities, as already mentioned. in this respect, the commission has noted at this stage the advocate-general’s opinion on the volkswagen law. the advocate-general considers this to be as an unjustifiable restriction that infringes eu law. the commission awaits the court’s judgment. as far as the directive on takeover bids is concerned, we know it aims at eliminating certain defences applied by companies in takeover situations. one such defence for companies is to leverage voting rights vis-à-vis capital, but experience shows that, faced with potential takeovers, the vast majority of member states are reluctant to neutralise their companies’ disproportionate voting rights. nevertheless, it is still early days for the implementation of a directive. the commission does not intend to reopen a debate on the takeover directive at this stage. whatever the policy indications the commission draws from the proportionality study are, they will not apply to takeover bids. the commission believes that these two should be considered as two separate initiatives. to conclude, i would like to emphasise that a decision on any future steps on the issue under discussion on the proportionality issue will be taken in the light of the outcome of the study. whether we present a proposal, and what the content of this proposal will be, will depend on the outcome of the study and of the impact assessment that is currently being carried out in parallel. we are therefore still at the study and first procedural phase. we will, as always, take very seriously the position and the views of the european parliament.

member of the commission. mr president, the commission is very well aware of the definite imbalance between male and female researchers. the latest available statistics show that, in all disciplines, over 50% of graduates, but only 15% of professors, are female. in science, engineering and technology, the figures are 34% for female graduates and 9% for female professors respectively. the commission agrees that this is a waste of talent and resources. since 1999, several documents by the commission have addressed the participation of women in european research. the commission is devoted to gathering reliable statistical data in order to view the complete situation and it publishes these results regularly in a brochure entitled ‘she figures’. this brochure was published in 2003 and 2006, and the next publication is expected in 2009. since the fifth framework programme, the commission has also provided financial support to studies and action in the field of women in science. in addition, under the sixth framework programme, a budget of eur 15.7 million has been devoted to women in science. several projects are ongoing: addressing the need to provide role models to encourage women to pursue a career in science, for instance. the 2005 competitiveness council conclusions led member states to set a goal of 25% of women in leading positions in the public sector. in this regard, an expert group on women in research decision-making has begun to look at the formal and informal barriers which make it difficult for women to reach top-level positions in research. under the new framework programme, a similar expert group will look at the issue of scientific excellence and potential gender bias in the evaluation of scientific excellence. in the seventh framework programme, the line of action with regard to gender issues is divided into three main areas of activity. firstly, in order to strengthen the role of women in scientific research, we will finance projects to compare positive action schemes for women in research decision-making positions, which will cover europe, the us, canada and australia. secondly, under gender dimension of research, the areas of action in the seventh framework programme will include gender issues as regards the definition and measurement of scientific excellence. for instance, an analysis of all research carried out in the eu on issues of discrimination and disadvantages for female researchers will be financed through this type of activity. thirdly and finally, as regards mainstreaming gender in community research policy and programmes, work programmes under the cooperation-specific programme encourage female participation. the commission also continues to have a target of 40% of females on evaluation panels and this is monitored regularly. in addition, we have planned to provide training and guidance to various researchers on how to mainstream gender in research. whatever we do in the seventh framework programme, it is and will be an important policy statement and will also be important for a number of research organisations who participate in the framework programme. we will have only a limited impact on the situation on the ground in europe. thus, we are also looking for new ideas on which the commission could take action or member states could take action with the support of the commission. therefore we intend to make this a question in its own right in the era green paper. the more the specific situation and needs of researchers in europe are recognised, with regard to mobility or portability of social security rights for example, the more scope there could be for addressing the specific role of women in research. the era green paper will soon be discussed by the commission and i would like to invite members to actively participate in the era debate which ensues. furthermore, i am relying on your strong support on this and other issues. in conclusion, i should like to emphasise that we have opted for a long-term approach based on constant efforts and continuous support in promoting the role of women in the world of science, using the measures and activities i have just explained.

the commission's vice-president mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in 2002 you approved regulation 1592/2002. this regulation establishes common rules on the airworthiness of aircraft and establishes the european aviation safety agency. you agreed that an optimal and uniform level of safety could only be achieved by extending the scope of this text, and thus the powers of the european aviation safety agency, which have been extended to flight operations, pilot licences and the safety of aircraft of third countries. and you have explicitly asked the commission to make a proposal to that effect. it's time to end an anomaly. while aircraft are now free to operate within a single market, the level of safety remains uneven across member states. you know as well as i do that the rules drawn up by the specialised intergovernmental organisations are implemented very differently within the community. the result is that there are wide national differences, and not always the most stringent standards are applied. you have asked for continued efforts to improve the general level of aviation safety in europe. that is the purpose of the proposal we are discussing, since it aims to extend the common rules to air operations, pilot licences and the safety of aircraft from third countries, in other words to provide the community with tools which should help to strengthen the safety of air transport in europe. the proposal also strengthens the obligations of member states in respect of inspection of aircraft and of third countries and member states. it gives the agency the power to carry out extensive inspections of all activities of the civil aviation authorities of the member states and their companies and airlines to verify that they comply with the common rules. penalty mechanisms, such as withdrawal of mutual recognition in case of non-compliance, are also provided for. the text is part of a coherent set of measures to improve aviation safety. i would like to remind you briefly of the following: the blacklist, which allows airlines that do not comply with safety rules to be banned from our countries, the strengthening of the mechanisms for inspecting aircraft safa directive and very soon the commission will propose to complete this regulatory framework by extending the powers of the european aviation safety agency to the safety of airport operations and air navigation, as set out in the communication attached to the regulatory proposal you are considering today. this will result in a coherent and uniform set of safety rules for the community by 2010 and a single body, the european aviation safety agency, responsible for preparing, implementing and enforcing them. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to congratulate you and thank you for your contribution to this strategy to strengthen european aviation safety. i shall be very interested to hear what you have to say on this subject, which is obviously of vital importance to the citizens of the european union.

deputising for the author. – mr president, we have asked for this debate to examine the background and the purpose of the green paper adopted by the commission on 6 december 2006. with the green paper, the commission intends to stimulate a debate over the use of trade defence instruments in europe: countervailing, anti-dumping and safeguard measures. i believe that this is a commendable initiative and i am convinced of the value of this debate. we need to talk much more about trade policy and about the choices made by the european commission and by the council and we need to ensure that decisions are properly discussed before this parliament. we need to give this parliament more power and to make trade policy more subject to democratic scrutiny. we are all living through a moment which many view as some sort of crisis period. we are living through a time when europeans are asking themselves: what does europe represent and why do we need such a complicated thing as the european union in the first place? and, when these legitimate concerns are raised, the importance of the role of a united eu in the globalised world and the importance of having a single voice to represent and defend the interests of 500 million citizens in any negotiation with other trade partners in the world market are vital factors to be considered. global trade and its impact on the lives of our citizens and on the future of our businesses, big, medium-sized and small, play an essential role in the anxieties felt by many over what we usually call ‘globalisation’. and, while many of us believe that some of the criticism is no more than cheap demagogy, we must understand those anxieties and we must oppose pure determinism in the way this new world develops, in the way trade takes place, in the way wealth and poverty are distributed.europeans who lose their jobs when a company suddenly decides to move eastwards in search of higher profits cannot simply be told that times have changed and that they cannot stand in the way of progress. they want to know what is going on and they must have their voice heard by those that ultimately decide. we should not forget that there is more than one recipe for economic growth and trade development. it is a matter of policy options whether the future of europe belongs only to huge retail corporations and to importers or whether we can preserve a model compatible with our most essential social and environmental concerns. our strong belief in free trade is perfectly compatible with the need to ask for a level playing field. even the most peaceful countries in the world – and europe among them – know that a full commitment to peace does not necessarily mean that armies are abolished and all means of defence are to be destroyed. so, we say yes to the huge benefits of free trade in our open world and we say yes to the fair implementation of the rules on which this global trade is based. we welcome the green paper, which has the merit of opening a debate on this subject. its text and the questions it raises already assume that something must be done to modify the current community trade defence system. this might be true. the recent footwear case has shown that the risk of deadlocks is real. they are clearly of no benefit to anybody. nobody here is blindly defending inefficient european production or supporting a protectionist approach to this highly sensitive matter. trade defence reform can be considered, if it is to be made more effective and more transparent. the green paper can be a good starting point if all the stakeholders’ views are properly taken into consideration and if the commission and the council do not entrench themselves behind preconceived ideological positions. the decision-making process can also be improved and we need to ensure that decisions are taken by member states based on the well-founded research carried out by independent community bodies, rather than on the basis of national interests, or, if you prefer, national selfishness. it is therefore important to improve and reinforce trade defence instruments instead of watering them down. on the other side, a fresh approach can be made to less traditional threats to a balanced and free world trade. practices such as so-called social or environmental dumping need also to be confronted and, when necessary, new means of tackling them should be seriously considered as a matter of community interest. the following are the questions i would like mr mandelson to respond to tonight. firstly, the doha negotiations have been restarted and i sincerely hope that they will result in a clear success. in this respect, would it not have been better to wait for the successful conclusion of multilateral negotiations before starting this exercise, which might weaken our position in geneva? secondly, can mr mandelson explain why his services are already applying quite a few questionable innovations mentioned in the green paper, even before the public consultation has come to an end and without any discussions either before the council, or before this parliament? thirdly, since the new trade defence system proposed by the commission assigns a role to all possible interested parties, including those not related to the production of goods falling under the scope of the investigation, do you not believe that the time has come to allow trade unions to lodge a complaint, as foreseen by the wto anti-dumping agreement? i conclude by formally asking mr mandelson to provide assurances that the european parliament will be kept informed at all stages of the process and that the views expressed by its members will be fully taken into account when discussing this highly sensitive matter.
mr president, i would like to congratulate mr voggenhuber on his report. saint teresa used to say that the devil is the detail. it is obvious that the european commission is not one day going to approve a piece of legislation that blatantly violates fundamental rights: nobody expects that. but, for example, we have situations, as in the case of restrictions on liquids in aeroplanes, where comitology has been used in a shameful way to impose, through a secret piece of regulation – and i emphasise, a secret piece of regulation – duties on citizens which cannot be reviewed by any court in europe, national or european. this is a case of the european commission not being a witness to a violation of fundamental rights but itself legislating in a way that goes against respect for fundamental rights and the most basic rules on transparency. these things happen, so let us stop the rhetoric and begin applying to ourselves what we pretend to apply to everybody else, to our neighbours and to our partners throughout the world.
the rapporteur. mr president, at the fourth european union-latin america and the caribbean summit held in vienna last spring, the green light was given to start negotiations for a strategic partnership agreement between europe and the andean community. in this report i propose some thirty recommendations for the council and the commission to take into account when they draw up the negotiating lines. we want a partnership that is ambitious, broad and far-reaching, in line with the twins, say, mercosur and central america, because we consider it a strategic need for both regions. latin america and europe are called by history, language, culture, beliefs and values, as well as by a common worldview, support for multilateralism and the united nations system, to become strategic allies in a globalized world. this is especially true for the andean countries where some of the continent's pockets of extreme poverty and the greatest inequalities are found. the agreement must have three pillars: one of a political and institutional nature, one of cooperation and one of trade. in the political and security field, we should achieve a euro-andean charter for peace and security, the establishment of a permanent political dialogue, the promotion of the quality of democracy, social cohesion, support for governance, poverty reduction, human exchanges, the fight against terrorism, conflict prevention and coordination for the reform of the united nations, together with civil and military crisis management operations. the second pillar is the promotion of sustainable human development and the progressive access of andean products to european markets, on competitive terms, taking into account the enormous economic asymmetries and the degree of integration between europeans and andeans, which will mean the review of the cap and subsidies by the union. the third pillar is trade itself, but unlike other models with third countries, for example the agreements of the andean countries with the united states, they must not be free trade agreements in the strict sense, or free trade agreements without more, but they must take account of the abyss that separates the two regions. without accompanying economic measures, cooperation and financial support, trade policies alone would not be able to fulfil their role as a contribution to development. the inclusion of labour rights, especially of indigenous and tribal peoples, the protection of decent working conditions, non-discrimination and equal employment between men and women and the eradication of child labour should be included in the agreement. it is also worth noting the importance of european investment as an essential element for the development of those countries and the need for european companies to apply the same standards as those applied in european countries with regard to working conditions. immigration, as a phenomenon and a source of opportunities, must be included in the agreement, with due regard for the rights of immigrants, and facilitating, reducing costs and making remittance transfers more transparent and secure. the environmental chapter, which should occupy a prominent place in the agreement, should include the pooling of policies aimed at energy saving, diversification, the promotion of alternative and renewable energies and the reduction of polluting emissions, in the direction taken by the last european council. in short, mr president, commissioner, the objective, in the opinion of this rapporteur, must be that at the fifth summit of the european union - latin america and the caribbean, to be held in lima in 2008, we should be able to sign this ambitious strategic partnership agreement between the european union and its member states and the andean community and its member states.
the rapporteur. mr president, it is obvious to everyone that this debate which is about to take place in the house is taking place at an important moment for latin america in general, whose peoples seem to be responding very strongly to the policy which has impoverished them: a policy of neoliberal recipes which are now in question. president bush's recent visit to latin america is more than clear evidence. the european union has a historic debt to central america, particularly in the context of the association agreement with central america. we played a very important role in the 1980s in the process of pacification and democratization in central america - the san josé and esquipulas agreements - in which the european union took off, with an autonomous position vis-à-vis the united states, and played a key role. the situation in central america is very clear: economic growth is very weak - we are at 0.6% - poverty levels are still similar to those of the 1990s, and inequalities are increasing. the verification of the peace agreements is still an open question, as are human rights, impunity and corruption, and regional integration is still very weak. in this context, this modest rapporteur opted for a specific report to specify the type of partnership. it was based on three fundamental pillars: political dialogue for good governance, development cooperation to help eliminate the structural causes of poverty and inequality, and trade in conditions of fairness and mutual benefit based on complementarity and solidarity. an agreement that is committed to regional integration that contributes to the equitable and fair redistribution of income and wealth in central america. that was the context. we wanted an agreement which did not become a free trade area agreement and privatisation of public services. in short, we did not want to subordinate cooperation and political dialogue to the prescriptions of free trade. i am convinced that a markedly neoliberal trade agreement between unequal regions - in every sense of the word - only leads to deepening that inequality and fosters the exploitation of a business elite, deepening a wider circle of dependence, exclusion, poverty and very high social and environmental costs. i believe that trade and cooperation should be based on sustainable development at regional level to the benefit of the people, and not a series of projects for the benefit of transnational capital such as the puebla-panama plan or the european investment bank. with that in mind, i have prepared this modest report, with the help of many civil society organisations in europe and central america. the report was, of course, followed up by the opinions of the committee on development and the committee on international trade of the house. i would like to thank all those who contributed to the improvement of the text, and i intend to continue to follow this philosophy throughout. i would like to express my special thanks to mr miguel ángel martínez for his always fair and supportive contributions, in this case from the committee on development. in the opinion of the committee on international trade, mr gianluca susta, he has introduced amendments into the text, very important amendments which really distort the report i intended to present to the house. the aim was to produce a balanced report based on the three pillars i mentioned earlier, but in practice the set of amendments constituted a document whose main aim was to establish a free trade area. at that point, finally, it was up to me to try to dampen that vision as much as possible, that is to say, to try to make central america see or believe that what we europeans were pursuing was, fundamentally, a free trade area. we have reached - and i thank him for it - seven amendments of compromise with mr salafranca of the ppe-de group, mr obiols of the pse group and mr susta of the alde group, whom i thank, and i sincerely urge them to do so, in order to get closer to a cushion and not to distort the report. but i also naturally welcome the amendments by mr obiols and mrs de kayser of the socialist group and mr romeva of the green group, because they add to and improve this interest by making the mandate a clear mandate for an association agreement on those terms, excluding the free trade area. this has been partly fortunate, because we have managed to cushion, as i said, such important points as point (v) where it was explicitly recommended that the free trade area should be a priority strategic objective, even making references to the alcac plan, and, logically, we have managed to cushion it but not enough. i do not know whether it has been done before, but i am going to recommend to my group that it abstain in voting on this report because i think that it does not really achieve the objective it was intended to achieve, namely that of a balanced report. i am very interested in the opinion of the parliament of central america, the parlacen, the political organizations of central america, and what i do hope and wish is that the european commission, when it starts the negotiations, will take into account that what we are being asked for here is not a photocopy of the united states, but an equidistant, different and autonomous position.
member of the commission. mr president, let me first welcome, also on behalf of my colleague, benita ferrero-waldner, the remarkable work of the two rapporteurs as well the constructive analysis and comments made by the committee on foreign affairs, the committee on development and the committee on international trade concerning the different aspects and perspectives for future agreements with these regions. the conclusion of association agreements with central america and the andean community is a long-standing strategic objective for both regions, confirmed repeatedly by the heads of state and government at the summits in guadalajara and vienna. with the negotiation of these agreements, the eu shows its commitment to the region and its determination to reinforce its relations with all latin american countries. europe and latin america are natural partners, and closer ties with central america and the andean community will contribute to a stronger partnership, both politically and economically. the agreements will be negotiated on a region-to-region basis in order to provide further impetus to the regional integration processes both in central america and in the andean community. as repeatedly emphasised, also by the european parliament, regional integration is key to political and social stability. it will also help to insert these regions more successfully into the world economy by developing larger and more stable economies able to attract investment. nevertheless, it is worth dispelling the idea that the eu tries to ‘impose’ its own model: regional integration should be developed by each region on the basis of its own ambitions and agenda. the association agreements are envisaged as comprehensive agreements, embracing the whole array of the multifaceted relations of the eu with both regions: political dialogue, cooperation and trade. the respect and promotion of democratic principles, fundamental human rights, the rule of law and good governance will remain at the core of our relations with central america and the andean community. in addition, the commission is of the opinion that the association agreements should pay particular attention to the effective implementation of internationally-agreed standards in the human rights, social, core labour and environmental fields in order to enhance sustainable development. concerning political dialogue, these agreements will aim to tackle a wide range of matters, such as climate change, energy, migration and the fight against drugs. these are vital not only for both our regions but also for the entire planet. an enhanced dialogue with central america and the andean community aims to seek constructive engagement towards effective multilateralism and international governance that may respond to the world challenges of the 21st century. the political chapter of the association agreements will be accompanied by measures aiming to enhance bi-regional trade and investment in a balanced and fair way. this should be pursued not only through the progressive and reciprocal liberalisation of trade in goods and services, but also by establishing a fair and transparent regulatory framework. asymmetries between our regions should also be taken into account. the trade part of the agreement will be fully consistent with wto rules and obligations, while going beyond its basic rules, so as to maximise the mutual and long-term benefits of bi-regional trade liberalisation. cooperation between the two sides is to be deeply rooted in the global objectives and principles established by our development policy, such as the european consensus on development, as well as by the international agreements to which we are party, including the millennium development goals, and the paris declaration on aid effectiveness. social cohesion will be a priority. the cooperation chapter should reflect the willingness to work jointly and to exchange experiences. it should also reflect solidarity towards the poorest and most excluded people. let me conclude with an overview on the preparation of these negotiations: the draft negotiating directives were adopted by the commission on 6 december 2006 and are currently under discussion with member states. the commission hopes to have the negotiating directives adopted and, if conditions allow, actually to start negotiating with these two latin american sub-regions within the first half of this year. if we manage to stick to this ambitious timetable, it will be largely thanks to your support and determination to enhance relations between the eu and latin america, in particular with these two regions.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat fraud. mr president, the initial report presented to us by mr willy meyer on the association agreement between the european union and the countries of central america formed the basis for the opinion we drew up in the committee on development. we have very broad agreement with their approaches and we have also agreed with a number of recommendations of our committee on development on this subject. mr willy meyer was very receptive and we jointly signed seven amendments to introduce the specific concerns of the committee on development. i must admit, ladies and gentlemen, that i find the text which has come to us in the house very decaffeinated in relation to the initial proposals, reorientating them to a large extent in a neoliberal way, perhaps reflecting the thinking of the majority of parliament. the truth is that we can live with these texts thanks to the commitments, we will vote for them, but we will vote for them without any enthusiasm, knowing that they do not fit the needs of central america or the aspirations of its peoples and knowing, also, that this text will not increase the credit of the european union in those societies. of the seven amendments proposed by the committee on development, three have been accepted, and they stress that the eu-central america association agreement must include the dimension of development cooperation and therefore, as the commissioner has said, include the priorities defined in the european consensus on cooperation: namely, the eradication of poverty and the achievement of the millennium goals. perhaps these recognitions and the need we feel for the agreement will save, in the text we are going to vote, the minimum requirements for our support.

mr president, commissioner, we are living in the era of globalisation, which certainly has its ups and downs, but which fortunately is making us aware of the great affections on the planet which human activity and development imply. among other things, the marine environment, so important to our food, our leisure and our transport, is under constant assault from pollutants, both from land and from the sea. the latter include some - the least - resulting from unavoidable incidents, while the majority are caused by ship owners and operators who continue to operate irresponsibly, disregarding international safety standards and practices. the specific cases of the prestige and the erika were notable, but we must not forget the pollution that occurs daily from uncontrolled dumping of waste from bilge tanks and tank cleaning. we therefore have an obligation to impose all the controls and means at our disposal to tackle these criminal behaviours, and we must require all flag states to fulfil their responsibility, to have qualified inspectors with the necessary experience, and to have their port authorities verify the reliability of vessel hulls and compliance with waste disposal regulations. on this last point, i would like to urge the commission to propose legislation to ensure that all vessels have automatic devices for recording the levels of liquid in bilge tanks and tanks every hour, like black boxes carried by airplanes, to detect criminal activities against the marine environment. this is the only way to achieve the goal. i would like to end by congratulating the rapporteurs on their excellent work.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner kroes, ladies and gentlemen, the existence of economic freedom, the functioning of the internal market and the sustainability of european development are inseparable from competition policy. since the signing of the treaty of rome 50 years ago, its importance has continued to grow. competition is an indicator of european vitality and excellence, a key policy for delivering on the lisbon strategy and achieving the union's objectives. the commission has also proposed that the commission should be given the power to impose fines on the infringements of competition law. it is important to have both deterrence and reaction capabilities. the treatment of infringements has been carried out mainly by means of public administrative actions. the centralisation of the application of article 81 (3) through a priori control by the commission, which was mitigated by the exemption regulations from the 1980s onwards, was a victim of its own success; the demand for more and better competition revealed its economic inefficiency and its legal insufficiency. the role of private actions was underlined by the court of justice of the european communities when the courage v crehan judgment of 2001 recognised the possibility for anyone to claim damages from the infringer before national courts. the modernisation of council regulation (ec) no 1/2003 broke the commission's monopoly and recognised a more open system, applied in a decentralised manner by the administrative authorities in the community competition authorities network and also directly by the national judicial authorities. the possibility of private actions is not something exotic, but a return to the classical case-law that community law imposes obligations on states and individuals, and produces vertical and horizontal effects which can be protected by judicial review. its use in the member states, according to the commission study, reveals a surprising diversity and total underdevelopment, in contrast to the united states, where nine out of ten enforcement procedures are judicial. the rapporteur welcomes the commission's publication of a green paper to identify obstacles to private action and to seek solutions to remove them. in an advanced competition system, public action against the impunity of offenders must be complemented by private action against immunity and compensation for the damage caused to the victims of their conduct. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the rules on competition are applied more effectively. it responds to reasons of efficiency and justice. the imposition of fines is insufficient if it is not accompanied by private actions which prevent the infringer from enjoying advantages over competitors because of the infringement and compensate victims for the damage caused. the report considers that public and private actions form two pillars with the complementary purpose of safeguarding the market discipline inherent in the public interest and protecting the private interests of the participants. the application of community competition law by administrative and judicial authorities should not lead to a breakdown in the uniformity of its implementation. a decision cannot vary according to the nature of the authority adopting it. this is a critical point. it is necessary to maintain the community acquis and the effectiveness of leniency programmes, to coordinate public and private actions and to intensify cooperation between all the competent authorities. the report proposes a community model in line with the legal culture of the union, which takes account of the legal traditions of the member states. it rejects a shift towards the north american model by not sharing the desirability of introducing its unique features such as the possibility of judicial authorities composed of non-professionals class actions, the fixing of compensation for triple damages, excesses in access to documents and the system of professional fees or procedural costs. we must compensate for asymmetries and avoid irresponsibility, without breaking the procedural principle of equality of arms or artificially stimulating litigation. it is about encouraging the rational use of legal action, not judicial activism, and above all, about promoting the amicable and early resolution of conflicts. community competence is an exclusive competence of the european union. national administrative or judicial procedures do not alter this condition and should not prevent common guidelines or guidance for sanctions, in accordance with the principles of better law-making. i would like to thank the rapporteur for the legal affairs committee, mr doorn, for his valuable cooperation, the help of the alternative rapporteurs and the contributions of the amendments. i appreciate the constant and exemplary dialogue with the commission during the drafting of the report and i encourage the commissioner to continue to demonstrate her commitment in the next white paper.
the commission has also taken the initiative of drawing up a report on the implementation of the budget for the financial year 2005 and has also adopted a number of amendments to the budget. i have to say that from a budgetary point of view 2005 was not a bad year. it was a difficult exercise, as the european commission and the college of commissioners were faced with not very simple circumstances, as this was the first full budget of the enlarged union and, moreover, it is the first budget to be implemented in full by this new college of commissioners. i should therefore like to start by saying that the european commission has done a good job. that is why this rapporteur proposes that we give discharge for the management of the community budget in 2005, and that is what will be put to the vote in the house. that does not mean, of course, that there is no strong and well-founded criticism, both in certain directorates-general and in a structural and possibly very difficult-to-solve criticism, on some of the financial control issues which should be improved by the commission in the coming years. i would also like to point out that the commission has reacted quite well to the court of auditors' report and has advanced a number of lines of its new action plan which i hope will allow positive control in the coming years. in my resolution i have basically dealt with the subject of national declarations. the national management declarations are of great importance to this parliament. they were set up in 2003 and are intended to provide a guarantee by the member states that they have effective audit systems for community expenditure. in addition, they should be signed by someone with some authority at national level and, although the treaty states that the european commission is responsible for managing the budget, we must not forget that 80% of it is managed in the member states. we therefore felt that a new initiative of national declarations was necessary. we support the courageous initiatives, in our view, taken by some member states - and i am referring in particular to the netherlands and the united kingdom - which have put forward in the council these ideas of national declarations of control which may not be followed by other member states, since their territorial distribution and organization are different. but it's a step forward. and what we propose in the report is that the type, the form of future declarations should be left open, so that they can reflect the realities of the political systems of each member state. but as a fundamental idea, we as the european parliament want these national declarations to go ahead, because that is the only way to really involve the member states in the responsibility for the control of community funds, which is really the basis of this declaration of discharge. and then there is a very important point about national declarations: the das, as we members understand it, is a dead end, and we members who have followed the declarations of reliability very closely for 12 years know this. today it is impossible to establish the legality of the underlying transactions in the member states, particularly in the structural funds. we therefore need to do something to improve the quality of the audit, the involvement of the member states and that is why we are asking the council to issue a national management declaration covering all the funds co-managed, based on the declarations of the various national bodies responsible for the management of expenditure. in conclusion, mr president, although my report covers more, i believe that we could achieve a positive sda in the coming years, which is necessary for the community institutions and, in particular, very necessary for public opinion, which wants to see reliability, transparency and control of every last euro of public funds administered by both the commission and the member states.

paid out and specific to each programme will be decided by the commission to address the infringement of the rules and the extent and financial implications of the remaining shortcomings. suspensions and reservations often lead to the necessary improvements. in 2005, for example, dg regio had reservations on the adequacy of control systems in spain. in 2006, the dg audited that again and found that progress had made it unnecessary to repeat the reserve. likewise, for the european social fund, in early 2006 the commission signalled its reservations on the systems in place in the united kingdom. improvements were made by the uk and the reserve could be lifted. these examples show that the commission can and does interrupt payments. the basis for decisions like these must be well justified and explained in a detailed manner. we have therefore made great efforts again this year to improve the quality of the annual activity reports of commission directorates-general. the court was rather critical of commission controls in the research area. this is direct management by the commission and we have given this issue the highest priority. an ex-post audit strategy is now in place across the research family of dgs for audits on the sixth framework programme (fp6). this is a robust strategy and is accompanied by a significant increase in the percentage of the research budget covered by ex-post audits. there will be 300 audits for fp6 in 2007, compared with 45 carried out in 2006. reflecting the priority given to this, the commission is reallocating a significant number of staff to audit tasks and undertaking the necessary additional recruitment. furthermore, serious consideration is being given to the gradual introduction of lump sums in certain specific areas of the framework programme. let me say a few words on agencies. the commission has noted the increasing concern in parliament over regulatory agencies. we already provide a lot of support to the the budget. we do so by informing you openly and honestly about our strengths and weaknesses. we are grateful for your fair recognition of both.

the rapporteur. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i sincerely believe that there is reason to be satisfied with the results achieved, the result of the collaboration and consensus that exist in this house on a matter as sensitive to public opinion as the safety of our seas. this is the feeling we must convey to the council, encouraging it to share this same attitude, because we must learn the lesson. we have to act now. we cannot expect the consensus that always follows disasters, the terrible images of our polluted beaches, the ships of our fishermen docked in ports faced with the impossibility of working, the families and regions living off the sea, broken by the pain of tragedy. the treatment we must give to these seven proposals is that of a whole, despite the complexities that may arise, because the intersections between the proposals exist; all the actors in the maritime transport chain are involved. it is therefore not a question of whether any of these proposals are unnecessary or untimely. each and every one of them is indispensable. however, there is one point which concerns me very much and which i would like to mention, because it concerns an essential aspect of the package. i am referring to the independence of the bodies and authorities which have been set up specifically to take the best decisions in the shortest possible time. in this connection, i am speaking specifically of the independent authority which is intended to be created to make permanent the ever so difficult decision to take a ship in danger to a place of refuge. i would like to express my disagreement with the attitude - which i consider to be voluntary - adopted by the committee on transport on this matter, which further weakens the already fragile decision-making structure for safe havens proposed by the european commission. ladies and gentlemen, it would be useless to create an authority that is independent of the influence of political power if it were not provided with the necessary resources and capacity to take decisions. but it is even more serious to give it powers if, at the moment of truth, it is left with only one option: to take the ship by force, even if it is uninsured and without guarantees. the whole burden therefore falls on the member state concerned, which is ultimately the victim of the ecological and social damage which may result from hosting a vessel in a place of refuge, in addition to having to deal with the coverage of such damage. let's be realistic and address the history that is so often repeated. in spain, in the last three months, we have had two cases of vessels in distress close to our coast, and in both cases the competent authority, on the basis of a detailed assessment of the emergency situation, decided, in order to minimise the risks, not to bring the vessel close to our coast. it is not necessary to say how relieved the civilian population in the area is to see the ships moving away, because it is one thing to see your beaches surrounded by luxury motorcycles and unprecedented perfumes, and quite another to see your beaches, your marine environment and wildlife impregnated with potpourri or your fellow citizens affected by toxic gases. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishing fleet is not affected by the crisis. that said, i appreciate mr. sterckx's tenacity in this difficult undertaking he's had to deal with. i congratulate him in particular on the progress made in the monitoring of vessels, which is essential to prevent dangerous situations. before i turn to my report, i would like to commend the work of mrs vlasto, mr kohlicic and, of course, the enormous work of mr costa. we hope that this proposal will be successful because now more than ever, after what happened in the last few days with the sinking of the cruise ship in greek waters, it is necessary to go further in protecting the rights of travellers. i shall now turn to my report. as you will recall, we have been working on the fourth revision of directive 94/57. this is the vital role played by so-called classification societies. from now on, recognized organizations. the evaluation carried out by the commission over the last six months has revealed that serious deficiencies remain in the process of inspection and safety certification of the global fleet. in view of this, it is our duty to reinforce the activities of these organizations, more and better. to this end, the european commission is proposing a series of reforms which i have endorsed and which have been strengthened as a result of the dialogue with the commission and the positive contributions of the parties concerned and the members of the transport committee. only in this way have we succeeded in strengthening the monitoring mechanisms of the recognised organisations by setting up an independent evaluation committee with permanent powers and autonomy of action. only in this way can we achieve a more flexible and equitable system of sanctions, which is ultimately more effective, since it sanctions those who do not act as they should, but it does so in accordance with the seriousness of the infringement committed and the economic capacity of the organisation. and only in this way have we been able to make progress on the thorny issue of the recognition of certificates of classification, by setting out the conditions under which recognised organisations will have to recognise each other, without jeopardising maritime safety and taking the most stringent rules as a reference. thank you very much.

ladies and gentlemen, madam president-in-office of the council, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the prestige disaster in 2002 marked, like the erika disaster in 1999, a before and after in the adoption of community legislation on maritime safety, and this parliament can be proud of its role in this regard. the first paragraph of the third resolution on the prestige, which was adopted by this house in september 2003, called on the conference of presidents to give a favourable view to the request for the creation of a temporary committee to look into the causes and consequences of the disaster in greater depth, so that such a thing would never happen again. the temporary committee, which was a very difficult one to set up, was very positive for this house. it has enabled us to assume our responsibility for the political control of a european-wide disaster and to play a role in promoting a genuine european maritime transport policy, because the investigation and technical and professional analysis of accidents and incidents -
