member of the commission. mr president, i am really very pleased to be here today to discuss with you this very important topic of how we can improve consumer confidence in the digital environment. i would like to start my speech by thanking mrs roithová and all the shadow rapporteurs for their excellent and very close cooperation – and this is not just a matter of courtesy, but a sincere recognition of very hard work. i am glad that the commission and the european parliament agree on a common line in approaching this very important and challenging issue. this is clearly an important and ambitious report, and i think we all broadly share the same objectives and analyses of the problems. the digital economy – and more specifically e-commerce – has great potential to improve consumer welfare by making a greater range of products available, boosting price competition and developing new markets. it is also central to completing the retail side of the internal market. at present, retail markets are still fragmented along national lines into mini-markets, as mrs roithová indicated. this makes no sense in the age of e-commerce and the internet. e-commerce is changing the face of retail, but only at national level. the internet is borderless but consumers, businesses and regulators are not. fifty per cent of european consumers who have a computer at home have made an e-commerce purchase in the previous 12 months, but only 12% of those with a computer at home bought cross-border. this indicates the need for action to increase consumer confidence on the retail side of the internal market and the necessity to solve the fragmentation of the market to achieve finally a citizens’ market. as you know, since the beginning of the year we have launched two major initiatives for consumers: the consumer policy strategy and the consultation on the review of existing consumer protection legislation. our objective as a commission is to help the eu rise to the challenges of growth and jobs and reconnecting with its citizens. this objective will be met if, by 2013, we can credibly demonstrate to all citizens that they can shop from anywhere in the eu – from corner shop to website – confident that they are equally and effectively protected. the need to improve consumer confidence in the digital economy runs through every aspect of this strategy. mrs roithová’s report shows that the obstacles – including regulatory obstacles – are numerous. my predecessors made progress in tackling some of them with the unfair commercial practices directive and the regulation on consumer protection cooperation, which established the european consumer centre (ecc) network. my priority now is to tackle the remaining obstacles, with the reform of existing consumer protection legislation related to consumer contracts. as you know, we have initiated a broad consultation on the future of consumer protection, and we have started to analyse reactions from the stakeholders. we are looking forward to mrs petre’s report after the summer. your views and your support will be an important reference for our follow-up work and for specific proposals. the commission’s follow-up to the review of the acquis is a basis on which build consumer trust. the development of standardised consumer contracts may be something to investigate further once this solid base is established. one of the aims of this exercise is to reduce the regulatory fragmentation of the internal market by targeted harmonisation of issues that cause particular problems for consumers and businesses. we will, inter alia, consider whether standards and standardisation can play a role in this process. similarly for self-regulation. the commission has done some important work to establish a best practice model for self- and co-regulation, and we will continue to do so in the future. i share your concerns about the interplay of different legislation governing online transactions or digital goods. there are many precise laws, and consumers and businesses may not be sufficiently aware of their rights and duties in the digital environment. i will examine how best to clarify these issues with my colleagues, mrs reding and mr mccreevy. thanks to your input, we will explore the idea of a practical guide which would cover information society services and help citizens to understand their rights better. i would also like to thank you for insisting on the importance of enforcement – i fully agree with you. quality legislation is not enough if it is not backed up by effective enforcement. we have set up a network of national enforcers in the european union and we will now gradually enlarge the network to third country partners in order to enhance its efficiency. in conclusion, i would like to thank you for your commitment to helping european citizens to enjoy all the benefits of the internal market and the digital economy. i look forward to opinion of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights. - mr president, the committee on legal affairs was asked by the chairman of the committee on the environment, public health and food safety to give its opinion on the appropriate legal basis for the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing a uniform authorisation procedure for food additives, food enzymes and food flavourings. the committee on legal affairs has studied the matter and, firstly, we find that it is perfectly possible to have two different legal bases. we have, for example, the court of justice's decision of 1988 in the case of commission v council, which provides for this possibility of a dual legal basis where the objectives of the protection of individuals and the functioning of the internal market coincide. we believe that this directive is a coincidence. it is not simply a directive aimed at maintaining the internal market but also a directive which aims to provide the highest level of legal protection. there is no difficulty in the procedural aspect, because the procedure is the same: the codecision procedure. however, we believe that the legal basis of article 95 'based exclusively on the internal market' is not sufficient and that it should therefore be reinforced by article 175 (1), which concerns the protection of the health of individuals.
mr president, commissioner, i shall be speaking on the flavour regulation, and i should like to thank the rapporteur, mrs murko, for the cooperation we have had and the good agreements we have reached. firstly, i have to welcome the commission's proposal, because it updates the legislation, while simplifying the approval procedures, centralising the risk assessment for marketing flavourings and the establishment of a positive list in the european food safety authority (efsa). the contribution of parliament to this report is also important and has been very well coordinated by mrs murko. we think that the comitology procedure is appropriate and we agree with it, provided that it does not deprive parliament of the possibility of examining it when it deems it appropriate. it is necessary to extend the application of the regulation to frozen spices and herbs, as technology requires. natural aromas must be labelled as such, because the consumer has a right to know this. as regards foods and food ingredients derived from genetically modified organisms (gmos) which meet the requirements of regulation (ec) no 1829/2003 on genetically modified food and feed and those of this regulation, they should be subject to a single efsa assessment valid for both authorisation procedures. they should not be subject to two different procedures for the same purpose. natural herbs and spices have very particular characteristics and i think the solution that has been reached, namely to remove them from the annex, is a good one. the transitional period, which is not provided for in the regulation, is also a necessity as long as the existing legislation is in force. the amendments tabled by the european people's party go in this direction.
the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the energy package, which is a package of measures to be taken by the member states to ensure that the union's energy supply is not affected by the consequences of the crisis. the report which this house will adopt tomorrow answers the main questions raised by the commission in relation to this last paragraph, the internal market. the text adopted in the committee on industry, research and energy, agreed with all the political groups, shows that there is clear agreement on most of the issues and we hope that commissioner piebalgs will find our contributions useful in the run-up to the adoption of the third liberalisation package in september. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the protection of the euro against counterfeiting is a very good one. the current system 27 member states, 27 different rules is a serious obstacle to the internal market, in particular as regards cross-border trade and the promotion of interconnections. it is therefore proposed that a european-wide body be set up to deal with these issues. we also welcome the council's firm commitment to achieving 10% interconnections between member states, which is of particular relevance for the peripheral states. at national level, it is called for national regulators to be fully independent of governments and industry and for their powers to be strengthened so that they can ensure that the law is complied with. regulators must ensure that markets are transparent, open to all and that there is no abuse by existing companies. we also agree that regulated tariffs should be phased out. this is the case in several member states where this type of tariff is used to prevent new companies from entering the market; in some cases it is so low that it does not reflect costs, which sends a false signal to the consumer. we are in a period in which a radical change in consumption habits is necessary and to achieve an optimisation of energy resources it is necessary that citizens are fully aware of their real value. the report also introduces a social chapter, reminding member states that the completion of a competitive energy market must not in any case lead to a weakening of consumer rights and that obligations towards the vulnerable sections of society must remain in place. the most hot topic in the report is the separation of ownership between the generation and transmission levels of electricity. it is the majority view of the committee on industry, research and energy that this separation of ownership provides us with an appropriate measure to achieve greater transparency, to secure investments and to guarantee access for new entrants to the market. these are the main points of the report, mr president, and i can only thank the directorates-general for translation and publishing and the bureau of this parliament for their invaluable help. without it it would not have been possible to conclude this report in just four months, in time to achieve an effective presence in the legislative process. i would also like to highlight the excellent cooperation with the alternative rapporteurs and the political groups. it has been a real pleasure to negotiate this report with them and let us hope that the vote tomorrow will bring a happy end to all this work.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to reduce the use of mercury in the manufacture of products. it is appropriate to introduce restrictions at community level on the marketing of measuring and control equipment containing mercury for use by private individuals, with some exceptions in the health sector. we want to prevent considerable amounts of mercury from entering the waste stream. in this way we will contribute to ensuring a higher level of protection of the environment and human health and to the preservation of the internal market, in accordance with article 95 of the treaty. mercury and its components are extremely toxic to humans, ecosystems and nature. mercury pollution, which began as a diffuse local problem long ago, is now recognized as a global, chronic and serious problem. as regards the possibility of a total ban on the use of mercury in all measuring devices covered by this proposal, it should be noted that the experts consulted have concluded that hospitals need very precise devices to treat potentially life-threatening conditions such as hypertension, arrhythmia and pre-eclampsia. mercury sphincter manometers ensure the precision and reliability necessary to preserve patient safety, so for the time being in this proposal we advocate exempting these instruments from the ban until there are full guarantees about the operation of possible alternative instruments. i would also like to stress again to the commission the need for it to take short-term measures to ensure that all mercury-containing products currently in circulation are separately collected and safely treated, otherwise this directive would lose its practical effect. on the production of new traditional mercury barometers, which has been the most controversial item in this parliament, we proposed an agreement that there should be a two-year transitional period for manufacturers to adapt to the new standards. unfortunately, not all the political groups have signed it, although i believe that we will have a sufficient majority in this house to approve it. as for the manufacturers of these barometers, i would like to say that they will have this two-year transitional period to stop using mercury in their industrial processes, which will not cause them any competitive disadvantage or economic damage, since we know that they have been manufacturing this type of barometer for some time without using mercury. it is necessary to remind our citizens that these devices can be a danger to health and the environment, since they can easily break and end up in landfills, or, worse still, when they are incinerated, mercury is dispersed into the atmosphere, polluting the air, the soil and the water. this is how mercury enters the food chain, first in fish, and then in us humans. as this house is well aware, the committee on the environment has rejected by a majority, at this second reading, the amendments tabled to allow the manufacture of new mercury barometers to continue. i think it would be irresponsible for us to accept this request and i therefore ask all the honourable members to vote against it, as the council and the european commission also propose, and i thank them for all their efforts to avoid a possible compromise. finally, i would again ask the commission to raise public awareness by organizing information campaigns on the health risks of exposure to mercury and the environmental problems that this substance can cause, since i fear that the public is still not sufficiently informed about its toxicity. i am grateful to the commission for its work and for the opportunity to reach an agreement at second reading. i would also like to thank the council and the political groups who have supported this proposal.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i would like to congratulate my colleague, mrs wallis, on the work she has done. i think we will get a good agreement, that parliament will support this proposal by a majority and that we will have a new regulation on non-contractual liability. i would point out, however, that this regulation is only going to be the beginning. there is a fundamental difficulty in the whole field of private international law and in the conflict of laws, which is the sheer inability of judges to apply a law other than their own. in the european union as in general we have trained judges to apply their own law. as soon as a question arises in which they have to apply foreign law, there are enormous difficulties. it is clear that if two englishmen have a traffic accident in france, they will apply the french traffic rules - they could not consider that the driver on the left is the one who acted correctly. now, in the second part, with regard to the civil liability to be determined, if the judge is english, i have great difficulty in thinking that he would accept the application of the rules of limitation of liability which exist in french law and that he would not apply the rules of english law. so i think, as i said before, this is a work in progress. commissioner frattini referred to a subsequent study by the commission - which is also referred to in the draft regulation - which is the applicability of the law by the courts. i think this is the second part, a second essential part. those of us who have worked in this area have seen that there is a general tendency for courts to apply their own law, the law of the forum. therefore, this convention or this regulation cannot be interpreted without taking into account the applicable jurisdiction at any given time. in large part, the court will determine the applicable law because judges usually resort to any subterfuge. here, for example, we have eliminated the subterfuge of referral, but there is still the whole issue of public policy - the public policy clauses - which contain the mandatory provisions of national law contained in the draft convention. i therefore have the impression that, on the basis that this parliament will approve by a large majority the proposal put to us by mrs wallis, once it has been approved we will have to continue working on this matter. we are certainly looking forward with great anxiety to the commission's studies on this subject and, above all, to an important element, namely the work with the people who will have to apply this regulation: the judges themselves. we wonder what the attitude of the judges is and what the practice will be in applying this regulation, since the experience with international conventions and with the application of the rules of private international law of the states shows us this general tendency for the judges to apply their own national law.

the rapporteur. - madam president, i would like to comment on amendment no 2, which refers to the role of the transmission system operators, in the text of the report the word 'institutional' appears. in the language of the european union, 'institutional' has a very specific meaning which is too high for what is intended here. so what i suggest is to replace the word 'institutional' with 'official'. the commission therefore welcomes the proposal to give the existing tso associations an official role, with formal obligations and objectives (etso+/gte+ solution).
mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate jacek protasiewicz on the consensus effort he is trying to make and which i hope will be successful tomorrow. there was no doubt that a joint reflection was needed on what the rules meant for regulating the labour market, and i believe that the green paper has provided a good opportunity to do so. since the luxembourg summit, new challenges and problems have emerged, for example immigration and an ageing population, and in 1997 - we remember - the aim was simply to encourage job creation. today, in a period of greater economic dynamism, we are not only opting for full employment but also for quality employment. i am referring to the fact that we are seeking better working conditions, more efficient business management, a balance between work and family life, lifelong learning and also stability. and therein lies the first flaw i find in the report. stability cannot be at odds with parttime contracts. the report disqualifies this type of contract and only defends full-time contracts, forgetting how necessary these types of contracts, which can also be indefinite and stable, are for reconciling work and family life. the report also criminalizes and forgets temporary contracts, which are necessary, indispensable and irreplaceable in some sectors, such as tourism, hospitality, construction or agriculture, where it would be unthinkable to have indefinite contracts, because of the very function that is performed. i would also like to point out - and this is another point that can be made - that we know that in different countries the labour systems are different, very different from one country to another. the relations between the various social partners are also very complex, which makes it very difficult to legislate jointly at european level. we are more in favour of subsidiarity, but we are also in favour of the open method of coordination and of agreement between the social partners. we certainly do not want to give the commission a blank cheque so that it can act on labour law issues without taking account of the different countries and the different characteristics of each of them.
on behalf of the alde group. i have had the opportunity to read a newspaper article which said that the origin of man is in water, that without this liquid element we cannot live and that we adult humans are 75% nothing but water. in addition, three quarters of the surface of our planet is covered by water from the seas and oceans, and there is a constant cycle of water being transferred from the oceans to the atmosphere, from the atmosphere to the earth and finally back to the sea via the rivers. this makes it imperative to focus all our attention on the sustainability of the marine aquatic environment, especially when all the alarms have been sounded worldwide for some time now about the deterioration of the environment in general and climate change in particular. we believe that measures to improve water quality must be taken rapidly at all institutional levels - community, national, regional and local - and at the private level. in this connection, we wish to express our concern about the broad timetable contained in the proposal for a directive on a marine strategy. we believe that, as with air pollution and the ozone hole, we have little time left to act and reverse the current trend. if we don't do this soon, i'm afraid the degenerative process will be irreversible. we have therefore proposed that the timetable for drawing up the action plans for the new marine strategy be adapted as a matter of urgency, bringing them into line with other important union programmes, such as those financed by the erdf, the cohesion fund and also the agricultural policy, since there are also agricultural activities which end up dumping waste into the sea. we also believe that more accurate information on what is happening in the seas and oceans is needed. we are in favour of better coordination and networking of all european marine research institutes, either by promoting a european network or a european consortium and creating a maritime database accessible to all of them. we must improve training and information at all levels and disseminate best practice in pollution control and control. i would like to stress once again something i have been saying for years, namely that it is necessary to make it compulsory to install on ships devices - which have already been invented - for monitoring the emptying and cleaning of tanks and bilges, in the form of non-manipulable black boxes, which will be the best method of preventing deliberate dumping, and i say this without underestimating that this will be complemented by satellite inspection and monitoring. we must not forget the professional fishermen, who are an important population group whose way of life we must ensure for the future, avoiding the depopulation or invasion by wild urbanism of coastal or island populations. finally, we are in favour of applying the 'polluter pays' principle to the marine sector and of creating a community fund for the rebuilding and conservation of marine flora and fauna, based on the contributions of all industrial activities - energy, tourism, recreation and all kinds of activities - that pollute our seas.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, only a few months ago, not many observers were fully convinced that the european council could successfully relaunch the treaty review process. opinion across europe was fragile and there were wide divergences of views but, thanks to the admirable determination of chancellor merkel and the german presidency and through a real collective effort by member states and our institutions, the european council last month reached agreement on a clear and stringent mandate for a new igc, and it is important that we today recognise this success. yesterday, the commission adopted its opinion on the igc and, today, you are discussing parliament’s opinion. this process will allow the portuguese presidency to launch the intergovernmental conference later this month, but it is not only on timing that our institutions walk side by side. we also do so more importantly on the substance. the commission shares the globally positive assessment of the igc mandate which mr leinen’s report provides. the mandate contains many positive elements which are to be welcomed. like any compromise text, it is also a carefully crafted balance between different interests, between ambition and political realism, and this means that some of the changes agreed in the 2004 igc were not retained. it is also the reason why a number of derogations were granted to individual member states. i shall set out four reasons why the commission believes that this mandate will allow us in the igc to provide the european union with the sound institutional and political basis which we need to meet the expectations of our citizens and the challenges of our societies. firstly, the mandate will lay the ground for modern and more accountable institutions for the enlarged union. we warmly welcome the provisions which will refresh and reinforce the european union’s democratic legitimacy, a stronger and wider role for the european parliament, transparency of council deliberations, more codecision, more decisions taken by qualified majority, a clearer division of competences. national parliaments will have greater opportunity to be involved in the work of the european union, while the role of the european institutions will be fully respected. we are also very pleased to see that the innovations of the constitutions on democratic participation, including the citizens’ initiative, have been safeguarded. secondly, the union will have a charter of fundamental rights to protect the citizens, not just a declaratory text but one which will have legal force. citizens will be able to claim before the courts the rights enshrined in the charter. the charter will be binding for the european institutions and for member states when they implement eu law, even if this does not apply to all of them. thirdly, the union will be able to speak with one single voice on the global scene and be better able to protect the european interest. if we really want to tackle globalisation and address common concerns on sustainable development, climate change, competitiveness and human rights in the world, the union should use to the fullest its great potential to act collectively. my fourth remark concerns the policy areas, because the mandate develops the union’s capacity to deliver swifter and more consistent decisions in the area of freedom, security and justice. furthermore, it reinforces the legal basis to deal with the challenges of energy policy and climate change. how can we assess these changes? in our view, the overall balance is positive: the disappearance of some elements, including some of a symbolic nature, as well as the changes that reduced the readability of the text, were necessary parts of a package agreement which could be subscribed to by all member states. without an effort to compromise from all those involved, success would not have been possible. the european train is back on track, but we are not yet at the end of the journey and the citizens must be on board. the mandate is not yet the final product. to steer this new consensus to a successful igc will require intensive efforts from the portuguese presidency, the member states and our institutions. we particularly welcome the decision of the european council to strengthen the involvement of the european parliament in the igc. however, our collective negotiating efforts on their own will not be enough. we all – the commission, the member states and parliament – should draw some lessons from the previous ratification process and from the listening phase of plan d. i am glad to see that the european council has recognised the importance of communicating with citizens, providing full and comprehensive information on the eu and involving them in a permanent dialogue. this should be even more important in view of the changes that have reduced the readability of the treaty text. in the coming months, the commission will present some ideas on how a debate around the reformed treaty could be organised during the ratification period. we want to work closely with you in the european parliament, all the member states and other institutions. together, we should use this window of opportunity; together, we should engage in this new process without any delay and with all our energy. acting president of the council. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, on 6 december 2006 the council asked the european parliament to give its assent to the commission proposal for a council decision on the acceptance, on behalf of the european community, of the protocol amending the trips agreement concluded in geneva on 6 december 2005. the council requested such assent under the relevant provisions, namely articles 133 and 300 of the treaty establishing the european community. at the political level, the community was one of the strongest advocates in the drafting and negotiation of the said protocol, which will increase access to affordable medicines for all citizens in developing countries, one of the major successes achieved in the run-up to the wto ministerial conference in hong kong in december 2005. the handling of this important issue for developing countries by the body responsible for international trade rules is a practical application of the principles of policy coherence for development laid down by the european council, agreed in 2005 between parliament, the council and the commission, and is also an important concrete step towards achieving the millennium development goal of fighting hiv/aids, malaria and other diseases - objective 6. several wto members, including the united states, have already ratified the protocol and it is desirable that, once its internal procedures at the level of the commission, council and parliament have been completed, the european community, as the main proponent of the measure, ratifies the protocol as soon as possible, by 1 december 2007. as regards both the technical issues and the broader policy issues raised by the honourable members, the assessment of the technical effectiveness of the mechanism, established by the wto decision of 30 august 2003, is not a matter for the council. the council recognises the complexity of the issue but also stresses the fundamental political importance of ratification of the protocol for developing countries. the council does not intend to alter the mandate given to the commission for the purpose of economic partnership agreements, as they are in the final stages of negotiation. the member states, meeting with the commission in the edf committee, will endeavour to ensure that adequate resources are channelled towards the achievement of millennium development goal 6, in particular for the acp states. the council takes this opportunity to urge the european parliament to play its essential institutional role so that the european community can accept this important protocol and the rules of trade can be changed to better serve the interests of millions of human beings in developing countries.
member of the commission. madam president, the commission shares parliament’s view that access to medicines for poor developing countries is a matter of huge political and humanitarian importance, and the commission has taken a number of initiatives to facilitate access to medicines for poor developing countries through existing programmes. from the outset, the european community has been at the forefront of the debate on trips and access to medicines. in the wto, we played an active role in bringing together almost irreconcilable positions. developing countries were grateful to the european union for our role as an honest broker. the debate in the wto first led to the adoption of the declaration in doha in november 2001. this declaration reaffirms the right of wto members to use, to the full, the flexibilities contained in the trips agreement, including the use of compulsory licensing. for those countries with no manufacturing capacity in the pharmaceutical sector and that could not make effective use of compulsory licensing under the trips agreement, a temporary waiver from the normal rules of patent law was adopted in august 2003. parliament, together with the council, implemented this waiver decision by adopting it at first reading – regulation (ec) no 816/2006 – to allow manufacturers of generic drugs to produce patent medicines for export to countries in need without sufficient capacity to produce them. the protocol amending the trips agreement aims at transforming this decision into a permanent and legally secure solution. this flexibility, to be introduced into the trips agreement, can help save lives without undermining the patent system, which is one of the main incentives for the research and development of new medicines. we are now at the very end of this wto process. the last step is the acceptance of the trips amendment. i come now to the specific questions raised in the oral question, and i have discussed these responses with my colleague, mr mandelson, who is in charge of trade policy in the commission. i should like to make four specific, concise points. first, the mechanism created by the wto decision of august 2003 and the protocol to the trips agreement is the result of long and difficult negotiations between almost 150 countries. it represents a balance which was difficult to strike. this mechanism must be seen only as a part of the wider issue of access to affordable medicines for developing countries, which goes far beyond the issue of patent law. second, the commission can confirm that the european community is committed not to include, in the economic partnership agreements and in other future bilateral and regional agreements with poor developing countries, any trips+ provisions which could affect access to medicines or undermine the trips flexibility contained in the doha declaration on trips and public health. third, the commission encourages pharmaceutical companies to adopt schemes, such as tiered pricing, under which medicines are sold in poor and developing countries at considerably lower prices than in developed countries. fourth, the commission supports local production capacity. local production can promote competition and make pharmaceutical products more affordable. it is also important to encourage technology transfer to ensure that locally produced pharmaceutical products can meet internationally agreed standards. to conclude, i hope that parliament has been reassured that access to medicines remains a priority for the commission. now that the european parliament has all the elements in its hands to make a well-informed decision, and given the role played by the european community in forging this permanent solution, it would be regrettable if the european community could not accept it in time. it is essential that parliament and the commission continue to cooperate closely to facilitate access to medicines for poor developing countries.
acting president of the council. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, as i have already said, at the political level the community was one of the strongest advocates of this protocol in the preparation and negotiation of this protocol, which we believe will increase access to affordable medicines for all citizens in developing countries. commissioner olli rehn has also made it clear here that this result has been obtained after long and difficult negotiations and we believe that the result achieved, in the face of the circumstances, is a balanced result. i therefore have no choice but to appeal again to this parliament to accept this important protocol and so that the rules of trade can be changed to better serve the interests of millions of human beings in developing countries.
member of the commission. madam president, thank you for this very responsible debate on a very important issue. i would like to give a response to an issue which was raised by david martin and some other speakers concerning what the commission is doing in order to support technology transfers leading to the local production of affordable key pharmaceuticals. the issue also concerned what we are doing in the field of prevention, treatment and care as regards hiv, malaria and tuberculosis. this is one of the objectives of a specific initiative dedicated to aid for poverty-related diseases in the developing countries which provided a combined total of eur 81.2 million over the past two years. the european union is also a major funder of pharmaceutical and health-oriented clinical research including health systems research and capacity building in various sub-saharan african countries through the european developing countries clinical trials partnership. moreover, during the period of implementation of the sixth framework programme for research, eu support for r&d devoted to poverty related diseases amounted to more than eur 455 million. for the same period an additional eur 78 million was spent by international scientific cooperation on various projects covering the fields of neglected infectious diseases, health systems policy research and reproductive health. as you can see, the commission is doing a lot to help developing countries, in particular the least developed countries, to enhance their access to affordable medicines, including local production capacity. is that enough? probably not. is the commission ready to do more? yes, provided we have the resources needed. and this is an area where parliament has a key role to play. there was another important issue raised concerning the fact that the mechanism has not yet been used, which implied that it does not work. it is important to understand how compulsory licensing works. the mechanism can operate without any compulsory licence actually being granted. the usefulness of compulsory licenses comes mainly in the leverage they give to developing countries in price negotiations with pharmaceutical companies. in other words, compulsory licenses can deliver the expected results, i.e. make medicines more affordable without being actually granted. finally, i hope that parliament has been reassured that access to medicines remains a very strong priority for the commission and for the european union. we hope that parliament will give its assent to the protocol as soon as possible. the outside world would not understand a delay or refusal from the european union. this would undermine the eu’s credibility as a whole in this field and as an international partner in general.

the rapporteur. - mr president, my report is a contradiction because i use an expression which is contradictory: 'indicative right'. the law is not indicative, the law is coercive. the fact is that the european union's jargon has been using this expression: 'instrument of indicative law'. and what does that mean? this means, in particular, documents from the commission: some of an interpretative nature, others of an implementing nature, others merely preparatory documents. the problem is that, in view of the confusion and ignorance about the nature of community law in many jurisdictions - including the court of justice itself - these indicative legal documents are given binding legal status. this is a breach of the fundamental principles of the law of the member states of the european union and of the european union as a whole. the only legitimacy at present for legally binding rules is the will of the people, both at national and union level. and the will of the people is usually expressed through representative bodies, which can be either, in this case, the european parliament, directly elected by the people, or the council, made up of governments which are dependent on and elected by the people of their respective countries. it is clear that the commission has an important role to play in the implementation of european law, it is the guarantor of the application of the treaties, but it must do so together with the legislative bodies and, in any case, it cannot replace the legislative power conferred by the treaties on parliament and the council. the concern we have in the committee on legal affairs is that, on the one hand, we do not want to impede the commission's initiative, we do not want to impede the commission's implementing functions, we do not want to limit the possibilities for development, but we do believe that it is important to draw a conceptual distinction between the two types of instruments and that, when the commission considers that it has to resort to this type of act, it should at least establish collaboration with parliament and, of course, in any case with the council, so that the preparation of these acts does not give rise to misinterpretations or interference. of course, what is not right in any way is what has been called the 'open method of coordination'. the open method of coordination can be an effective instrument for achieving the aims of the treaty, but it can only establish obligations between those parties which participate. these would be contracts between parties, for example between social partners. just as an agreement between, for example, trade unions and employers may have binding value for the parties involved, the open method of coordination is used to draw up such contracts, but subject to community rules and, in no case, can replace them. and the european union, as a community of law, needs the adoption of legal texts. it is not enough to say 'let's use the open method of coordination', because it is an effective instrument for achieving the objectives of the european union. it is not an effective instrument, because the european union can only function as a legal order. the european union has no army, no police force, it has operated on the basis of the assumption by the member states of a series of obligations which are fulfilled by the institutions of the member states and whose fulfilment is monitored by the commission and the court of justice. but the open method of coordination is not a legal method, it is not a legal instrument to give general rules and one cannot confuse one thing with another. the committee on legal affairs - as mr gargani said earlier - is concerned about this anti-legal drift within the european union. the european parliament wants to cooperate with the commission in achieving its objectives, in its implementing tasks, in its tasks of preparing legislative texts, but it cannot and must not condone the use of techniques which are not in keeping with the development of the rule of law, the development of the construction of the european union as a community of law, a community which must have a clear regulatory hierarchy: treaties - which i still call constitutional, despite everything - which lay down the fundamental rules, european union legislation which meets all those areas in which the european union must intervene, while respecting, of course, the principles of proportionality and subsidiarity, but maintaining the union's competences and setting out action at the legislative level, leaving then for implementation instruments such as this method of coordination or any other instrument which the commission may consider adopting to lead to the achievement of the union's objectives. the rapporteur. - mr president, this afternoon we are discussing a sector which is key to european growth, competitiveness and employment: logistics. logistics is essential to the quality of life of our citizens, even if they do not perceive it clearly enough. this exercise seeks, among other things, to make it more visible to the public. this sector accounts for around 13% of the european union's gdp and has a major economic impact, accounting for between 10% and 15% of the final cost of finished products in europe. in some sectors, such as the important automobile sector, it is even now more important than social costs. it is also a sector which, until now, seemed to be a matter for industry and the market alone, and its success and growth potential seemed indisputable and should therefore remain so. but in keeping with our firm conviction that the best market is one which is well regulated, which facilitates and promotes positive capacities and, on the other hand, avoids possible risks before they become obstacles and impediments to the necessary growth, creativity and development of our citizens, we therefore welcome the commission's decision to address the treatment of this sector in so far as the european union can contribute to it, in order to multiply the potentials and limit the obvious risks, given the forecasts of growth in the transport sector in europe. there is now talk of a 50% growth between 2000 and 2020. it will therefore be able to exploit and increase its opportunities in a scenario which appears to us to be defined by five fundamental axes. the first is the recent enlargement to the east, which increases distances and creates peripherality but at the same time also creates new market opportunities and exchange in the diversity of the cultures of our citizens. the second axis would be globalisation, which accelerates exchanges, diversifies needs and relocates territories and populations. i am thinking that my country, for example spain, appears to be on the periphery in the case of enlargement, and yet globalisation has repositioned it at the crossroads of such important areas as latin america, africa or trade with asia. another key focus for this approach to logistics is climate change and current energy needs. we need to make more efficient use of infrastructure, better traffic management, limiting empty travel, and logistics, as it is being developed today, can make a great contribution to all this. the fourth axis would be the r & d & i opportunities we are looking for in europe, in the framework of the seventh framework programme and the whole future of the knowledge economy. logistics represents precisely that intelligent transport, that transport which includes planning at its base and which is increasingly based on intelligent transport systems. sesar, safeseanet and track and trade are all mechanisms and new technologies that are being successfully applied to this sector. finally, demographic changes and the expectations of young people in employment, to which logistics can also contribute in a definitive way. in this respect, the proposal for a report is precisely trying to follow the commission in identifying bottlenecks and in trying to put forward new proposals. the case for avoiding excessive administrative burdens, through the application of precisely these intelligent systems, of reduction and limitation, although it is still complex, especially, for example, in the case of customs and maritime cabotage, but i believe that the commission is in this case in its action plan presenting approaches which can be very positive. another bottleneck, for which we also propose a number of solutions, would be the lack of infrastructure and its poor financing. in this sense, we still demand the need to complete this network of transfrontier networks where some of the historic passes, in the case of the pyrenees or the alps, have yet to be opened, which we believe would also help, by reducing congestion on some of the roads through the opening of railway tunnels. in this connection there is also a specific proposal, which i particularly support, and that is the proposal for a dedicated railway freight track system. we encourage the commission to submit a draft to us in this respect. as regards the whole question of the need for financing, we would like the logistical factor to be taken into account in the debate on the future financing of a sufficiently ambitious european transport policy, and we would therefore like it to be a priority element as well. as regards the shortage of labour, we support the commission's approach to making this profession more attractive, but we would like to see more than just training, but also improvements in social and working conditions. finally, we also want to follow the commission and encourage it in this respect, pointing out to it the need for a specific chapter on urban logistics in the future treatment of urban transport. we believe that our citizens suffer daily from congestion where this logistics that appears invisible in the positive part appears instead in its most negative aspect. we believe that it is time for logistics to take its place in the european debate.
mr president, commissioner, i am one of those who believe that without ambitious objectives, progress and prosperity cannot be achieved, but i also believe that the community and the european union are too often given to grandiose and unrealistic agreements and objectives. this is what happened, in my view, in 2000 with the lisbon strategy, which by 2010 was to position us as the most competitive and dynamic global economy in the world; or in 1994 with the essen agreements on the transeuropean transport networks, most of which are still pending. in march of this year, the european council set the target of a 20% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions and energy consumption, whereas in reality we are failing to meet the much more modest targets we committed ourselves to in kyoto. we are now discussing freight transport logistics in europe as a key element for sustainable mobility, something that is essential for our growth and development; and given the significant growth expected for freight transport until 2020, we cannot ignore logistics, as it is a necessary tool to increase accessibility, efficiency and safety - as well as sustainability - of freight transport. but at the same time, persistent shortcomings need to be addressed, such as the throttling of the transeuropean road network at biriatu pass in the basque country or elsewhere, or the lack of freight corridors on the rail network which do not need to be high speed to compete, or the very low interoperability of railways or the lack of efficient transhipments. we must strengthen intelligent transport systems, apply the potential of the internet to the management of freight transport, standardising weights, measures and loading standards, reducing bureaucratic red tape and creating one-stop shops. we must promote the co-modality of the different modes of transport, not forgetting the motorways of the sea and inland waterways, and above all integrate all real costs, including environmental costs, into the price of their use. and all this cannot be done by cutting the contributions of the member states to the community budget.

vice-president of the commission. madam president, the european court of justice plays an important role in safeguarding the legality, implementation and application of third pillar instruments. under article 35 of the treaty, the court has jurisdiction, upon request of a member state’s court or tribunal, to give preliminary rulings on the validity or interpretation of framework decisions and decisions, on the interpretation of conventions established under title vi of the treaty, and on the validity and interpretation of the measures implementing them. however, this jurisdiction only exists for those member states which have declared that they accept the jurisdiction of the court. moreover, those member states, having accepted the jurisdiction, may limit it to the highest national courts or tribunals. at this moment, unfortunately, only 16 member states have accepted the jurisdiction of the european court to give preliminary rulings on third pillar instruments, and two of them have made a limitative statement. this is really insufficient in my view and does not allow for appropriate dialogue between the court and the national courts applying european law on a daily basis. in addition, the european court has jurisdiction to review the legality of framework decisions and decisions. both member states and the commission may bring an action before the european court to challenge the legality of these measures. in practice, the commission has made use of this possibility twice. i refer to the cases regarding the request for annulment of the framework decision concerning the application of criminal law with respect to the protection of the environment and ship source pollution. but, in my view, these provisions also need improvement. in particular, the present treaty does not provide for a mechanism similar to the infringement procedures for community legislation, in order to monitor the implementation of the instruments in member states’ legislation. i have expressed my view on the gaps with respect to the jurisdiction of the court in the area of freedom, security and justice in two communications i submitted to the commission in 2006 and july 2007 on the implementation of the hague programme. the commission therefore welcomes the mandate agreed by the member states for an intergovernmental conference to finalise details of a reformed treaty. under the reformed treaty, i would expect the court of justice to become fully responsible in all justice, freedom and security areas. this is important to tackle poor national implementation of previously agreed work.

which is the eighth since the adoption of the convention. you will know that the council supports the adoption by this 8th conference of the parties of the strategic plan and the ten-year framework to implementation or process of the un convention to combat desertification. they will also be aware that the conference of the parties will address the relationship between poverty and desertification, identifying the specific contribution that the convention can make to the fight against poverty in close cooperation with other relevant global and regional actors. the council considers it important to reach consensus on an improved monitoring system of the convention based on standards for the conservation, management and sustainable use of drylands. such a system will make it possible to measure the progress that has been or is being made. the role of the committee on science and technology is essential to strengthen the knowledge base of the convention and to enable more informed action and decisions to be taken. the council of the european union considers that the challenges of desertification, climate change and biodiversity are complementary and should be addressed in a coordinated manner by relevant policies in order to develop synergies and increase their effectiveness. the availability of adequate financial resources, effective management and financing of initiatives to combat desertification, and an effective and efficient secretariat for the convention are also vital elements, in the council's view. along with desertification, drought is also a serious cause for concern. the council is fully convinced that only by strengthening international cooperation can these threats, namely drought and desertification, be effectively tackled. that is why the european union is pursuing its objectives in this field in collaboration with third countries. i would remind you that the acp-ec council of ministers adopted a joint declaration on combating drought and desertification at its annual meeting on 25 may this year. this joint declaration between the acp countries and the european commission recognises the importance of the united nations convention to combat desertification for poverty reduction and the pursuit of the millennium development goals set by the united nations. the declaration also supports the adoption by the conference of the parties of the decade strategic plan and calls upon all parties to work together to enhance the effectiveness of the united nations convention. the definition of a limited number of implementation priorities to be identified on the basis of scientific data and the use of indicators to measure progress made are elements which we believe are of great importance in this context. on the other hand, greater involvement of civil society and better communication and a more in-depth dialogue between all the parties involved will also, in our view, contribute significantly to the effectiveness of the united nations convention to combat desertification.
member of the commission. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, since its signing in 1994, the european community has attached great importance to the role of the united nations convention to combat desertification in poverty alleviation. the convention was developed as the main tool to contribute to the objective of sustainable land use, in order to fight against hunger and poverty. the commission continues to regard this convention as a key building block in the joint fight against poverty and desertification. the convention remains a unique forum, with the competence and experience to learn lessons and design new approaches to how to address land degradation. current work within the convention is focusing on key issues in the implementation of actions, such as integration and coherence of actions within strategic cooperation frameworks. the countries concerned, as well as the donor countries, need to ensure that the development of the convention is closely linked to other key development initiatives and, in particular, they need to ensure that the country concerned owns and leads the process itself. as regards the european union's objectives for the madrid conference, firstly, the commission is particularly pleased that four members of the european parliament are part of the community delegation attending the conference. the convention is entering its second decade and needs to adapt to meet new challenges and take advantage of new opportunities. this means reviewing action through the convention, in order to maximise the effectiveness and efficiency of our work in combating land degradation and poverty. in this regard, the union's main objective at the madrid conference is the adoption of the 10-year strategic plan to strengthen the implementation of the convention, a plan developed by a working group in accordance with the conclusions of the last conference of the parties, which took place in 2005. this plan, which is strongly supported by the european union, represents the parties' common and renewed vision of the strategic direction to be taken over the next ten years. if this common vision is adopted, as we hope, we will need to develop on behalf of the pse group. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, according to the united nations environment programme, desertification threatens a quarter of the world's land, 250 and poor practices are all factors that are deteriorating land productivity. i therefore hope that in madrid, more than 13 years after the birth of the un convention to combat desertification, the causes of the depletion of many arid, semi-arid and dry lands. these causes are leading us inexorably to a growing desertification of the planet, which we must try to stop by all means. in this acting president of the council. the implementation of the set of actions provided for in the council conclusions of 18 june 2007 shall be carried out by the institutions of the european union within the limits of the competences conferred on them by the treaty, in cooperation with the member states and, where appropriate, with the third countries concerned. the responsibility for the control and surveillance of the external borders lies with the member states. however, all member states participating in schengen cooperation, and not just those with external borders, have an interest in effective external border controls and some measures have been taken to promote solidarity and cooperation between member states in this area. the establishment of a european agency for the management of operational cooperation at the external borders of the member states of the european union, commonly known as frontex, by regulation (ec) no 2007/2004 is an important step towards promoting such solidarity. in this context, the capacity of frontex was further strengthened by the adoption on 12 june of the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council establishing a mechanism for the establishment of rapid border intervention teams and by the creation, during 2007, of a centralised register of available technical equipment, known as the toolbox, held by the member states and which could be made available to other member states. the launch of joint operations and pilot projects shall be carried out with the agreement of the member states concerned. rapid border intervention teams shall be established in response to a request from one or more member states. the role of frontex is to coordinate these activities. there are currently no plans to extend the scope of the decision-making powers of the commission or frontex in this context. in addition, the adoption of decision (ec) no 577/2007/ec of the european parliament and of the council, which established the external borders fund for the period 2007-2013 as part of the solidarity and management of migration flows programme, is another important step towards promoting solidarity and will create a new means of providing financial assistance to member states applying the schengen provisions at their external borders.

the european union is born of values that cannot be surrendered. just as we are closely watching that our member states do not violate the right to liberty, or to life, or to democracy, we must decisively influence, through dialogue, those countries with which we have political, commercial, economic, partnership relations, etc., to be also respectful of human rights. within the complexity and scale of the union's external relations, the space occupied by human rights dialogue and consultation with third countries may go unnoticed or take a back seat. if that were the case, and we allow it, we would be making a very serious mistake. this report deals with the aspects necessary to improve a task which is an obligation of the european union, according to article 11, and which also falls within the field of political ethics. human rights must become the banner of european foreign policy and the union must use its influence to improve the living conditions of the people of those countries with which we have relations. this is one of the key policy points of this report. when we sit down to negotiate economic or trade agreements with a country in which fundamental rights are being violated, we cannot put figures, agreements and contracts on the table while shamefully hiding under the carpet the situation of its citizens. if we leave human rights out of the negotiating room, we are falling into the most macabre cynicism. we must also take a close look at the role played by civil society and human rights defenders, who are sensitive and essential voices for the advancement of all oppressed societies. the report we are discussing today evaluates one of the main instruments available to the european union for the objectives i have mentioned and also for clearly defining the role we want to play in the world order. only through respect and reciprocity can we advance in the task of promoting human rights. it is not at all a question of acting through impositions or patronizing. we are not in a position to give anyone too many lessons, but we are obliged to maintain consistency in our external action and to favour relations with those countries which are making progress, avoiding imbalances and tailor-made recipes which undermine our credibility. the report i am presenting to this house today calls for action at three levels: more coherence in the conduct of dialogues and consultations, which will require greater coordination between the council - which i miss in this debate - the commission and parliament, using some mechanism to facilitate fluid communication and to avoid contradictions between the various community institutions. it is a question of speaking the truth with one clear voice. the commission is also proposing to make the dialogue and consultations transparent, which should be a principle and not an exception in the field of human rights. the flexibility and pragmatism needed to achieve concrete results must not be matched by an opacity in the agenda, objectives or outcome of the dialogue. we call for a strengthening of the role of the european parliament, which, ladies and gentlemen, is largely absent from the management of this instrument, without there being any legal or formal justification for this. the european parliament is prepared to act responsibly in the area of its external competence. the european parliament has established itself as the leading european institution in the field of human rights, placing them at the centre of its attention, and is determined to use all the means at its disposal to assert its role as the political guarantor of the union's external action. the european parliament calls on the commission and the council to listen to and implement the recommendations contained in this report, which has been widely endorsed by all the political groups in this house. the voice of parliament, ladies and gentlemen, must be heard. we know that what we are asking for will require a great deal of effort and we therefore consider the need to increase the resources devoted to the human rights units, both in the commission and in the council, the latter being absent from this debate. however, this is the minimum required of a european union which intends to defend before the world that human rights are an indispensable european value. if we want to be credible, we have to work together in this direction.

the rapporteur. - madam president, let me say first of all that today a spanish fishing vessel sank off the coast of andalusia, killing three people and leaving five missing. i ask this parliament to join in the grief of the families and the desire for the rescue of the missing seamen. and with that, i move on to the report we are dealing with today. the first thing i would like to stress, as the commission itself acknowledges and as this parliament has expressed on numerous occasions, is the utter failure of the community fisheries management system which, throughout its many years of existence, has neither ensured the sustainability of resources nor supported an efficient and profitable fisheries sector. paradoxically, the management system is the only one that has not been fully involved in the great reform of 2002, and therefore the commission has to patch up here and there, tackling unsustainable discards, inventing control measures and introducing recovery plans every day, but without addressing the substance of the matter: the definition of a coherent and updated framework for the fisheries management model. in this context, the commission's communication opts for maximum sustainable yield as a benchmark for long-term fishing, a theoretical model that seeks to combine the most efficient exploitation of a species, while ensuring biological sustainability. the problem is that the maximum sustainable yield - which as an intellectual and theoretical concept may be beyond reproach - has revealed many contradictions in its practical application and, in fact, is now widely considered obsolete by much of the scientific community. the question would therefore be to redefine the model in such a way as to adapt it to the reality of community fisheries. and here we have a series of questions about how to do that, which the report we are presenting today has tried to highlight and which are not answered in any way by the commission's communication, which is very ambiguous and very vague. it is clear that we are not criticizing the commission's intention here to impose a new management model but its inability to explain to us how it will overcome the difficulties of putting it into practice and of overcoming the pitfalls that the very maximum sustainable yield contains in its very formulation. among them, we know that maximum sustainable yield requires long series of reliable and accurate scientific data, whereas for the vast majority of species, such a degree of certainty is not possible. on the other hand, the model was created on the basis of exploitation of a single stock, whereas the vast majority of community fisheries are multi-specific, which means that many of them are overexploited or under-exploited, which is clearly contrary to the very definition of maximum sustainable yield. it is also not good for pelagic species, and we also know today that the state of populations is influenced by other factors, such as recruitment failures or environmental factors, which can lead to erroneous definitions of maximum sustainable yield. what is certain is that strict application of the maximum sustainable yield will in the short term result in a reduction, sometimes drastic, of fishing opportunities and therefore of the activity, income and employment of the community fleet. madam president, allow me to thank all my colleagues for their contributions and to ask for the adoption of a report in which the committee on fisheries would ask the european commission to first clear up all these uncertainties before introducing a military version of a model whose effectiveness for many fisheries is scientifically and economically in question to some species of great economic importance; to first seriously tackle a clear fisheries management system with an ecosystem approach, and then decide on the adaptation of the reference points and the model chosen, whether based on the msy or another, and not without first - i insist on this - accompanying it with a socioeconomic analysis of the repercussions of its implementation and the measures to counteract its impact, all of which are issues of great concern to our sectors and to us ourselves right now.

acting president of the council. we believe that the association agreement between the european union and mercosur must be comprehensive in all its aspects, that is, political, economic and cooperation, and aim not only at promoting trade and investment but also at strengthening in a decisive way the strategic relationship between the european union and that region. this agreement will create the largest free trade area between two regional blocs, with a population of about 700 million, strengthening economic and social integration, facilitating investment and providing significant economic growth for both regions. the results of the doha agenda negotiations have certainly shaped the negotiating process. however, we cannot look at the association agreement from an economic perspective alone, and it is necessary to stress the importance of its political dimension. the balance between the political and economic components is essential if we are to achieve the qualitative leap forward we all want in the relationship between the european union and mercosur. it is inevitable, however, that after seven years of negotiations we are at an impasse. this deadlock is the result of a discrepancy or difference between the bids submitted. on the one hand, the european union's policy covers all sectors, and on the other, mercosur's policy omits sectors which are of great importance to the european union. the portuguese presidency hopes that the political commitment shown by mercosur will translate into an improved offer so as to enable the commission to resume negotiations with a view to a rapid conclusion of an agreement which is fair and balanced for both parties. the strategic partnership between the european union and brazil, which was established at the lisbon summit on 4 july, should be seen not only as a means of strengthening relations with brazil but also as a way of promoting the bi-regional strategic relationship between the european union and latin america and, in particular, the european union's negotiations with mercosur. the joint declaration resulting from this summit with brazil clearly demonstrates the commitment to the conclusion of the negotiations on the eu-mercosur association agreement. with regard to brazil in particular, and in view of the country's growing strategic importance on the international scene, this partnership, established under the portuguese presidency, marked the beginning of a new relationship between the european union and brazil, similar to the one already existing with russia, india and china. the partnership will be developed on the basis of an action plan which will include the strengthening of dialogue and cooperation in the areas of mutual interest set out in the commission's communication to the council on the eu-brazil strategic partnership, which of course includes the mercosur agenda.
member of the commission. madam president, i am grateful for the opportunity to discuss this very important topic. as has rightly been pointed out, the decision to establish a strategic partnership with brazil goes back to the commission’s first communication on brazil, where we proposed a way forward in our relations with brazil, and the first eu-brazil summit in lisbon has confirmed and cemented this new relationship. why a closer relationship with brazil? the eu-brazil strategic partnership is a natural reaction to geopolitical realities. today, brazil is becoming an international player with a strong weight on important global issues like climate change, the fight against poverty, peace, security and multilateralism. it is a respected voice in the developing world, as shown by its chairmanship of the g20 within the wto or as an active promoter of the south-south dialogue. it has forged new partnerships with all key players: china, russia and the united states. the european union has a lot to gain from a closer partnership with brazil in order to progress on global issues of common concern. the strategic partnership provides the appropriate framework, as experience has shown with all other members of the brics group. what effects will this partnership have on latin america and, more specifically, on the mercosur region? the promotion of regional integration is one of the cornerstones of the partnership. this is clearly stated in the commission’s communication, and it is also how brazil perceives it. president lula made this point very strongly at the first eu-brazil summit in july. i cannot stress enough the importance of the southern cone for the european union. besides sharing cultural and political values like democracy, human rights and social justice, there is a huge economic potential to explore between the two economically complementary regions. the eu is mercosur’s number one trade and investment partner. we have goods and services worth eur 50 billion crossing the ocean annually. in addition, the aggregate value of eu investments in the mercosur countries in 2005 was around eur 100 billion. also, and most importantly, we genuinely believe in the potential of an economically and politically integrated mercosur. the recent creation of the structural convergence fund and mercosur parliament are most encouraging signals. the eu is a firm supporter of this integration process, not just in words but also in concrete deeds. the european union has been and will continue to be the quasi-exclusive donor to mercosur integration. a sum of eur 50 million has been committed over the last five years and the same amount is available for the current financial perspective (2007-2013) to help build mercosur’s institutions, strengthen civil society and take economic integration forward. the conclusion of the eu-mercosur association agreement would be a colossal step forward in the integration process of the region. that is why the european union remains firmly committed to concluding the negotiations and is keen to advance in negotiations once there is more clarity in the doha development round. the strategic partnership with brazil is a decision in favour of brazil and in favour of mercosur. the two levels of relations – national and regional – will complement and mutually support each other. in no way does the partnership replace the biregional eu-mercosur negotiations. we are in full agreement with brazil that mercosur is and will remain the only platform for our bilateral economic and trade relations. i am convinced that by engaging with brazil, mercosur’s largest member, we can bring a real added value to the regional integration process. shared experience in a joint agenda with the eu will encourage brazil to better support mercosur efforts to build a common market and a political union.
