the rapporteur. madam president, mr vice-president of the commission, mr president-in-office of the council, mrs gruber, ladies and gentlemen, in the era of globalisation, to imagine the future of europe and our societies without immigration is to be out of touch with reality. immigration is both necessary and positive for the demographic stability, economic growth and cultural diversity of the union. now, we need legal immigration of workers with rights and obligations, not slaves. the development and success of a legal immigration policy depends to a large extent on a firm fight against the other side of the coin, illegal immigration. the management and control of these illegal migration flows exceeds the capacity of individual member states to act and is undoubtedly the most delicate dimension of the overall and common immigration policy to be developed by the european union. recent economic and social imbalances, international conflicts and climate change will increase the flows of illegal migrants into the european union. they are faster than our political response and they will not stop on their own. we have to act now. we welcome and share the commission's approach. its role is essential in the development of a more coherent and effective policy by the member states based on full respect for human dignity and fundamental rights, based on solidarity, shared responsibility, transparency and mutual trust. first, we must achieve secure land, sea and air borders through integrated control and surveillance. in this sense, frontex and rabit are the way forward. the path of solidarity and shared responsibility. ladies and gentlemen, frontex is working. where he has carried out operations, lives have been saved and illegal immigration has decreased substantially. the flows of smugglers have had to find other routes, as has recently been the case in spain and italy. frontex is a newborn child of the union, which can only grow and fulfil its role with the support of its parents, the member states, who we ask to fulfil their commitments by making available the necessary human and logistical resources. it is also imperative to establish a european return policy, fully respecting human rights, as one of the deterrents and to promote the conclusion of readmission agreements with third countries. we are calling for the adoption of the return directive during the portuguese presidency. ladies and gentlemen, we need political will and courage to tackle the biggest attraction of illegal immigration: illegal employment. we must beat the mafia and the unscrupulous businessmen who exploit illegal immigrants. there are huge amounts of money and hidden interests at play that demand forceful and energetic action. we must, as you have said, mr vice-president, apply zero tolerance to irregular employment in order to reduce the underground economy that causes the so-called effect. the psychological dimension is obvious. if there are no opportunities to work illegally in the union, the incentive to emigrate to the union is reduced. we also call on the member states to take decisive and adequately resourced action against trafficking in human beings through judicial and police cooperation and to pay particular attention to the most vulnerable people - women and children - and to facilitate their access to health and education. external action requires dialogue and close cooperation with countries of origin and transit. we must continue the path we have opened up at the rabat and tripoli ministerial conferences and at the brussels world forum, emphasizing the link between immigration and development. we must make immigration a factor of development for both the countries of origin and the countries of destination, and through co-development we must jointly tackle the root causes of illegal immigration. it is also necessary to maximise the positive impact of remittances from migrants on the development of their respective countries and to explore the use of micro-credit. we must also ensure a coherent foreign policy that ensures that trade and development aid objectives are compatible so that the least developed countries can export their products and do not have to export their citizens. ladies and gentlemen, i would not like to conclude my speech without expressing my gratitude to all the rapporteurs with whom i have had close and positive cooperation, as reflected in the high level of consensus reached in the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs. ladies and gentlemen, let us not make a mistake, we must fight illegal immigration, tackle its causes and its channels, but we must not fight illegal immigrants, they are not criminals; emigration is not a crime. let's take a look at the populist and xenophobic rhetoric that associates immigration with insecurity, crime, terrorism or unemployment. he never emigrates on a whim, always by obligation. let's make it a personal choice instead of an obligation. what is the appropriate response to this situation? it is right to think that either the situation has the air of déjà vu, heralding a repetition of the violent repression of 1988, or that this is a historic turning point. however, events in myanmar/burma seem to be heading towards unpredictable developments. the fact that protests of such a scale - 100,000 demonstrators on the streets of rangoon crisis. it is also necessary to encourage asean to make its voice heard more strongly. any deterioration of the situation in myanmar/burma can only have negative consequences for the whole region. acting president of the council. thank you very much. mr president, mr president-in-office, i would like to thank the honourable member on behalf of the council for his question on the question of the bluefin tuna recovery plan. that plan was drawn up in accordance with the advice of iccat scientists, who recommended that immediate and strong action be taken to prevent the current collapse of bluefin tuna stocks in the mediterranean and eastern atlantic. the iccat adopted the recommendation for the adoption of a 15-year recovery plan at its annual meeting in dubrovnik in november 2006, and the european community, as a member of icat, assumed the international obligation to transpose that recovery plan into community law. in commercial terms, the consequences of failure to comply fully with this obligation would be serious for the position of the european community on asian markets. this obligation was fulfilled for 2007 by the adoption of council regulation (ec) no 643/2007 amending the regulation on tacs and quotas. the council, on the basis of a commission proposal, is currently examining the necessary regulations to allow the plan to be applied on a permanent basis for a further 14 years from 1 january 2008. the rules apply to the various zones in different ways, in order to reflect the respective differences in fisheries types, activity levels and stock situation. it should be noted that these fisheries vary between high-tech industrial fishing and traditional non-industrial fishing. the iccat teams have determined the plan on the basis of scientific advice which draws certain distinctions between the mediterranean and the eastern atlantic. the council is therefore of the opinion that iccat has sought to follow this scientific development while differentiating the elements of the recovery plan to mitigate its socio-economic consequences. the council is fully aware that this important recovery plan has socioeconomic consequences for the fishing communities concerned. these consequences would also be felt in the event of a further collapse of bluefin tuna stocks. during the negotiations leading to the adoption of council regulation (ec) no 643/2007, the council and the commission agreed to introduce a provision for the recovery plan to be recognised as such by the european fisheries fund, which will allow member states to use part of their resources from the fund to help mitigate the economic consequences on the affected fishing communities. this provision is intended to remain in force until 31 december 2014.

vice-president of the commission. mr president, thank you for this interesting debate. you always learn a lot of new things and i can, of course, promise that i will report back to the commission. i have taken careful notes so that we can follow up also at the meeting that will take place in luxembourg next monday. i have heard three direct questions that i would like to respond to as well as i can. the first one alludes to parliament’s involvement in the procedure of appointing the first high representative. the treaty here reproduces the 2004 text. i am sure that everybody will want to find a pragmatic political solution that can satisfy all sides when this moment comes. you may remember, of course, the precedent of commissioners appointed after recent enlargements. there, too, parliament got satisfaction in practice, although the legal texts were not clear. i think it is in our interest to make sure that there is a satisfactory role for parliament in this whole procedure. the second question had to do with article 24 of the treaty, on protection of personal data in the field of security. here, at least, i can respond for the commission, which understands parliament’s concerns on provisions relating to the transmission of confidential data by the member states. as it stands now, article 24 of the eu treaty allows the council alone to define the rules in this field, with no possibility of involvement of the european parliament. this new provision, of course, stems from the igc mandate. it applies to member states only, whilst the european institutions remain subject to the general regime, and the foreseen procedure complies with the very specific regime that exists on the common foreign and security policy. here, it means that the competence of the court is restricted. i am afraid that there is little margin to change the substance agreed in the mandate, but, in any event, i want to reassure you that we do not read this article as covering, for example, the eu agreement with the united states on passenger name records. that agreement currently has a third-pillar legal base and, therefore, in the commission’s view, it will therefore be covered by the normal competence of the ep and the court in the future. so this is how the commission sees those issues. i am seated so that i can actually watch all our visitors. i am not sure that we can always explain very clearly what we are discussing here, but i am sure that the visitors have felt the type of frustration that comes from this debate and the fact that some are very happy with this, they say it is a good compromise; others are not pleased at all and say that this is not good enough; others say that we are going too far. of course, it reflects the political situation and the difficult political game that comes after a long period of actually having discussed how we can adapt our decision-making procedures to enlarge the european union of 27 member states; how we can actually incorporate also the new issues that have emerged lately, like climate change and energy; how we can be more open and effective. all the visitors also remind me that, whatever the outcome – and we think and hope, with the help of the portuguese presidency, that we will have a good outcome, that we will be able to agree a new reform treaty – we will have to communicate; we will have to engage with citizens to try to do our best to explain. i hope that the commission and the european parliament will be able to plan also the communication activities together by making sure that we also provide a text which is as accessible and readable as possible; that we can create a debate which is european, so that you can, hopefully, follow the debate in other member states as well – and with a political commitment from all of us, all the institutions, to engage with citizens: to explain, to advocate and also to listen. this is our role from now on. this is only the beginning. we also have the ratification and the implementation awaiting us. but, for me and the commission, we believe that this is a good reform treaty – not a perfect one: it is, of course, a compromise; we would have wanted no opt-outs but really good support for what is in there on the charter of fundamental rights especially, but we have a compromise, we have an agreement between all the member states – and now we will make the best of it. the rapporteur. - madam president, although the murder of women is a global problem, there are areas of the world which have become, both because of the scale and complexity of the phenomenon, paradigmatic cases. such places are also, much to their chagrin, mirrors reflecting many of the ills that affect, to a greater or lesser extent, societies where social patterns based on a patriarchal culture prevail. this is the case, for example, in mexico and the countries of central america. in fact, it is precisely in mexico that the concept of femicide is beginning to take shape, especially when - and i quote - 'the special commission to investigate and prosecute cases of femicide in the mexican republic, chaired by congresswoman marcela lagarde, established that this concept referred to the whole of crimes against humanity which include the murders, kidnappings and disappearances of girls and women in a context of institutional collapse'. this is, in short, a breakdown of the rule of law which favours impunity. although the concept is in full evolution, there are those who defend the use of the term "feminicide" to oppose it to "homicide". i'd like to ask for a little silence in the courtroom. president. - thank you, madam president, i will continue. i said that although the concept is a concept that is in continuous evolution, in fact there are those who raise the need to speak of femicide to oppose it to homicide, it is relevant that what it reveals is the existence of the most worrying phenomena of our days: the murder of women for the simple fact of being women. the european parliament has been working hard on this issue for the past two years, and it will have an important turning point when the plenary adopts tomorrow, 11 october, the report on the deaths of women in mexico and central america and on the role of the european union in combating this phenomenon. the report is the result of a long and intensive process of dialogue with all the sectors involved and of numerous commitments between the political groups. i would like to take this opportunity to thank all the speakers in the shadow for their support and to inform them that we are joined in the chamber by marjo searle and arsène van nierop, the mothers of brenda and hester, who were both killed in mexico. the adoption of this report will put the european parliament in line with other institutions which have already spoken out on the subject. this is the case with the council of europe or the united nations, as well as various parliaments and governments around the world. and, by its content, it will mean considerable progress, both in defining the problem and in the assumption of responsibility by various actors in the fight to eradicate it. one of the principles of the report is precisely to recognize, as the starting point for all analysis, the multiplicity of causes and types of crime of this kind. it is true, for example, that the highly publicized case of ciudad juárez - more than 400 women murdered since 1993 - has a lot to do with the fact that it is a border town with problems typical of this type of area. however, there are also many other factors which require a concerted effort and integrated public policies. these policies include: prevention; investing in equality education and reversing the culture of patriarchy; improving forensic data collection and investigation; facilitating and speeding up the filing of complaints; training police, judges, prosecutors and doctors in this type of crime; monitoring local and multinational companies operating in the area, many of which subject women workers to conditions of enormous vulnerability; legislative reforms and transposition of rules to the relevant levels; and, finally, placing special emphasis on accompanying and supporting victims and their families. in relation to this last point, however, i would like to denounce and deeply regret that, on numerous occasions, the victims are belittled and even criminalized; and their families are persecuted, accused even of damaging the good image of a city or a country, simply because they want to make the problem visible and because they want to demand - and demand - justice. it is clear that the main and most important responsibility for implementing all the measures proposed is the governmental institutions of the countries directly concerned, and in this case it is obvious that it is mexico and the countries of central america. however, given that the european union has an association agreement with the former - an agreement which also includes a democratic clause and respect for human rights - and that a similar agreement is also being negotiated with the central american region, i believe that it is more than justified for the european institutions to take a stand and make concrete commitments in the face of this problem. no one should see this as an intervention by the european union in the internal affairs of another country, especially when, even if we acknowledge that important progress has been made - the commission's proposal for this report was based on a twofold legal basis: article 37 (2) on agricultural policy and article 152 (4) (b) on health protection. the committee on legal affairs has studied these proposals. there was a proposal, for example, from the committee responsible for the subject-matter, which proposed deleting rule 37 (2) and adding rule 175 (1) in addition, deleting rule 37 (2), keeping rule 152 (b) and adding rule 175 (1). the key to the legal basis is that the discussion should be in accordance with the object and content, and the committee on legal affairs, unanimously, considers that the applicable article is article 152 (4) (b), without any need to refer to article 175 (1). we think that this is perfectly clear and that neither the double legal basis proposed by the commission nor the double legal basis proposed by the committee responsible for the subject matter is necessary, but a simple reference to article 152 (4) (b) since the purpose of this proposal for a directive is the protection of human health.
madam president, commissioners, the proposal for a regulation which the european commission has drawn up to replace directive 91/414/ec achieves greater harmonisation of the authorisation procedures and at the same time ensures consumer protection. however, the result achieved in the committee on the environment not only fails to take account of this objective of greater harmonization, but unjustifiably radicalizes the measures to protect the consumer and the environment. the report starts from a total distrust of the agricultural production methods that already exist in the european union. but it is not just the farmer who will be affected: the consumer will be too, because many crops will become unviable and this will lead to imports, with a consequent reduction in food security. it has not been sufficiently assessed that the approval and use of plant protection products are already subject to strict controls both by the european food safety authority and by the competent authorities of the member states. in addition, this proposal increases the number of active substances from 1 100 authorized in 1991 to 148 which are included in annex i to this proposal. of these 148, only 34 are insecticides, nematicides or acaricides, which are the most necessary to be able to grow in mediterranean europe, where the level of insect attack is the highest in the whole union. insects not only cause pests on plants, they also transmit very serious diseases to humans. the commission's proposal to divide the european union into three zones for the mutual recognition of plant protection products must be reinstated. the exclusion criteria for pesticides should be established on the basis of genuine risk analyses. without a risk analysis it is impossible to know the impact of these substances on health or the environment. finally, i want to remind you that the poison is in the dose.

opinion of the committee on budgetary control. mr president, madam commissioner, the committee on budgetary control has focused its opinion for the 2008 budget on two key issues:the first is compliance with article 44 of the new interinstitutional agreement as regards the statement of assurance and the annual certification to be sent by each member state. we are here, with this amendment, to take up the conclusions and recommendations of the discharge for 2004 and 2005, which have already been implemented by a minority of member states, which we believe should be increasing. we know that the european commission cannot assess the extent to which the member states have complied with this commitment until 15 february. however, and perhaps to encourage the european commission to pursue this assessment without wasting time, we have introduced a reserve in the commission's staff costs. we are sure that the commission has as much interest as parliament in ensuring that the member states fully apply this article 44 in the field of shared management. so i'm sure we can come to an agreement on the reservation. the second axis is that of transparency. we believe that the more detailed the budget expenditure is, the easier it will be for the budgetary authority to monitor its implementation. that is why we have asked for the creation of new budget lines for sensitive matters, for categories of expenditure which are very sensitive to parliament, such as agencies, rural development or other categories, such as external action, seeking, i repeat, a very clear commitment from this parliament, from the committee on budgetary control, which was to contribute to maximum transparency, which is what public opinion demands of us.

vice-president of the commission. the commission fully agrees on the importance of combating the disappearance and abduction of minors. enhancing children’s rights, as you all know very well, is one of my personal priorities. the first action undertaken by the european commission in relation to this was to support, in 2001, the creation of a european network of organisations, the european federation on missing and sexually exploited children, which is now called missing children europe. to date, we have 21 organisations in 15 member states. then, with the financial backing of our community programme, the daphne programme, several centres were created or revamped from 2001 to 2005, with the aid of child focus. several member states have, over the last 10 years, set up emergency call lines in order to speed up searches and support families of missing children. cases of missing children and abduction can quickly become, and still become, cross-border phenomena. we therefore propose to have a single telephone number for urgent calls about missing children. to that end, the decision of 15 february 2007 on reserving the national numbering range beginning with ‘116’ for harmonised numbers for harmonised services of social value will be implemented. this is an important decision by each member state, particularly in relation to the 116000 number for hotlines to report missing children. you know that putting in place the services corresponding to a 116 number remains the responsibility of member states. there, unfortunately, i have to say that three member states have not yet responded. legal measures have been taken by 17 member states. there have been calls for candidates for the management of the hotline numbers in 12 member states, and only four member states have so far chosen service providers: belgium, denmark, greece and portugal. so i am not at all satisfied at the state of play in implementation of the decision taken in february 2007. in addition to these emergency phone numbers, a mechanism of assistance in the search for missing children is necessary. several systems already exist and can serve as an inspiration for a europe-wide action. you know about the american system, ‘amber alert’, the french ‘alerte enlèvement’ and the greek ‘amber alert hellas’ system, which are already in place. we support member states in putting similar mechanisms in place nationally. provided that all member states adopt such mechanisms and that interconnection schemes are put in place, resolving cross-border cases would be possible and easier. to that end, we have drafted guidelines describing our idea for a europe-wide child alert mechanism. the issue was discussed for the first time at the informal justice and home affairs council on 1 october 2007. finally, we support the creation of an international database of child abuse images, which will be a new tool to help identify victims and criminals. the feasibility study and implementation phase are funded by the agis programme and, since september 2005, this database used by interpol is funded mainly by g8 governments and private companies. so far this database has made it possible to locate and arrest several criminals in europe and outside europe, most recently a very well-known paedophile in thailand, and save victims.

member of the commission. mr president, i would like to thank mr mantovani and i would like to express the commission’s thanks to him and to the responsible committees for their proactive engagement and supportive stance throughout the negotiations on the european qualifications framework (eqf) for lifelong learning. this recommendation goes to the heart of what the eu is about: mobility, cooperation between countries, promoting prosperity and helping individual citizens. we propose the eqf because you, the european parliament, and the member states asked us to find ways of promoting mobility and lifelong learning, without which we cannot achieve the lisbon goals. the eqf has been developed within the education and training 2010 work programme, the education dimension of the lisbon agenda. the eqf seeks to overcome the barriers that remain to european workers and learners when they wish to change jobs or move to another country for work or for study. too often, europeans have difficulty in using their qualifications in another european country. even in their own country they find their educational pathways blocked by poor integration of the different parts of their national education system. the eqf will relate the countries’ different national qualification systems to each other, acting as a translation device. it will thus make other countries’ qualifications more readable and so enable individuals to move to another country if they wish to work or study. at the national level it will – indeed it is already doing this – stimulate the development of national qualifications frameworks. qualifications frameworks promote lifelong learning by, for example, making it easier for people to move between different types of education and training institutions, for example from vocational training to higher education. i should acknowledge that the eqf is a technical, even complex instrument. it will be used mainly by experts and educational authorities, but it is for the benefit of the citizen. what we are debating today is the product of a collective endeavour between the commission, countries, social partners, education and training associations and other stakeholders. the eqf has very much been built on a consensus and we have sought to carry stakeholders with us throughout the process. the eqf recommends that countries relate their qualification systems to the eqf by 2010 and ensure that individual national qualifications carry a reference to the appropriate eqf level by 2012. these dates were proposed by the council and parliament. we have also been happy to agree to the insertion of a new recommendation on quality assurance proposed by parliament, which we feel reinforces the importance of these principles. we also agree to parliament’s proposal to include a reference to credit systems which recognises the rapid development and application of these components of qualifications frameworks. we believe that parliament and the council have indeed improved the text. the approach adopted in the negotiations by the parliament, council and commission reflects the consensus behind the eqf across europe. there is now a momentum behind the eqf; the great majority of countries recognise its potential for mobility and as a lifelong learning instrument. a large majority are now developing a national qualifications framework related to the eqf, so this proposal is already having a major impact on europe’s education and training systems. i hope you can agree to support this proposal at first reading so that it can formally be adopted by the council in the coming weeks.
the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. i would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteur, mr president, mr commissioner, because he has really tackled a subject which goes far beyond what we can think of. in a globalised world, europe and the individual countries of the european union will be whatever the qualifications of their human resources are. if we were to sum up in one pillar what is going to enable europe to be competitive in this global world, and each of the countries that make up it, it is the qualification that the human resources, the european citizens, have. in this sense, it is absolutely essential that lifelong learning and lifelong learning be training adapted to the demands of the labour market and that these demands are constantly met. otherwise, it will be impossible to compete. we are also faced with the following paradox: people are getting older, but they are getting older and younger and potentially more active, and instead they have resources that are very insufficient to be able to continue to give back and to give to society, and to realize themselves in the world of work. in this sense, the first aspect is that lifelong learning, based primarily on a technological dimension, which is what brings added value, is a fundamental concern. but there is a second point, which concerns the future of europe, and that is the integration of these human resources into a competitive internal market, for which we need these certificates recognized by all the states, which will allow citizens of some countries to compete with others, on the basis of training recognized by all. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the use of cluster munitions. its use, in the summer of 2006, in the lebanon war, showed us the extent to which it could cause a humanitarian catastrophe. these are weapons that threaten civilians and military personnel, but in practice, 90 per cent of their victims are civilians, and 10 per cent of these deadly bombs do not explode, they remain in the ground and have an effect similar to that of landmines. therefore, cleaning up land contaminated by these munitions is dangerous, both for the populations and for international peacekeeping forces. these bombs are not only used in war, they are also a long-term obstacle to transport, agriculture, trade barriers and obstacles to humanitarian aid. so they are one of the main problems that stand in the way of the development of poor countries. because it is the poorest countries that are most affected by these bombs, and within them, the main victims are the poorest and least educated populations. we cannot say that peace-keeping or military intervention is no longer done efficiently by bombing the enemy from 10,000 metres above, by dropping bombs on the ground as if they were shower water. the deployment of peacekeepers and humanitarian aid are now essential to stabilize and rebuild the areas affected by the conflict and these bombs are now completely unjustified, even from a military point of view. today we are going to talk to the commission and the council precisely about the initiatives that have emerged in this general change of attitude of the international community towards cluster bombs. the european parliament has repeatedly taken a very clear position: we want to see a global international regulation prohibiting the use, production, transfer, financing and storage of cluster bombs. until we achieve this, the member states of the union should take unilateral action to prohibit the use and transfer of these bombs, as some states have already done and others are preparing to do. the european parliament, madam commissioner, mr minister, would like to thank the efforts of the presidency of the council, the commission and the member states to negotiate a new protocol to the united nations convention on certain conventional weapons, which addresses all the humanitarian problems associated with the use of cluster bombs. but unfortunately, we have to admit that, to date, there has not been much progress. that is why we need a solid oslo process, around which states, ngos, the red cross, international bodies, define and implement an ambitious agenda. so far, oslo has been supported by 80 states, including many developing countries, but it is not at all clear that this process will finally lead to an outright ban on cluster bombs. what is clear is that we need an integrated and comprehensive approach that is humanitarian in nature and that does not just talk about disarmament, that its main objective should be the protection of civilians, helping them to cope with the consequences of war, establishing the destruction of existing stockpiles of those bombs and the cleaning up of contaminated areas. in a context where important events are about to take place, such as the meeting in vienna in december, or in brussels next week, or on 5 november, world day against cluster bombs, acting president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to say on this question that, as you know, the current european union solidarity fund was set up to respond to the major disasters of extraordinary proportions caused by the floods that struck central europe in the summer of 2002. in 2002, following a proposal from the european commission, the council adopted a regulation establishing the european union solidarity fund. article 14 of the regulation, known as the 'solidarity fund', provides that the council, on a proposal from the commission, is to review the regulation by 31 december 2006 at the latest. in 2005, the commission proposed that regulation 2012/2002 be replaced by a new regulation on the solidarity fund. the new proposal would, inter alia, extend the scope of the instrument to cover industrial and technological disasters, public health emergencies and acts of terrorism and reduce the thresholds used to classify a disaster as major. the exceptional regional criteria of the existing regulation would disappear, but in exceptional circumstances the commission could recognise that a major disaster has occurred. the european parliament delivered an opinion on this in may 2006 and, in 2006, the council discussed the commission proposal and parliament's opinion at the appropriate levels, although it did not reach agreement. in this context, regulation 2012/2002 continues to apply, and the commission has already proposed its mobilisation during 2007. as i had the opportunity to say here last month on a similar question, as far as the council is aware, in the case of disasters provided for in the regulation, its application has been effective. the european commission regularly produces reports detailing the operation of the solidarity fund.
the council's proposal has been perfectly clear. we are very far behind in this new regulation. the supplementary and specific question i put to the council is this: this summer we almost burned down the cradle of western civilization, which is classical greece, including the olympic stadiums. is the council waiting for the vatican to burn, for the prado palace to burn, for the palace of belém to burn, or can we hope that before next summer we will have a regulation that can deal with this kind of catastrophe?

member of the commission. madam president, first of all i would like to thank the european parliament and in particular the rapporteurs, mrs gutiérrez-cortines and mr prodi, the committee on the environment, public health and food safety and the other committees for their contribution to the first reading. the commission's proposal for a thematic soil protection strategy is the result of work begun in 1998 at the initiative of the german ministry of the environment. the results of long consultations with stakeholders and member states were to recognise that land is a valuable natural resource and that its degradation in europe is becoming a problem. since then, the commission has worked with stakeholders, in particular the parliament and the council, to understand and reach a consensus on soil protection issues. the parliament's resolution on the 2002 soil communication gave the commission important guidance on the direction to take in achieving soil protection in europe. in the conclusions adopted in mallorca in 2002, the european council asked the commission to propose a comprehensive and far-reaching approach to soil protection, including general principles, appropriate quantitative and qualitative targets and timetables for measuring and evaluating the measures envisaged. i should now like to address a number of specific points. i am very pleased that it is recognised that land degradation is a very serious problem that needs to be tackled. given the keen interest of this parliament, for example, in desertification, it is important to show that here in europe we are reaffirming our commitment to tackling the factors that create this problem at home as well as internationally. climate change and some improper land management practices are putting our lands at risk. the identification of the extent of degradation and the subsequent development of methods to ensure sustainable land use are direct applications of the knowledge-based approach which parliament rightly considers valuable. it is also a guarantee of greater focus of effort and more efficient use of resources to serve our priorities. businesses are entitled to expect member states to apply community legislation consistently. the commission's environmental impact assessment estimates that there are some 3.5 million sites in the european union that are likely to have been contaminated. of these, a percentage, perhaps 15%, are actually contaminated. it is therefore important that undertakings have confidence that similar approaches to the identification of contaminated sites will be adopted so that they can plan their investments. we also have to take into account that there is a direct link between climate change and soil. for example, according to recent research published in the prestigious international scientific journal nature, in the last 25 years in the united kingdom alone, the soil has released 13 million tons of carbon dioxide into the atmosphere each year, an amount equivalent to adding 5 million cars each year. moreover, the capacity of soil to absorb carbon and convert it into useful soil organic matter has not yet been fully exploited. in this context, let me sum up the main objectives of the action of measures proposed by the commission: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the policy, by creating a framework for sustainable land use and by taking measures at source, will prevent further degradation of land and preserve its vital social, environmental and economic functions. secondly, to gather the necessary information on the state of the soil in europe to enable us to make informed policy decisions and to focus efforts where the most serious degradation has occurred. thirdly, to restore degraded land wherever possible, on the basis of an analysis of the state of the soil to be carried out by the member states. restoration shall aim at achieving a quality level of land at least consistent with its current and intended use. fourthly, to establish minimum common rules for the whole of the european union in order to ensure a coherent approach between the member states in terms of soil protection. the common rules will bring transparency and avoid distortion of the internal market. the strategy and the directive aim to launch a long-term policy for soil protection in europe so that within a few years all member states have made significant progress in this field. i would like to draw your attention to some key aspects of the framework directive on soil protection: first, the text resulting from the codecision procedure must be clear and provide legal certainty to the parties affected by the legislative act. we should avoid introducing amendments which leave a legal vacuum, unnecessarily restricting the scope of the directive. secondly, the proposal already contains a high degree of subsidiarity and flexibility. i understand that some amendments are proposed to increase the degree of subsidiarity even further. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented in all member states. this applies in particular to amendments concerning the programmes of measures in the priority areas identified in the directive. thirdly, in order to achieve a high level of environmental protection, it is necessary to agree on a consistent approach to be followed by all member states in the identification of contaminated sites. the proposed deletion of annex 2 would prevent us from achieving our objective. in conclusion, i should like to state at this stage that the commission will follow developments in the debate on its proposal in the council and in the european parliament and will take its position accordingly.
the rapporteur. - madam president, before i speak about the proposal which will be put to the vote tomorrow, i would like to thank the rapporteurs from all the political groups and, in particular, i would like to thank maruja sornosa of the socialist group and our friend mr prodi, who have really worked hand in hand and enriched the directive, as have the green group and many other members. the document to be voted on tomorrow is a document with numerous amendments which have been the result of an agreement and have therefore been enriched by the contribution of other political parties. it is a document, for the most part, consensual. and this is not common in an environmental policy which is going to generate, shall we say, a new european policy and open up a new road. this document is extremely novel because it responds to a new approach to directives. we were faced with the problem that out of 27 countries, only nine had legislation for soil protection. and this is a subject that we're going to have to address in the future. europe has developed asymmetrically and at the moment there are many countries which have already done their doctorate and others who are doing their baccalaureate in the field of soil policy. how can we achieve a policy of agreement, a common policy, with such great differences? that is the challenge we have faced. what was the solution? we have looked at the treaty and we have seen that article 249, when defining directives, says that directives are common objectives and, instead, implementation and enforcement can be left to the member states. and that is what has been done. articles 1 and 2 have been strengthened, up to 6 have been strengthened to make it clear what the common objectives are. i mean, we have the goal in sight. we know what the goal should be to which we have to go. and we have to recognize that sustainability is a process that has to have clear goals. but not all countries can keep up with the pace. those who have not walked before cannot be asked to do the same as others. we therefore ask that implementation be left to the member states, with full respect for subsidiarity, and that the fear of some countries - those which have already been through this - that their bureaucracy will be repeated is thus eliminated. those countries which have clear soil protection do not have to do it again. this policy of flexibility also applies to the recognition that given the climate and conditions of each country, they must be allowed to agree with their citizens to carry out these policies. so, for example, in article 8 we guarantee that farmers can agree with their member states on soil conservation and those who have already done so do not have to repeat the legislation. now, this means that at the same time we must ensure that there is a clear policy on contaminated soils and in that sense the health of the citizens is above all and the objectives of preserving health and having transparency to inform the citizens, this is clear. and why do i think it is important that there is a directive in the face of criticism that does not call for this? because, ladies and gentlemen, we must build europe on our strengths, we must go after the countries that have done things right. and if we do not legislate, we enter into uncertainty and insecurity. and insecurity and uncertainty for the market and for health is a weakness. let us build europe around strengths, not weaknesses. that's the way we should go. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. and it is the responsibility of the member states to make it happen. and that is that freedom is responsibility. in a europe of 27 we must learn that environmental policy cannot be made by judicially enforcing it. we cannot rely on the prosecutors and the court of justice alone to enforce it. we must rely on common policy, on faith, on credibility and on the ability of countries to get on their feet and implement the best policies. that is why we have turned to good practice in large measure. another innovation in this directive is that it addresses climate change in relation to soil for the first time. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat the problem of soil erosion. and there is something else to consider: europe and its landscape are the result of man's work, they are the result of farmers as gardeners of the landscape. we must bear in mind that the europe of the future must be made by the citizens and, therefore, we must, i repeat, set common objectives, but help them to follow a path which also guarantees health and a commitment to transparency. thank you very much and again, thank you to the political parties.
the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. thank you, madam president, and also thank you to commissioner dimas for his resolute push for this directive. we welcome the commission's proposal, since it is certainly intended to protect the soil and preserve its capacity to continue to develop its environmental, economic, social and cultural functions, all of which are essential for human activity. the commission has also proposed, as the commissioner has rightly said, a flexible regulation, ambitious in its objectives and not overly prescriptive in its content. within a common framework, of a minimum common denominator, member states will define their own level of intervention, allowing for a more efficient use of administrative capacities at national level. despite the exaggerated resistance of some sectors to this directive, it is clear that soil is a vital, essentially non-renewable resource and that it is undergoing increasing environmental pressure in which human action has a significant responsibility. it is estimated from the reports discussed here that the cost of soil degradation amounts to approximately eur 40 billion per year, costs borne by society in the form of damage to infrastructure, increased health care costs and many other elements. this directive is, of course, based on the precautionary principle and preventive action, on the principle that environmental damage must be rectified at its source and that the polluter pays. this regulation will help to reduce the cross-border effects of soil degradation, which also exist, and will help to ensure a level playing field in the internal market. i would like to stress this point, because the different obligations which may be imposed on economic operators under the different national soil protection regimes may lead to distortions of competition. in conclusion, the soil protection directive is a step forward which will allow for more transparent competition and protect areas of common interest such as water, food safety and human health.

have specific community legislation, whereas land as a resource does not. it is time to redress this imbalance and i therefore thank the commission for the proposal and i thank the rapporteur, mrs gutiérrez-cortines, for the work she has done. soil, as many of us have said, is a non-renewable and therefore limited natural resource which fulfils many important ecological and economic functions and is the basis for virtually all human activities. the involvement of the european institutional regulatory system in this area will undoubtedly serve as an incentive to improve the legislation that is being implemented in many countries, by framing it in a coherent framework and supported by regulation and, possibly, resources of european origin. as regards the immovability of the soil, which acting president of the council. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the first euro-mediterranean ministerial meeting on migration will take place in santa eulália, in the algarve, portugal, on 18 and 19 november this year. put that way, it sounds like the most banal of advertisements, but it's not. we have managed to hold this high-level ministerial meeting and we have succeeded after this was set as a priority by our heads of state and government in november 2005, some two years ago, on the occasion of the 10th anniversary of the barcelona process summit, which recognised the growing importance of migration issues within our euro-mediterranean partnership. later, as you will remember, ladies and gentlemen, in rabat, in tripoli, we had the opportunity to reaffirm our common political agenda. we have done so in a realistic and lucid way, in the council's view. today, on both sides of the mediterranean, there are considerable immigrant communities who play a very important role in our societies. we have a duty to give a new impetus to the partnership which can take advantage of the existence of these strong communities. the complexity and significance of migration issues require the attention of all parties involved, both the countries of origin, transit and destination, and at this first meeting in the algarve, the council believes that the debate should focus on the most pressing issues and only those, in a step-by-step approach to the issues. the main items on the agenda will be in the priority areas agreed at the tampere ministerial, namely immigration and development, legal immigration and the fight against illegal immigration, and will include such important areas as the framework for the issue of migrant remittances, the new micro-credit challenge, the opportunities we are creating in the european union and on both sides of the mediterranean for legal immigration, the essential issue of document security just mentioned here by mr frattini, on another occasion, the security of travel documents is a crucial point for the safe development of migration flows and the very important issue of return conditions when it comes to this. i think that the preparatory work carried out over the last few weeks has led to a positive conclusion, which bodes well for the debate to be held in the algarve. there is a very clear determination on both sides to find positive solutions, to find concrete measures, to agree on these concrete measures and to implement them. the council therefore expresses its conviction before the european parliament that the meeting will be able to agree on concrete measures which will enable us to take our partnership forward. we hope that this effort will culminate in a final statement. this final declaration has a careful preparation process that will culminate in the algarve with its ministerial approval. this declaration will clearly define the main priorities and will also determine the concrete projects to be implemented in the short term. we therefore believe that this initiative is developing in a positive framework and will be, in itself, a mobilizing and significant moment in our euro-mediterranean relationship. that is the council's duty, and that is also the outcome we hope for, which is entirely within our reach.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, improving migration management in the mediterranean region will certainly be one of the priorities for the eu and its euromed partners. too many people are drowning, and we are not benefiting sufficiently from the potential that well-managed migration can bring. at the summit in 2005, which was just mentioned, the euromed heads of state and government adopted a work programme that set goals for cooperation on migration, social integration, justice and security. now, thanks to the excellent initiative taken by the portuguese presidency, ministers responsible for migration will have the opportunity to take the next steps in making the cooperation more concrete. it promises to be a big milestone. i welcome the presidency’s emphasis on concrete operational outcomes from the conference, because our citizens want to see very concrete results. the three themes for this meeting are well balanced and fully in line with the global approach. first of all, legal migration: we live in a world of increasing mobility, and well-managed migration is in the interests of all partners. the european union needs migration in full respect of the law. the need for workers in many member states of the eu is already evident, for example, in agriculture, health care and tourism. however, the european union needs to be able to manage and integrate these migrants. we need to match skills better than in the past and we have to prepare migrants for their life in the eu and their eventual return if their migration is temporary or circular in nature. no migratory strategy is possible unless a european policy towards integrating migrants who live and work in the eu is in full respect of the law. we will be discussing how to use the european integration fund that, for the first time, is available in the eu, thanks to a proposal made a year and a half ago by the commission and endorsed by the council and this parliament. we need to make europe more attractive to legal migrants. our recent proposal for a european ‘blue card’ for highly skilled migrants is the first example and relevant to the euromed context. next year’s legislative initiatives for unskilled and seasonal migrants and remunerated trainees will follow. the proposals to launch discussions on these matters with our euromed partners seem to me logical and timely. the second point is migration and development. in order to be successful in managing migration, we must also address the main roots of migration, such as economic disparity, lack of career opportunities, instability, poor governance etc. good cooperation with partner countries and detailed knowledge of the situation on the ground in terms of labour needs, skilled shortages and capacity-building requirements are essential to this effort. that is why ministers will discuss with the commission the concrete proposals on migrant remittances and how they could be made more productive for development – a debate that is to be welcomed. the third area of discussion is illegal migration, because to be comprehensive we must also tackle illegal migration and protect european external borders. our euromed partners are countries of destination, transit and origin. we should aim to establish cooperation to prevent people drowning at sea. at the euromed conference we will be talking with ministers about cooperation and a possible new role for frontex in search and rescue activities, not only in patrolling and the return of illegal migrants. in doing so, we need to ensure that we respect our obligations when it comes to international protection and human rights. we would support a development whereby frontex becomes a tool of support for third countries in their efforts to better manage migration and control their borders by fully respecting international obligations. we are looking forward to this ministerial meeting. migration is a subject of vital interest to us all, and that raises strong passions at member state and community level. it is no different in our partner countries. however, working together is the only way to move forward. i would say cooperation alone is no longer sufficient. we need partnership based on shared goals and on equality of all partners. we need political packages, including measures to improve both the movement of honest people and respect of national and european laws, and to increase local growth rates in the origin countries. finally, i believe that the ministers will be successful in identifying concrete areas for cooperation. the commission stands ready to support the implementation process, including in financial terms. we are committed to supporting such actions through the meda programme, as well as the european neighbourhood and partnership instrument and the new thematic programmes.

vice-president of the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your kind words. the evolution of the euro exchange rate naturally affects the relative price of european tourism products for consumers from third countries. although the euro exchange rate is not a political instrument but is freely formed on the foreign exchange market, the impact of the recent appreciation of the euro against the dollar on tourism should be considered in a differentiated way. firstly, fluctuations in the euro exchange rate have only a very small impact on tourist flows within the european union. according to available data, around 70% of the revenue generated by crossborder tourism in the european union is generated by tourists from other eu member states. secondly, we should not focus solely on the euro versus dollar exchange rate. calculations of the effective exchange rate of the euro show that the overall trend is much smoother. the appreciation against the chinese yuan, for example, was much lower this year. nevertheless, the total revenue attributable to tourists from non-eu countries only slightly doubled between 1995 and 2005, while the revenue attributable to tourists from china increased by 12 times. the commission is aware that price is an important competitive factor. the commission's vision of the future of european tourism, as set out in the recently adopted communication, is not based on low costs but rather on high quality. we are convinced that europe will remain the world's number one destination even with a strong euro, if europe makes the right use of its advantages: its historical heritage, its beautiful nature, its geographical concentration of attractive places and its reputation for high service levels.

the rapporteur. - madam president, i would like to thank, first of all, commissioner dimas for his comments, his reflections, and allow me, ladies and gentlemen, to begin - as it could not be otherwise - by thanking all those who have made this report possible, from the staff of the secretariat to all the colleagues who have taken part in the committee discussions and who have enriched this report by introducing amendments to improve it. to all of them, thank you very much. ladies and gentlemen, i am submitting this report in accordance with rule 192 of the rules of procedure of the committee on petitions for 2006. this report summarises the main elements of the committee on petitions' work during the past year. it is a question of the quality of the work, and i would like to stress that the commission is not only responsible for the quality of the work, but also for the quality of the work. the committee on petitions is the committee closest to the citizen of all the committees of our parliament. citizens can approach the committee individually or collectively and the committee itself tries to provide petitioners with the most appropriate solutions, ensuring that petitions are handled in a transparent and efficient manner and that citizens get understandable answers to the issues raised. as set out in articles 21 and 194 of the treaty on european union, the right to petition is an important element of european citizenship, since it enables any citizen of the european union, and any natural or legal person residing or having its registered office in a member state, to address the european parliament here, in relation to matters falling within the sphere of activities of the european union. i would therefore like to point out, and i am positive, that the statistics show, once again, a constant number of requests. for example, last year, 2005, there were 1 032, and 1 016 in 2006. approximately one third were not admitted to the proceedings and it should be noted that the petitioners' main concerns remain, fundamentally, environmental and the free movement of goods, persons and capital. petitions provide an important picture of the implementation of european legislation and its impact on citizens. through their petitions, european citizens point out the shortcomings and difficulties in the transposition and implementation process and are in an ideal position to monitor the implementation of community legislation at national level. the proportion of petitions not admissible also indicates a continuing need to increase public awareness and better inform european citizens about european union legislation and policies, as well as their legitimate right to petition the european parliament. and to achieve that objective, to achieve that objective, it is necessary to make a joint effort at the level of this european institution, but also at the national level, of the different national institutions of each country of the european union. i would also point out, in relation to the european commission, that the committee on petitions relies on the expertise of the european commission to investigate possible breaches of community law that petitions have brought to light. the recommendations of the european commission remain fundamental in defining the most appropriate response to the problems of the petitioners. however, the committee on petitions has continued to encourage, and we continue to encourage, the european commission to avoid non-personalised and sometimes quite general responses based on a strict interpretation of its powers and on information provided by the member states. the committee on petitions has continued to stress the need for petition assessments to focus more on the real problems of citizens and to ask the european commission to carry out independent investigations which will allow some issues to be raised in a more coherent way. i also wanted to make it clear that the committee on petitions, in its dialogue with the european commission, has not failed to stress the importance of petitions in achieving the common objective of bringing europe closer to its citizens. it should also be noted that the committee on petitions has had a constructive relationship, in dialogue with the european ombudsman, of mutual respect, one might say, of mutual respect for powers and prerogatives, and has submitted two reports.

the next item is the debate on the statements by the council and the commission on the situation in pakistan.
acting president of the council. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, as you know, the european union has been following with great concern the recent developments in pakistan, in particular those which led to the declaration of a state of emergency in that country on 3 december and, consequently, to widespread social unrest and a number of arrests, in particular the arrest of the 'chief of justice', who is currently under house arrest. there is no doubt that there has been a serious setback in the structure of the rule of law and the democratic process in pakistan which constitutes, i would say, a coup de grâce to the hopes of the pakistani people in the first place and of the international community in general in terms of strengthening the legitimacy of democratic institutions in pakistan. that is why the presidency issued a statement on behalf of the union on 6 november expressing our deep concern at the imposition of the state of emergency and the suspension of the pakistani constitution and fundamental freedoms. on 4 november, two days earlier, the heads of mission in islamabad, but also the high representative javier solana, had already expressed their concern at the course of events. our words, the words of the union, thus joined those of so many others, reiterating the importance of restoring the constitution and civil order, guaranteeing the independence of the judiciary, freedom of the media, the release of all political prisoners, journalists and human rights defenders, and demanding that the necessary conditions be created for the legislative elections to take place as planned, that is, in january 2008. we have no doubt that only in an environment of full democratic credibility can the stability and development of any nation be guaranteed. we are gravely concerned by reports of numerous arrests, the boycott of freedom of information, the repression of citizens' indispensable freedom of expression and attacks on professional classes such as judges and lawyers, journalists and human rights activists. however, at the same time, we cannot but make a strong appeal to everyone to exercise the utmost restraint and to join forces in the process of identifying a democratic and peaceful solution to the present crisis that will allow a rapid return to normalcy. while recognising the challenges pakistan currently faces in its security situation and the sacrifices and efforts made by the pakistani people in the fight against extremism and terrorism, the union firmly believes that the solution to these challenges cannot be achieved by disrupting the democratic process. we must not, however, fail to recognize the ally we have always been able to count on in the fight against extremism and terrorism. it is therefore important to keep it engaged in the fight against this global threat, in which international cooperation is an indispensable instrument. the union hopes that the current climate of uncertainty will be resolved quickly and peacefully and calls on president muscharraf to honour his commitment to remove his military uniform and to relinquish his post as army chief.
member of the commission. mr president, pakistan is on the agenda of this plenary for the third time within a few months. this bears witness to the very difficult transition the country is currently going through. the imposition of emergency law by president musharraf on 3 november in his capacity as chief of army staff has sent a deeply worrying signal to europe and the wider world and has damaged the course of democracy in pakistan. before the emergency was imposed we had witnessed some encouraging developments, with hope for a more inclusive political process and stronger democratic institutions, but regrettably this has now been put in question and today we ask ourselves whether this situation is still reversible or whether it is not too late to restore confidence and conditions in advance of the parliamentary elections. president musharraf, in his televised address on the night of 3 november, told us that he was suspending the constitution because of threats to the nation due to a visible ascendancy in the activities and incidence of terrorist attacks. there is no doubt that pakistan is currently facing a very serious threat of religious extremism and violence as recent events in the north-western frontier province and the attack on ms bhutto’s convoy on 18 october in karachi have clearly demonstrated. but what we are also witnessing now is the arrest of thousands of lawyers, journalists, political party workers and human rights activists, including such distinguished persons as ms asma jahangir, the chair of the human rights commission of pakistan, or mr aitzaz ahsan, president of the supreme court bar association. these are people who stand for an open and tolerant pakistan. they are not terrorists and it is wrong to detain them. they should be set free immediately. i would regard the drastic action taken against pakistan’s judiciary as particularly serious. rule of law is at the heart of any democratic process and the functioning democratic system cannot be sustained without an independent judiciary. the statement by the presidency, just mentioned also by our president on behalf of the eu, is therefore very clear, and this remains our position. last sunday president musharraf announced at a press conference that he hopes parliamentary elections can be held in pakistan by 9 january 2008. this would be a step in the right direction but there are a lot of remaining problems. when can we expect the state of emergency to end? how can we have free and fair elections when print and electronic media are censored, other civil rights and liberties suspended and the independence of the judiciary has been undermined? how will parties be able to campaign when freedom of assembly is curtailed and party leaders like benazir bhutto are kept under house arrest? these issues are not at all clear at this stage. to end this uncertainty it is of fundamental importance that a firm date for elections should be announced as soon as possible, along with a clear timeframe for ending the emergency. for these elections to have any chance of being at all democratic and transparent, it will be essential for all restrictions on political rights and fundamental freedoms to be lifted. and, as things stand, at present it seems it will not be possible to deploy an election observation mission. certain minimum conditions laid down in the commission communication on eu election assistance and observation for the holding of democratic elections are not met. however, if the emergency rule was lifted rather quickly and conditions were significantly improved soon, i might yet be able to review the situation. in any case i have made the necessary preparations for possible deployment of an eu election observation mission to pakistan should the conditions noticeably change for the better quickly. but, as i say, i am very much concerned as to whether this is likely to happen. there have been calls to suspend or review our aid to pakistan, and some eu member states have taken steps or are considering some action in this respect. the european commission’s support to pakistan focuses, i would like to remind you, on key issues such as poverty reduction and education, including in the north-west frontier province and baluchistan, which are the most disadvantaged provinces in pakistan. therefore, i think we will need to consider how best to proceed but, given the nature of this assistance, i think we have to reflect very carefully on that.

the rapporteur. - madam president, i have inherited the co-authorship of this report from our colleague mr beglitis, who is now in the greek parliament, and i did so with some concern, but i must now say that i am very pleased with the result achieved. firstly, because of the good synchronisation with mr tannock, the co-rapporteur, also because i have had the opportunity to work with a group of extremely competent assistants and officials, and finally because a high level of consensus has been reached in the preparation of this report. the majority of the amendments tabled were accepted with a unanimous vote and the result seems to me to have been satisfactory. the report supports the commission's december 2006 document on the evaluation and future development of the european neighbourhood policy and, in view of the consensus reached, it can now be said that parliament and the commission share the same vision, the idea that the european continent and the mediterranean are interdependent realities that cannot be viewed in isolation and that the neighbourhood policy offers new avenues of relationship and collaboration with societies facing common challenges and problems, but also great opportunities for shared progress. the text sets out some elements to give the european neighbourhood policy the greatest possible strength and ambition. i will list five very quickly: first, the principle of a broad policy design, but also in the framework of differentiation, a principle of differentiation, so that the european neighbourhood policy is not seen as a standardized and mechanical routine, but as the way for the european union to organise relations with its neighbours on the basis of the flexibility necessary to be able to respond successfully to disparate situations. secondly, the idea of a balance between the countries of the east and the countries of the south. we must not give priority to one perspective over the other, but always have a fully balanced approach. thirdly, to reinforce, with the neighbourhood policy, the design of the euro-mediterranean policy, which is what i have worked on most concretely in this report. it is not a question of overlapping policies, of creating a baroque and overly complicated framework, but of creating synergies in such a way that the european neighbourhood policy can mean a strengthening of the general design of the euro-mediterranean partnership or association policy. fourthly, the idea of moving from cooperation to integration in everything that is possible. in those sectors which are prepared to do so, the aim would be, in the years ahead, to share policy areas which can ensure the development of convergence and synergies in key sectors such as energy, transport networks, intercultural dialogue, the environment or education. and finally, the criterion of involving, not just the management of governments or parliamentary institutions, but, to the extent possible, the more active sectors of civil society involved as possible, the better. in this context, the european neighbourhood policy should also address the basic question of communication and visibility. i would say, the overall narrative of europe's policy towards its neighbours. i would like to point out, finally, that this is now facing a first challenge of visibility, of narrative, with the proposal launched by mr sarkozy for a mediterranean union. we heard the french president yesterday, and i think he made very positive points in saying that his proposal for a mediterranean union excludes no one, firstly, secondly, that it must be added to the acquis of euro-mediterranean policy and, thirdly, that it must try to go further. i could not agree more with this approach, which seeks to simplify the overall political and institutional framework of european neighbourhood policy and, in particular, of the mediterranean area.

i would like to thank mr tannock and mr obiols for their report and to inform them that my group is critical of the development and direction of the neighbourhood policy. critical because in 2004 we welcomed the possibility of establishing this neighbourhood policy based, fundamentally, on the promotion of human rights, specialised technical advice, a greater balance in the relationship between goods and people in the migration flow, but the truth is that, since the adoption of the financial instrument document, we seem to have given the impression that we were primarily interested in establishing free trade areas, free trade agreements and strict control over migration flows, leaving aside everything related to the promotion and demand for respect for human rights. there are two fundamental examples, to the west and to the south, and that is the conflict in the sahara, which mrs ferrero-waldner has mentioned, and the conflict in israel, or the responsibility, in other words, of morocco and the state of israel for two conflicts: the occupied territories of western sahara and in connection with the palestinian conflict. i think that, frankly, the neighbourhood policy would have to be much more demanding of these two states if they were to take responsibility once and for all for conflicts which have been going on for almost a century, and the other for forty or fifty years without a solution. we therefore believe that from this perspective we would have liked the european union to have taken a much more demanding position in establishing this neighbourhood policy.

mr president, it is very important that our neighbours form a circle of prosperous, stable, peaceful countries in which power is based on democratic formulas and on full respect for fundamental rights. this idea should be a cornerstone of the european neighbourhood policy, which should encourage and help our neighbours to carry out the reforms necessary to make the values i mentioned above effective. the question of political, economic and social reforms is, in my view, an essential aspect of the report we are going to adopt tomorrow. a second point: the neighbourhood policy must take policy. the neighbours on the southern shore of the mediterranean have felt a certain fear that enlargement to 27 could lead to a certain marginalisation by the enlarged union, and we can in no way acting president of the council. as the honourable member will be aware, in may 2007 the commission presented to the european parliament, the council and also the committee of the regions a communication on circular migration and mobility partnerships between the european union and third countries. in its communication, the commission considers that circular migration is a useful tool to be developed at community level for a more effective management of migration flows. in its june 2007 conclusions on the enlargement and strengthening of the comprehensive approach to migration, the council stressed that the possibilities of legal migration, including well-managed circular migration, can benefit all stakeholders. the council therefore considers that all possibilities for well-managed circular migration should be explored in close cooperation with all relevant stakeholders, with a view to adopting council conclusions by the end of 2007 at the latest. the need to examine these circular migration possibilities, on the basis of the commission communication of 16 may 2007, was also reiterated in the conclusions of the european council of june 2007. the issue of adopting specific instruments and measures to facilitate circular migration is currently being discussed in the council. the question of how measures to facilitate circular migration can be implemented is also being examined in the council. the commission has not yet proposed any specific measures.
