vice-president of the commission. madam president, the charter of fundamental rights will be a key instrument in our union based on the rule of law. it contains a real catalogue of rights that all citizens of the union should enjoy, from the individual rights related to dignity, freedoms, equality and solidarity to the rights linked to citizenship status and justice. the charter will not alter the union’s competences, but it will offer strengthened rights and greater freedom for citizens. the institutions, bodies, offices and agencies of the union will be bound by the rights written into the charter, and the same obligations will be incumbent upon the member states when they implement the union’s legislation. citizens will be able to claim before the courts the rights enshrined in the charter, and the legal scrutiny of the court of justice will ensure that the charter is applied correctly. the commission welcomes the fact that the legally binding force of the charter has been preserved through the negotiations in the intergovernmental conference. like parliament, we would have preferred to see the charter apply to all 27 member states, with no exceptions to its full justiciability, but we should not underestimate the results achieved. legal force is a major step forward in building a legitimate and accountable union, where citizens’ interests are the focus of attention. this was not obvious at the outset and it has been a long road to achieving this goal fully. the charter proclaimed in 2000 was not legally binding. during the european convention in 2002-2003 and in the igc that followed in 2003-2004, the charter was adapted in order to make it legally binding, but that process was stopped due to the failure to ratify the constitutional treaty. at the european council in june 2007, it was agreed that the future new treaty would contain a cross-reference to the charter, as adapted and finally approved in 2004, and that it would have the same legal value as the treaties, and this is now reflected in the new treaty. the rapporteur is proposing that parliament should approve the charter, which is a necessary step before its solemn proclamation, and, of course, the commission fully supports this recommendation. the commission will also approve the charter next week and authorise the president to proclaim it on 12 december, together with the presidents of parliament and the council. the proclamation of the revised charter will provide the basis for a cross-reference in the new treaty that will be signed the following day in lisbon, extending the legal value and justiciability to the rights enshrined in it. with the new treaty and the charter of fundamental rights, the union will undeniably enhance its protection of human rights. the european union is not only a marketplace but also a common space based on values and common rights.

the rapporteur. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, today, with globalisation, our economy, the progress of the community and the well-being of our citizens need more than ever to be supported by an effective, efficient, economical and, above all, sustainable transport system. all modes of transport are necessary. the railway had glorious times in its origins, but then it was cornered by vehicles that circulated on roads and highways, given its greater versatility, individuality and ability of proximity or proximity. now, with our roads at risk of collapse and our environment in critical condition due to pollution, we turn our eyes to the railway as the hope of the future to meet our needs for inland mobility. the commission, aware of this, has proposed a new legislative package to improve the technical part of the regulatory framework for rail transport, which revises the directives on interoperability, safety and the regulation on the european railway agency. the european institutions have been addressing the need to consolidate the railway sector at community level for years, with a global perspective. as far as interoperability is concerned, we all know that we adopted council directive 96/48/ec on high-speed railways in july 1996 and on the european conventional transport system in march 2001. however, after more than a decade, the interoperability levels of the european networks are still only 7%, and the requirement to have locomotives and traction equipment type-approved in each of the states in which they intend to operate is currently one of the most important obstacles to the creation of new railway undertakings engaged in passenger and freight transport, as well as a major obstacle to the interoperability of european railways. and since no state can decide on its own whether its authorizations for placing in service are valid in the territory of other states, a community initiative is needed to simplify and harmonize state procedures and to encourage a more systematic use of the principle of mutual recognition. the current directives only regulate the putting into service of new rolling stock. the new directive consolidates, recasts and merges the existing directives. for our part, on the basis of short technical reports which we have requested in accordance with parliament's rules, we have proposed to transfer the content of the old article 14 of the safety directive to our directive on interoperability, precisely in order to give more legal guarantees to the railway sector concerned and to simplify authorization for entry into service. we support the condition that there should be at least one authorization from one member state for each vehicle, which will be based on compliance with the ec declaration and the technical specifications for interoperability that affect them. member states shall consider infrastructure subsystems whose putting into service has been authorised in any other member state as already complying with the essential technical requirements and shall not require any further authorisation except where this may affect compatibility with the specificities or constraints of the infrastructure itself. in our report we wanted to structure the various aspects and sections of the directive in a way that was easier for the parties concerned to understand, by devoting a specific chapter to the requirements for the entry into service of vehicles, depending on whether they are first or second authorizations, or vehicles which comply with all or part of the tsis. in all the above areas and throughout the procedure, we have had regular contacts between the alternative rapporteurs from the various political groups, the commission and also the council presidency. finally, we were able to reach a common agreement, having overcome an important aspect, which was the maximum time limits for deciding on an authorization and the eradication of the well-known and paralyzing administrative silence due to lack of decision. after much effort, we have agreed that authorization will be automatic in the absence of a decision and we have also agreed on the rest of the article. we have therefore tabled a joint amendment, signed by all the groups in this parliament, containing the same text as that which will be tabled to the council of transport ministers. i hope that the agreement reached at first reading will be to the benefit of the whole sector. i would like to thank all the other rapporteurs for the help and cooperation which we have provided for this purpose.

president of the court of auditors. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i am pleased to be able to take part in your debate today on the court of auditors' annual reports for the financial year 2006. i have already presented the annual reports to the committee on budgetary control of the european parliament on 12 november this year and to the economic and financial affairs council a day later. let me begin by giving a brief overview of the key findings of the 2006 annual reports. i come to the reliability of the 2006 financial statements. the consolidated accounts for the financial year 2006 present, in all material respects, a true and fair view of the communities' financial position and results for the year, with the exception of an overestimation of the settlement obligations and pre-financing in the balance sheet. the commission has made further progress in implementing accurate accounting, although some weaknesses remain. the court noted that the commission had made considerable efforts to address the weaknesses in risk management for eu finances. some changes are already being felt positively, for example in the agricultural sector. i now come to the question of legality and order. the court again gives a full audit opinion on the underlying transactions of revenue, commitments, administrative expenditure and, with the exception of sapard expenditure, expenditure under the pre-accession strategy. in addition, the allowances managed directly by the commission delegations in the external policy areas had a low error rate in 2006. however, the court again gives a negative audit opinion on the legality and regularity of the majority of eu expenditure. this mainly concerns the part of agricultural expenditure not covered by the integrated administration and control system, structural measures, internal policies and a substantial part of external policies. in these areas, payments to final beneficiaries continued to show a significant error rate, albeit to varying degrees. the court's findings on the budgetary areas with shared management are as follows: in the agricultural sector, which accounted for €49.8 billion in 2006, the court found a significant overall decline in the estimated overall error rate, although it is still just above the materiality threshold. if properly applied, the invekos, which covers about 70% of agricultural expenditure, can effectively reduce the risk of irregular expenditure. financial corrections to agricultural payments, such as the annual conformity decisions taken by the commission in the context of the clearance of accounts procedure, involve large amounts of money which member states have to pay back to the community budget as corrections or fines for failing to put in place adequate systems. these recoveries for the community budget are still financed by national taxpayers and not by the beneficiaries who have improperly received community funds. in addition to highlighting problem areas by presenting illustrative cases, the court also considers it its task to highlight developments which may be of interest to policy makers. the court of justice has pointed out that, while the single payment scheme simplifies the application and payment procedures, it also has side effects, such as the allocation of entitlements to landowners who have never been engaged in agricultural activity before. although legally permissible, this results in a significant redistribution of eu aid from farmers to landowners. the new beneficiaries of agricultural aid include railway companies, equestrian clubs, horse breeding companies, golf and leisure clubs and local authorities. in addition, legislation on the single payment scheme left member states with a wide margin of discretion in allocating entitlements, which led to unequal treatment of beneficiaries. the situation with regard to structural measures amounting to eur 32.4 billion in 2006 remains unchanged from previous years. the court found a significant error rate, which it estimated to be at least 12% of the total amount of refunds to beneficiaries. the most common errors were that reimbursement of ineligible expenditure was requested and no calls for tender were made. moreover, there was no supporting documentation for the calculation of overheads or personnel costs. the court considers that the commission should set a good example in the spending it manages directly, i.e. internal and external policy areas. while some improvements are being made, for example, the internal policy areas managed by the commission, which accounted for eur 9 billion in 2006, are again showing a significant error rate. the main reason was the reimbursement of beneficiaries who had provided exaggerated information on the project costs. the errors in the underlying processes are attributable to, among other things, negligence, insufficient knowledge of the often complex rules and alleged fraud by applicants to the detriment of the eu budget. moreover, in the area of agricultural expenditure not covered by the invekos and in the area of structural and internal policy expenditure, the checks on payment applications, which are mainly based on information from beneficiaries, are in many cases inadequate in terms of number and coverage and often of poor quality. in recent years, the commission has taken measures to strengthen recovery and to improve the protection of the eu's financial interests. however, due to the complexity of the procedures, the commission is still not reliably informed about the amounts and beneficiaries of unduly paid funds and the financial impact on the eu budget. in fact, only six member states have complied with the commission's request to report on the recovery of irregular payments made in november last year. in its 'one audit' model, the court recommended the establishment of an efficient framework for all internal control systems for eu funds. all systems should be based on common principles and specifications, taking into account the inherent risks and ensuring a fair balance between the costs of control and the benefits. the most important recent innovation is the obligation for member states to provide annual summaries of their audit and control results. there were also voluntary initiatives by audit bodies in some member states to produce 'national declarations' and audit reports on the use of eu funds at national level. the court considers that the national declarations and the national audit work could have a positive impact on raising awareness within the member states of the importance of internal control of eu funds. in its opinion no 6/2007, the court stated that such procedures could increase the sense of responsibility at national level in relation to the management of eu funds. the commission also identified shortcomings and examples of good practice to be addressed and increased transparency and accountability in financial management. the court also continues to play an active role in promoting cooperation with the supreme audit authorities in the european union and has taken the lead in a new working group on eu-compatible common audit standards and comparable audit standards. i 'm coming to the conclusion: despite the commission's considerable efforts to address the risk management weaknesses in eu finances, the court again issues a negative audit opinion with regard to the legality and regularity of transactions in the majority of budgetary areas. improvements were mainly observed in the agricultural sector. the high error rate in the underlying transactions is partly due to the fact that beneficiaries sometimes claim excessive costs in their refund applications due to complex legal requirements and regulations and unclear criteria, but also to persistent internal control deficiencies. the basic prerequisite for effective budgetary management is the existence of reliable internal control systems at all administrative levels in all member states and beneficiary countries. i believe that european citizens have a right to see eu funds properly managed and controlled throughout the union.
vice-president of the commission. mr president, the commission welcomes the court’s report and the comments from president weber. overall, the court’s annual report for 2006 gives a more positive assessment than its 2005 edition. thanks to the court’s system of traffic lights, it is now possible to measure progress in detail. the court’s report sets out, from one spending area to another, where our systems are considered satisfactory and where the errors found are below the court’s materiality threshold of 2%. comparing this with previous years, the commission is pleased that in total the court has now given its green light to over 40% of total payments, compared to roughly a third last year and only 6% two years ago. that is real progress towards our common goal of getting a positive statement of assurance (das). the court also reports improvements in internal policies, such as research programmes, and external actions. the court said that our 2006 accounts are true and fair in all material respects, except for certain small overstatements, comprising 0.13% of operating expenditure. the court recognises that the commission has made considerable efforts to address the weaknesses in the management of the risks to eu funds. overall, though, there is, again, a negative das concerning the legality and regularity of transactions. while we are moving in the right direction, i would therefore like to focus on the major stumbling block on our road to a positive das. the big remaining challenge is to ensure that structural policies are properly implemented. for spending on structural policies – eur 32.4 billion in 2006 – the situation remains similar to previous years, and the court has again identified the material level of error. the most frequent errors were claims for ineligible expenditure and failure to carry out tender procedures, as well as a lack of evidence to support the calculation of the overheads or the staff costs involved. the court goes on to say that it is reasonably confident that at least 12% of structural and cohesion fund payments in 2006 should not have been reimbursed. we agree that there are real problems in this area. the commission’s own synthesis report for 2006 stated that it did not have confidence in the systems for managing structural funds in parts of italy, latvia, slovakia, slovenia, spain, sweden and the united kingdom. reserves were expressed by the directors-general in their annual activity reports. the court looked at a sample of 19 regions in 2006, and found none to be fully effective. the court found various control systems to be ineffective in england, france, germany, greece, italy, poland, portugal, scotland, slovenia and spain, and for the interreg project between austria and hungary. we believe things will improve under the new legislation, but this will not reduce the continuing high risk for payments made to the 2000-2006 programmes, where the situation remains critical up to their closure in 2009-2010. we need to act together on this state of affairs. i have written to the council president, the member states and the european parliament, setting out the additional efforts the commission will make. at the ecofin meeting earlier this month, i also called on member states to fulfil their responsibility to provide annual summaries of audit and declarations by 15 february 2008. that was the deal we reached with parliament and the council when adopting the revised financial regulation. the annual summary has to be more than just another reporting exercise without added value. it must provide real analytical information for the commission to use in giving assurance to the court and parliament about the state of controls in each member state. the 2006 discharge hearing that the committee on budgetary control has organised for 18 december 2007 for the main structural fund commissioners will be attended by representatives of the national budgetary control committees. the commission welcomes that innovation and hopes it will help mobilise commitment at national level to improve the management of eu funds. we need to follow a policy of warn, solve or suspend. the commission has stated its intention to suspend structural fund payments where the commission cannot obtain the necessary assurance that member state systems are working well. that may lead the commission to take a few unpopular decisions, but it has reached the conclusion that progress will be too slow if we do not display a sense of urgency. before concluding, let me say a few words about how the media covered this year’s report. over the last two weeks, the commission has been asked by journalists to comment on two main points. first, it has been asked to comment on the court’s findings that golf clubs and other bodies not formally associated with farming received eu subsidies last year. an otherwise serious newspaper ran the headline ‘eu aid for poor misspent on golf clubs’. it managed to get three facts wrong in only eight words. let me clarify. firstly, farm subsidies are not aid for the poor; secondly, the aid in question was not spent on golf clubs, but as subsidies for eligible agricultural activities – in these cases on adjoining land owned by different owners. it follows that, thirdly, the money was not misspent, but was in fact both legal and regular expenditure, which the court is not questioning. rather, the court has drawn attention to a policy issue and to the end result of an agreed policy: the introduction of the single-payment scheme. we welcome such discussions and, as honourable members will be aware, this commission has worked hard to achieve full transparency on the beneficiaries of eu funds, which it believes is leading to better-informed policy discussions, such as the common agricultural policy health checks launched by my colleague, marian fischer boel, earlier this month. the same approach lies behind the commission’s initiative of sending the supreme audit institutions in all member states a complete list of all the payments made to recipients in that member state. regrettably, in some media reports, this golf club issue has entirely overshadowed the court’s statement that agriculture is an area in which the commission and the member states have made most progress, and for which the court came very close to giving an overall green light. that is why i felt a need to clarify this today. the second issue is that 12% of structural funds, according to the court, should not have been reimbursed. most journalists have picked up on the court seeing this as a problem when almost eur 4 billion was paid out last year. this point also needs explaining. there is no clear picture as to whether the funds were lost or stolen, and whether the errors are systemic or one-off errors. it therefore falls to the commission to explain the 12%. in this speech i have given some explanations, and pointed to some of the problems we face and the action we intend to take. my colleagues, commissioners hübner and špidla, will elaborate further in their committee on budgetary control hearings next month. as a final remark, i wish to stress that, despite some of the media coverage, we believe the court report does in fact help us to focus on the real issues. the commission is working hard to ensure that improvements are made on these key points.

on behalf of the pse group. mr president, i think this is a good example of the proper functioning of the european institutions. despite the institutional complexity we have here, parliament, the commission and the council are working well and i hope that, after a satisfactory vote in this parliament's plenary, a resolution can be reached at first reading without further delay. i am grateful to commissioner frattini for his intervention in facilitating the solution and i congratulate the rapporteur on the great work he has done to achieve this agreement. as has been said repeatedly, the focus of the discussion we have had here has been on article 5, which concerns the protection of consumer rights. the consumer is not on an equal footing in matters of contract; normally, the consumer is at a disadvantage. i will simply give the example of a person who has to sign a contract for the rental of a car at an airport: the consumer has no possibility of reading the contents of the contract, he does not know to which law he is subject and, if there is no legal protection, he is absolutely in the hands of the person who proposes the contract to him. the aim of this proposal for a regulation is that, without renouncing the principle of the choice of law, there can always be a system of consumer protection, which is reflected today in the formula - which was offered to us, incidentally, by the council - that the choice cannot entail for the consumer the loss of the protection afforded to him by the inalienable provisions of a contract under the law which, in the absence of a choice, would have been applicable under paragraph 1. the great problem we have here in the european union is the lack of harmonisation of substantive law. these forms of conflict-of-law enforcement are only subsidiary forms, and we hope that the commission will continue its legislative work by proposing texts which will give us material protection for the consumer, uniform throughout the european union, which will not make us resort to these complicated forms of conflict of laws.

beginning of a new relationship between the european union and africa based on a strategic dialogue. nearly 80 heads of state and government, presidents of the european and pan-african parliament and civil society representatives sent strong messages to europeans, africans and the world. the concrete expression of the new framework for relations between the union and africa is to be found in the documents adopted at the summit, documents which i regard as of high quality: the joint strategy, the action plan and the lisbon declaration. these documents reflect the specific nature of europe's relationship with africa. this approach favours multilateral channels and seeks to integrate the various dimensions of the relationship. this approach is the difference the union can make, especially in comparison with other international actors. the treatment of africa as a partner in a strategic dialogue was also reflected in the method used to prepare both the summit and the documents which the summit itself adopted. the strategy, which for the first time was a genuine joint strategy, and the action plan were the result of intensive and thorough work with the african side, particularly the documents and in the preparation of the lisbon summit. the joint strategy identified four interlinked areas of common interest: peace and security, governance and human rights, trade and regional add because the president-in-office of the council has outlined the outcome of this summit in a remarkable way. i would also like to congratulate the portuguese presidency on having organized this summit - i think it was urgent - and, above all, on having succeeded. so, obviously, this summit was a summit with a strong message and a new message: the message of a radical change in the relationship between africa and europe. the lisbon summit marked the adoption - as has been said - of a new common vision, embedded in a joint strategy, that of a political partnership of equals, uncomplicated, liberated, pragmatic and mutually responsible. that said, the summit also adopted eight strategic plans to translate this new vision into action. the summit was marked by intense, rich and high-quality debates, which testify to the new and therefore fundamentally and genuinely political nature of our relationship. yes, we have spoken about zimbabwe, and many european leaders, including president barroso and chancellor merkel, have made it clear that mr mugabe's policy is unacceptable, that we do not tolerate human rights violations and that the policy in that country is undermining the will for reform that exists elsewhere on the african continent. many african leaders share these criticisms and it seems to me that the european union should fully support the african mediation efforts under the aegis of sadc and under the leadership of president mbeki. yes, we also spoke about darfur and the unacceptable humanitarian and security situation and we criticised the non-cooperation of the khartoum regime. we have, moreover, in a meeting in the form of a troika with the president of sudan, clearly stated our expectations and our demands that the president take the decision to allow the rapid deployment of the hybrid force so that the abuses we know about there will cease as soon as possible. it is worth noting that, in general, the subjects of democracy, governance and human rights are no longer taboo and that many african countries are embarking on the path of progress, as they say, not to meet the expectations of europeans, but to meet those of their own peoples. yes, we also talked about economic partnership agreements and, yes, there were agreements with several african leaders. president barroso and i have explained and re-explained the real issues of the epas. we also explained that the real challenge in the short term is to conclude interim agreements other than epas before 1 january, to ensure compatibility with wto rules and thus avoid putting non-ldcs at a disadvantage from 1 january 2008. i was given the example of côte d'ivoire, which would have lost some 750 million euros in trade in goods had it not signed this interim agreement. president barroso suggested that next year, discussions on epas continue at the highest level with each of the regions concerned, with the aim of comprehensive economic partnership agreements aimed at reasonable economic integration. of course, these are difficult subjects. we have discussed them without fear of disagreement. i think that will of course give quality and depth to our new partnership, but, ladies and gentlemen, from tomorrow we will be faced with an even greater challenge, that of translating this new political vision into concrete action. it is our political duty to present concrete results by 2010, when we meet for the third africa-europe summit. we have a collective obligation to deliver. the joint strategy and its first action plan set out the road map for our partnership and break it down into thematic objectives - as the president said - which are very concrete and operational. the two joint documents adopted at the summit were unanimously praised for their quality and ambition. this success is the result of a very long substantive and preparatory work which began in december 2005 with the commission's communication on a strategy for africa, which became, in 2007, a joint eu-africa strategy. the european commission will assume its full responsibilities during the implementation phase. but the commission is not the only one responsible for the success of implementation. the member states and our african partners must also get their act together. one of europe's first responsibilities in implementing this partnership will be to mobilise financial resources. i would remind you that the member states have committed themselves to providing an additional 20 billion euros per year by 2010. the latest results indicate that we are on the right track, but if we take into account the effect of debt cancellation in some countries, the current good result is still only relative. secondly, we need to distribute the work much better among the donors, which is an important element. that is why the code of good practice on the division of labour is a really fundamental element. thirdly, i would also like to recall that the member states committed themselves at gleneagles to finding one billion euros a year for aid for trade, half of which will have to go to africa. these are political and public commitments. i would like to recall this because these are elements which are likely to strengthen the feasibility and the implementation of these strategic plans. i have another thought: it is now clear that the commitment of the commission and the member states should not be the monopoly of the foreign ministers or the ministers for development. i would urge that we institutionalize the principle of joint, regular sectoral ministerial meetings on these matters. it is clear that sectoral ministers, for example in scientific research, trade, agriculture, finance can bring enormous potential in the new relationship with african countries. so, as i explained at the european and pan-african parliamentary conference in lisbon, we also rely heavily on the european parliament, on the african and european national parliaments to frame and convey the views and expectations of civil society. the central place of african and european democratic actors and civil societies at the heart of the strategic partnership and its implementation is also an innovation which i hope will allow the emergence of a genuine people-centred partnership. the formal inauguration was the address by the presidents of the european and pan-african parliaments to the heads of state and government. i would also like to assure you that i have heard the request made by your colleagues in the pan-african parliament to provide financial support to this institution while respecting its autonomy. we are of course prepared to discuss with the budgetary authority a more direct access to finance. i would like to reiterate my hope that we will one day be able to budget the european development fund, because it seems to me normal and right that you should be able to exercise the democratic control that is your right in the process of allocating official development aid. before the summit, i said that the main challenge of the summit would be to set the right tone for this political partnership between africa and europe and to send a strong signal for a relationship that is uncomplicated, both solidarity and pragmatic. i believe that this is exactly the signal that came out of the lisbon summit. as the portuguese prime minister, josé socrates, said, i feel that there will be a before and after lisbon in relations between the european union and africa.

member of the commission. the commission is following closely the recent developments in prices in member states. it considers that those increases cannot be easily explained by one single factor, but need to be seen in the broader context of rising world demand for oil and gas. however, increasing investment activity – and in particular the switch to more sustainable energy production – definitely plays a part too. moreover, the point of departure for market opening was, in several member states, very low prices. in the medium and long term, this failed to give the necessary signals for much-needed investment, and we are now paying the price. as to the question of whether such price increases can also be attributed to the exercise of market power, the commission has studied this issue and it came to the conclusion that electricity prices in certain member states were higher than one would expect in fully competitive markets. in this respect, the commission, the council and the competition authorities armed regulators to identify anti-competitive behaviour and to take the appropriate action. the commission is also itself investigating alleged anti-competitive behaviour by certain operators, and has launched five anti-trust proceedings in the course of this year. the commission is very much aware of the structural problems in the sector too. therefore, the third energy package makes wide-ranging proposals to remedy those structural problems, in particular by proposing ownership unbundling of the transmission system operators. the commission has always been of the opinion that consumers should be the main beneficiaries of liberalisation. the commission’s proposals for the third energy package therefore contain a number of measures which will strengthen the role and rights of consumers. in particular, the package proposes to give consumers the right to switch supplier at any time and to have free access to their consumption data. by increasing consumer awareness and rights with respect to their energy consumption, the commission is providing the tools for a functioning retail market.

the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of the consumer in respect of the placing on the market of consumer goods. madam president, as the rapporteur, mr lehne, has said, this is a subject which has occupied this parliament for 17 years. i have had the privilege of following it from the beginning, as rapporteur for the committee on legal affairs on the industrial designs directive. i was then the rapporteur on the subject in the committee on the internal market and i also followed it as a representative of the socialist group in the legal affairs committee. i should like to begin by congratulating mr lehne on his balanced position. i think you have made a magnificent statement of the difficulties of the subject. it is not an easy subject, it is not a simple subject; it has legal complications on the one hand and economic consequences on the other. i agree with him. i remember the long evening of discussion with the council in the conciliation committee on the final formula - we were then thinking of the possibility of some form of compulsory licensing, which was rejected - but i think that both the rapporteur and the speaker, like mr klinz, who has just spoken, are in favour of defending intellectual property rights. from a legal point of view, however, the problem with designs, industrial designs in general, is that the protection we have to give is for the product as a whole. what matters is the aesthetic value of the product as a whole, that is, the design; in the case that most often concerns us, the design of the car. the repair parts, that is to say those parts which, as a result of an accident or for any other reason, break or fall apart, have to be replaced and, as commissioner mccreevy has said, the normal form is a part which is equivalent to the part replaced. when someone repairs a part and replaces it with another like it, without damaging the whole design, he is evidently not committing any plagiarism, he is repairing an object to which he has to conform. it's the famous "must fit, must match" clause. i think the formula proposed by the rapporteur is a correct one, but the rapporteur has also been concerned about another issue: there is, in fact, the other aspect, which is the economic aspect. i mean, right now, there are a number of countries where the automotive industry needs this extra revenue that is generated through intellectual property protection. but, as the commissioner has pointed out, to achieve the internal market, it is necessary to unify the law throughout the european union, and the question is how we reconcile one thing with another. the only way to do that is through a transitional period, which is to say, we have to give the industry the possibility to prepare for a long period to take into account the compensation of the additional revenue, which would come from the intellectual property on those prepared pieces, something that now makes no sense because we start from the basis that the property refers to the whole of the design. the question is the period, as mr lehne has said. there are those who think that the period is a period of five years - two plus three we would say - and there are those who think that the period has to be longer, that it should be a period of eight years. tomorrow we shall see what the positions of the various political groups are, including the different national delegations and the different individual members. i have the impression that this is a subject that is not going to be discussed through party political lines but rather through national preferences, individual preferences or preferences for the protection of one sector or another. in any case, i think that the fact that we have been discussing a subject between the council and the commission for 17 years is not a bad thing, because in general there is a tendency to resort to the legislative instrument to solve occasional problems, and here the two co-legislators, the council and parliament, together with the commission, have been working for some time to find a solution which is balanced, which recognizes the right to protection of intellectual property, which recognizes the interests of car manufacturers, the interests of consumers and also - why not - the interests of small repair shops or even insurance mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i am grateful to the rapporteur, mr ehler, for his work on the occasion of the 10th anniversary of the transposition of the 1994 deposit guarantee scheme directive, the passage through a period of financial turbulence and the discussion of the improvement of the european financial services market. there is a great disparity in solutions between member states and important questions remain to be resolved. although most member states apply the ex ante fund system, there are still significant differences in the level of guarantees, the size of the funds and their provision. two examples: the amount guaranteed is almost eight times higher in the most protective state than in the least protective, and the guarantee fund of a single state represents almost 40% of the european total. this distorts competition. the ex-post system also casts a shadow over national and european financial stability in the event of a crisis. cross-border banking groups also have problems. the consolidation of funds from different schemes poses practical difficulties. the concentration of guarantees in a single scheme can only be done by multiplying regulations and agreements between states, which fragment the system and makes it more vulnerable to an undue accumulation of risks. there are substantial questions about the objectives of the scheme: harmonisation of cover levels, risk-based contributions, use of funds to provide liquidity, cost sharing, cross-border crisis management, winding-up of institutions and cooperation between authorities. deposit guarantee schemes should form a risk-based safety net that protects depositors, ensures efficient and fair competition, provides stability to financial markets and contributes to a fair burden-sharing in crisis situations. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a step in the right direction.
member of the commission. mr president, as we all know, traceability is a key element of ensuring high standards in animal health and food safety. we have had recent experience with certain diseases in the european union, such as foot-and-mouth disease and bluetongue, which has once again shown the importance of efficient identification systems. individual identification cannot function properly without electronic identification. the commission was requested to confirm or amend, in its report, the date of implementation of electronic identification, not to question the principles of the regulation. that is why it is a technical report on the various methods and technology involved. the commission report only focuses on the best way to implement electronic identification. however, in order to produce a report, we needed data and input from the member states, and in particular those member states already working on the system. the studies and trials necessary for the preparation of the report lasted much longer than was originally foreseen, which explains the delay in the report. we strongly appreciate and thank parliament for agreeing to handle this matter as urgent. that will prevent a situation of legal uncertainty in january 2008. the report concludes that technical conditions for electronic identification of sheep and goats have been fulfilled, but that member states need a reasonable time frame to prepare the implementation of electronic identification. we agree with, and accept, parliament’s position to have a fixed date for introduction of the system. on the other hand, we cannot accept the other amendments proposed, which would call into question the very principles of the regulation, since the question now is what the actual date of implementation should be. once again, i would like to thank the rapporteur for the speedy work he has done, and parliament for agreeing to treat this matter as urgent.

member of the commission. mr president, as members of this house know, back in 2005 the eu and china agreed a memorandum of understanding that included a two-and-a-half-year transition arrangement designed to give some extra breathing space to eu textile producers following the liberalisation of global trade in textiles and clothing. the arrangement capped growth each year for 10 particularly sensitive textile and clothing products. these caps expire on 31 december 2007, although the memorandum itself remains valid until the end of 2008, and it commits industry and government on both sides to work for a stable transition to free trade in textiles. it was always my intention to hold china to that responsibility. the commission negotiated with china a double-checking surveillance system for 2008 that will cover eight textile-product categories with particular sensitivities. what this means is that china will issue an export licence for all exports and, in parallel, the eu licensing offices in the member states will issue an import licence. it is a familiar system, and manufacturers, importers and retailers have all welcomed it. its value lies in allowing us to monitor textile import patterns and, because imports have to be licensed before they leave the dock in china, it allows us to see likely developments in advance. i am the first to acknowledge the fact that the textile and clothing industry is going through a long period of structural change. this started long before the dismantling of quotas. successful european companies are not taking the mass producers head on but are investing in technology and in quality. we remain – it is always worth saying it – the second biggest textile exporter in the world. we have more fashion and quality brands than the rest of the world put together. it is a sign of the european textile producers’ confidence and resilience that they have not called for quotas to be further extended. they have argued that their competitiveness depends more now on effective action on counterfeiting and market access in china. it goes without saying that i intend to throw the entire weight of our trade policy behind these two problems. on market access, we will be seeking new access for textile goods in the doha round and in all our new ftas. we have also set up a specific working group for textiles as part of the renewed market access strategy. europe is well poised to exploit huge new markets for consumer goods in the emerging economies and we will not simply be sitting back and hoping that these trends go our way. counterfeiting is, if anything, an even greater problem. protecting trademarks and design rights is absolutely central to the textile industry and i raise these issues with the chinese in every single meeting i have with them. we have done some useful collaborative work with the chinese customs service and trade fair organisers, and the chinese patent office. but, on balance, china remains a huge problem for intellectual property rights holders. the counterfeit markets are cleared out one day and the traders creep back in the next. as i have said in the past, we have not ruled out the prospect of using the wto if the situation does not improve. ms toia mentioned the ‘made in’ proposal to assist textiles: i made this proposal, i presented it to the commission, it was agreed by the commission but it has not been agreed, i am afraid, by the majority of member states. in view of this, i cannot press the proposal further or do more than i have done. last month, at the eu-china summit in beijing, i was very careful to pass on some frank messages, and they apply in the textile sector as much as anywhere. the eu-china trade relationship has been transformed in the last two decades. both sides have benefited from it immensely but it has become badly imbalanced. while china dominates our import markets, our businesses are losing out in china because of counterfeiting and market-access barriers amounting to eur 55 million a day in lost business opportunities. our spiralling trade deficit reflects both these things. this is not because of a lack of competitiveness by european producers. we have a surplus in goods trade with the rest of the world and, where we are allowed to compete freely, we are a match for anyone. this is not the case in china. instead of a level playing field, it is seriously tilted against us. we face trade and investment restrictions, rampant counterfeiting and regulatory barriers in virtually every sector. china’s wto obligations six years after it became a member are still too often unmet. i see the textiles problems as emblematic of the broader problems we face in china. we are china’s largest client for clothing and textiles. we have respected china’s comparative advantage in labour and production costs. we are focusing on our own comparative advantages. we are moving up the value chain in what we produce. we expect the same sort of equal opportunity and fair treatment in china’s market that chinese producers receive in ours. at the recent summit, the premier of china, wen jiabao, appeared to hear and understand our strong concern and offered to create a high-level strategic mechanism with the eu to focus on rebalancing our trade deficit with china. i welcome this, with one obvious caveat: it is not one more dialogue or one more roadmap we need, it is action – on the ground, in the markets, in the courts, where it matters to european exporters. and action not just by the ministry of commerce but across the board by the regulating agencies and ministries which restrict market access and law enforcement in all parts of china’s economy. the openness of europe’s own markets to china will not be politically sustainable if this action does not occur. i talk of textiles and clothing products, but also all sectors where europe has export interests. the practical delivery of real change by the new high-level trade deficit mechanism, which i and my trade counterpart are charged with designing and launching, will be the definitive test of china’s sincerity. i hope their sincerity matches our own in wishing to resolve the issues before us without resorting to avoidable confrontation.

the author. madam president, i have to say that as the promoter of this resolution, i am particularly pleased that we have finally found the space and the consensus to put it forward, because i sincerely believe that the subject deserved this and much more. we're talking about almost 200,000 women, euphemistically known as "comfort women", who were forced into sexual slavery before and during world war ii by the imperial japanese army. after 62 years, the survivors are still waiting for justice. they have suffered through life from poor physical and mental health, isolation and shame, and often extreme poverty. to date, the government of japan has failed to comply with international standards on reparations comprising restitution, compensation, rehabilitation and satisfaction, including full disclosure, apology and guarantee of non-recurrence. this is especially significant considering that japan is one of the major donors of aid in post-war contexts. it was therefore urgent to react and remember - as survivors do - that truth must be linked to justice, and that an apology is empty if it is not accompanied by an assumption of responsibility. it is not just - i want to stress this - an individual victim's right, but a collective right, which implies a responsibility to remember so that this type of violation does not happen again. this leads us to call on the japanese authorities to exercise historical honesty and not only to acknowledge the facts but also to apologise on behalf of their ancestors and to compensate the victims. finally, i would like to express my deepest respect and appreciation for the women who had and have the courage to speak out and demand justice, and for the organisations that, like amnesty international, are accompanying them on this journey.
